## FI13. Amendment — the corpus-marked run, and the one test that fails

`pytest -m corpus` on the final tree:

```
$ python -m pytest -m corpus -q
FAILED tests/test_parser_parity.py::test_detect_sweep_stays_affordable_for_the_discovery_run
1 failed, 13 passed, 3035 deselected, 1 warning in 2809.79s (0:46:49)
EXIT=1
```

`corpus_gate.py` itself — the substantive gate, and the 13 tests that passed —
is GREEN (FI10). The single failure is a WALL-CLOCK THRESHOLD:

```python
worst = 0.0
for markdown in sources.values():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    for registration in registrations:
        registration.detect(markdown)
    worst = max(worst, time.perf_counter() - start)
assert worst < 0.25
```

It is not caused by this cell, and this cell makes it cheaper. Measured
paired and interleaved in ONE process — both marker sets timed alternately,
trial by trial, so load drift hits both arms equally:

```
documents 103, registrations 53, 7 paired trials
  trial 1:  NEW   214.3 ms   OLD   238.4 ms   delta   -24.1 ms
  trial 2:  NEW   201.1 ms   OLD   212.8 ms   delta   -11.7 ms
  trial 3:  NEW   253.1 ms   OLD   185.8 ms   delta   +67.3 ms
  trial 4:  NEW   170.0 ms   OLD   220.9 ms   delta   -50.9 ms
  trial 5:  NEW   186.6 ms   OLD   217.5 ms   delta   -30.8 ms
  trial 6:  NEW   228.1 ms   OLD   228.4 ms   delta    -0.3 ms
  trial 7:  NEW   203.8 ms   OLD   203.4 ms   delta    +0.4 ms

NEW (this branch)   min 170.0  median 203.8  max 253.1
OLD (base d70efbe)  min 185.8  median 217.5  max 238.4
paired delta (NEW - OLD): median -11.7 ms
```

The reason is in the marker itself. The marker this cell removed called
`t.upper()`, which allocates a full uppercase copy of every document before
testing it:

```
worst per-document marker cost
  first_citizens OLD (t.upper() copy)     0.157 ms
  first_citizens NEW (substring only)     0.060 ms
  citizens OLD                            1.166 ms
  citizens NEW                            1.176 ms
```

(`citizens` is unchanged in cost: its `t.lower()` call — the expensive one at
~1.1 ms — is in the domain marker, which this cell did not touch.)

**The real finding is the margin.** 53 registrations sweep the worst document
in ~200 ms against a 250 ms budget, and the per-trial spread on this machine
exceeds 80 ms; five consecutive trials during heavy parallel-cell load
measured 280.6 / 496.5 / 376.6 / 280.6 / 314.8 ms. The assertion therefore
reports machine load, not registry cost, and it will fail intermittently for
any cell — the corpus-marked run that produced it took 2809 s against the
761 s recorded earlier in this log, i.e. the box was ~4x loaded.

Two things follow, both for Ocean rather than for this cell, since
`tests/test_parser_parity.py` is not this cell's file:

1. The threshold needs either headroom or a load-independent measure (CPU time
   rather than wall clock, or a per-registration cost budget). Retuning
   another cell's assertion mid-wave is not this cell's call.
2. **The budget is genuinely close.** Every cell in this wave adds
   registrations, and the sweep is per-document overhead on 3,506 discovery
   documents. `citizens`'s `t.lower()` alone is ~1.1 ms of the ~200 ms; a
   sweep-wide pass replacing whole-document `.lower()`/`.upper()` marker calls
   with case-sensitive substring tests, or normalising the text ONCE in
   `admissible_text` and handing the normalised copy to every marker, would
   likely halve the sweep. That is RFC risk 7 coming due.

## FI14. Corrections from adversarial review

Verdict was SHIP conditional on record corrections. Four claims in FI0–FI13
were wrong or overstated; each is corrected here and at its original site.
Nothing in `analysis/` changed except the module docstring that carried the
overclaim, and one test comment.

### FI14.1 — "field movers: 3" is true of the Statement, false of the document

FI10 reported three movers because it diffed `Statement` fields. At document
level the flattened descriptions move **six production metrics** on the pinned
statement, all classification-driven, none audited by either oracle — which is
why the gate stayed GREEN and why they must be named here instead:

```
  nsf_count                 1      -> 0
  effective_nsf_count       1      -> 0
  insurance_count           1      -> 0
  insurance_total           494.00 -> 0.00
  pos_count                 18     -> 0
  ach_debit_count           5      -> 0
```

Consumed at `analysis/metrics.py:208-251` via `analysis/detect.py`
classification, surfaced at `webapp/app.py:503/549/563`. Every one is keyed on
merchant text: the classifier is handed `Other Debit` where it used to be
handed `Overdraft Charge`, `Auto-Owners Ins. Prem`, `POS Sig ... Visa #8269`.

Measured across the family (all 35 parsed documents, not sampled), the same
collapse is total wherever a metric depends on description text:

```
  zero on 35/35 : nsf_count, effective_nsf_count, insurance_count,
                  insurance_total, pos_count, pos_credit_count,
                  ach_debit_count, ach_credit_count, atm_withdrawal_count,
                  loan_count, verified_revenue_count, verified_revenue_total
  survives      : check_count      non-zero on 27/35
                  unverified_deposit_count non-zero on 35/35
```

The two survivors are exactly the two that do not need merchant text: cheques
keep their printed serial, and deposits are counted whatever they are called.
`verified_revenue_*` at zero across the family is the sharpest edge of this —
revenue verification is not possible for this bank until descriptions come
back.

**Recovery path, and it is the same card as FI6:** a `+first-citizens-layout`
extractor in `ocr/native_text.py`. `pdfplumber` already reads these rows as
`03-02 POS Sig 02/27 Visa #8269 Cucina 100 864-6019606 SC 92.61`. Restoring
per-posting descriptions restores all six metrics on the pinned document and
unlocks the twelve across the family. It moves pinned ADB evidence, so it is
Gustavo's ceremony, not a cell's.

### FI14.2 — reconciliation is NOT independent for this bank

FI0/FI6 and the object-level test claimed the rebuild made
`analysis.reconcile` an independent test of the detail. That is wrong, and the
reviewer's proof is simple: `_matches` already requires each section's parsed
total to equal the printed total, and the printed summary closes on its own
arithmetic, so for any statement the parser ACCEPTS,

```
sum(postings) = printed credits - printed debits - charge
beginning + printed credits - printed debits - charge = ending   (summary closes)
=> beginning + sum(postings) = ending                             (forced)
```

Reconciliation restates the gate one layer down. The single path that can
still fail it is a billed service charge whose itemisation cannot be located,
where `_service_charge_posting` omits the row rather than date it by guesswork
(0 of 35 today).

What the rebuild actually bought, stated without inflation:

- the gate moved from **four constants memorized off one statement** to **the
  control record each document prints**, so a misread section is rejected
  rather than silently reconciled, and the check travels to all 39 documents
  instead of one;
- the balances are **read, not derived** — the old parser's
  `beginning = ending - credits + debits` made the walk true for any input
  whatsoever, including a parse that had recovered nothing.

The object-level test is kept but renamed
`test_first_citizens_balances_are_not_derived_from_the_postings` and
re-documented: it pins NON-DERIVATION, and says explicitly that it does not
demonstrate independence.

### FI14.3 — count_semantics: MAPPING, not COMPARABLE

FI10 recommended a COMPARABLE entry on the strength of `19 + 97 = 116` on the
pinned document. That document bills no service charge, and generalising from
it is exactly the error this cell was sent to fix elsewhere. Measured over all
35:

```
  counts agree exactly : 26   (all with a zero service charge)
  counts off by +1     :  9   (all with a billed service charge)
```

Every one of the nine is off by exactly one in the same direction: the printed
per-direction counts exclude the service-charge row, which this parser emits
as a posting. A COMPARABLE entry would therefore manufacture a flag on 9 of 35
— 26% of the family — which is the precise failure mode
`count_semantics`'s docstring warns about.

Corrected recommendation: **a capital_one-class MAPPING entry** — printed
counts denote the four posting sections and exclude the billed service-charge
row. COUNTS-P3 material, with the 35-document evidence above. The table stays
untouched and the counts stay inert (`UNSURVEYED`, `comparable=False`).

### FI14.4 — the calendar baseline misdescribed itself

FI8 and FI11 said `first_community.py` carries "a memorized page number and a
memorized posting date". Measured with the shipped `CALENDAR_RE`:

```
  HIT 1  line 28  '70'  in  'BUSINESS PLUS CKG-(\d+-70)\s+...'
  HIT 2  line 37  '10'  in  '...(?=\s+10/31 Ending Balance\s+\$?\d|...'
```

Only HIT 2 is a calendar literal. HIT 1's `70` is a **product-code suffix** —
a false positive of a rule that claims to find pinned calendar fields. And the
`--- Page 12 ---` marker sitting in that same string is **invisible** to the
scan: the `12` is followed by a space, not a regex date separator. The rule
finds pinned calendar FIELDS inside patterns, not every memorized number.
`CALENDAR_BASELINE`'s comment now records this, including the false positive,
because a ratchet that misdescribes what it excuses is worse than none.

### FI14.5 — carried, measured, not fixed

**D2 — the service-charge date contradicts the bank's own printed daily
chain.** The Daily Balance Summary is an in-document cross-check this parser
does not consult. Re-read with the parser's own section bounds (the audit's
`first_citizens_daily` needs an `^An updated` terminator that 5 of the 9
statements do not print, so a first pass was blind to them):

```
  statements billing a service charge : 9
  printed chain readable              : 9
  chain contradicts the charge date   : 4
  ADB impact                          : 0.15 to 0.73

  70e2b596__02_28_2026   charge dated 02-28, chain implies 02-27   0.41
  70e2b596__05_31_2026   charge dated 05-31, chain implies 05-29   0.52
  3df19105_Feb2026_0501  charge dated 02-28, chain implies 02-27   0.73
  3df19105_May2026_0501  charge dated 05-31, chain implies 05-29   0.15
```

In all four, moving the charge to the day the chain implies resolves EVERY
divergence (0 remaining). So the printed chain is a usable oracle for the
posting date, and consulting it would both fix these four and give the family
a genuine second check — the one thing FI14.2 says the parse currently lacks.
Card it.

**D5 — the ending-balance sign line is dropped.** `_summary` classifies block
cells by token shape; a lone `+`/`-` on its own line matches none of
`_BARE_MONEY_RE`, `_SIGNED_MONEY_RE` or `_DAY_COUNT_RE` and falls through. The
BEGINNING sign survives because it is the control row's leading token, but a
statement closing overdrawn has its ending sign only on that dropped line, so
the ending is read positive. Confirmed by construction: such a statement fails
the summary identity and is DECLINED, not misread. Fail-closed today and
unreached in this population — but an overdrawn month-end is an ordinary
event, so the class is reachable. Card it.

**Wall-clock affordability test (FI13) — direction right, magnitude wrong.**
FI13 reported a paired median of −11.7 ms in this branch's favour over 7
trials. The reviewer's paired run puts it at **−2.1 ms**, and further finds the
BASE arm breaches the 250 ms threshold more often than this branch's. Both
agree on the sign and on the conclusion — this cell makes the sweep cheaper,
by removing a whole-document `t.upper()` — but −11.7 ms was noise-dominated at
7 trials and −2.1 ms supersedes it. The substantive finding is unchanged and
is the margin, not the delta: ~200 ms against a 250 ms budget with per-trial
spread over 80 ms, so the assertion reports machine load. Reviewer's numbers
stand as the record.

## DB12. Amendments from adversarial review

Ocean's verdict was SHIP with five closures, all reviewer-evidenced, all in
these two files. Each is closed below with the fixture the review asked for.
Containment after the closures is unchanged: **improved 28, regressed 0** over
the 96-document family, **0 outcome movers** introduced by the closures
themselves, and archive-wide **0 documents changed outside the two folders**.

**C1 — the printed sign is read, not flattened** (`capital_one.py`).
`abs(_money(fees))` mapped `($15.00)` and `$15.00` onto the same published
15.00. That mattered *because of my own widening*: before `_SUMMARY_CELL` an
unbracketed non-zero cell did not parse at all, so the collision was newly
reachable and I introduced it. The signed value is now read, and the
cycle-charge guard tests SIGN rather than magnitude.

**C2 — one stated rule for every summary cell** (`capital_one.py`).
`stated_total_credits` was the single summary cell read without `abs()`, so a
bracketed `Deposits/Credits` would have published −500.0 with no summary
identity check downstream to catch it. The rule is now written down at the top
of the reader and applied identically to all of them: **balances are published
SIGNED** (an overdrawn account really does print `($59.78)`), **totals are
published as the POSITIVE MAGNITUDE the schema specifies**, and the printed
sign is still read and used to CHECK that each cell points the way its column
requires. A cell contradicting its column is refused rather than normalised —
no such document exists in the archive, so publishing a guess about one would
be inventing a reading.

**C3 — matching an amount is not identifying a fee** (`capital_one.py`).
The arithmetic arm re-dated ANY debit equal to the printed charge inside the
window, and relabelled it with a `(printed …)` annotation: the reviewer's
$12.00 STARBUCKS purchase against a printed `($12.00)` charge was silently
moved onto the cycle end and presented as a service charge. My negative
fixture used a different amount, so it covered the amount axis and nothing on
this one. The arm now additionally requires the row to be **worded like a fee**
(`_FEE_SHAPED_RE` — the bank's own fee lexicon, which is what admits
`Cash deposit limit exceeded` and rejects a merchant name). The reviewer's
exact same-amount fixture is pinned, plus a parametrised set of ordinary rows
that must never be adopted however well the amount agrees.

Latent, not live: no document in the archive had a non-fee debit matching its
printed charge inside the window — the only five rows in that window across the
whole family are genuine fees, so nothing published was ever wrong on this
axis. The fixture exists so it stays that way.

**C4 — a product line is product-SHAPED, not merely product-POSITIONED**
(`us_bank.py`). The anchor published whatever line sat above the header block;
with the product line replaced by prose it published a marketing sentence.
The anchored line is now validated structurally — U.S. Bank sets its product
register in capitals, so a line carrying lower-case words is prose — and an
unshaped line publishes `None`. Refusing the NAME never refuses the statement:
a pinned test asserts the money is published exactly as before.

**C5 — the hardcoded `account_name`, the R-1 class still standing in the other
file** (`capital_one.py`). The parser published
`account_name="Business Basic Checking"` on every document. Measured over the
22 documents it validates: the phrase appears in **0 of 22** — only 4 contain
the word "checking" at all, and in every one of those it is inside a
transaction description (a counterparty named `Delve Checkings`). Its one
occurrence anywhere in the family is in a FILENAME, which `analyze_markdown`
strips at the admissibility boundary before any parser sees the text, so it was
never evidence. This is a worse instance than the us_bank one, which at least
named a product 4 documents really printed.

The literal is gone, along with the account-number regex that was keyed to the
same phrase (it matched nothing, so `account_number` was None on all 22 and
still is). A structural `_ACCOUNT_LINE_RE` reads a printed
`<Product Name> <account digits>` line where a layout prints one; the native
layout prints none, so all 22 publish `account_name=None` — the honest reading.

**Movers introduced by the closures: 22, all `account_name`, nothing else.**
`Business Basic Checking` → `None` on 12 previously-validated and 10

# §MONEY-GRAMMAR — the shared money grammar: a sign class, two bounds, and a marker

MONEY-GRAMMAR, 2026-08-14. Branch `wave3-money-grammar`, base `d70efbe`
(current main). Brief: `docs/agent-handoffs/MONEY-GRAMMAR.md`. Single
integration owner for `analysis/money.py`, which ~20 parsers import — so
every card here lands behind one archive-wide byte-identity proof.

## MG0. Summary

Four defects in the shared grammar, each characterized on the base tree
before a line was written, each fixed at the grammar rather than in a
parser, and all four landed behind a single sweep over **3,367 documents**
(the entire claimed population of 2,100 — validated 2,030 / review 10 /
withheld 60 — plus all 1,267 `failed`; the 13 documents not covered are
`deferred` intake rejects with no cached OCR document, none of them
claimed).

**Result: 3,364 / 3,367 byte-identical. Exactly 3 movers, all
`chase_export`, all named — the three the brief predicted. Zero unexpected
movement anywhere in the archive.**

| Card | Defect | Direction of the fix |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | No grammar knew U+2212 MINUS or U+2013 EN DASH | the sign is a CLASS, normalized once |
| 2 | `parse_money("34.9")` returned `34.0` | a money token is two-or-three decimals, unadjacent (MG3) |
| 3 | 26+ integer digits crashed `adb.py` | bound token acceptance at the grammar |
| 4 | The debit-marker rule was "contains a D" | match the marker token, exactly |

## MG1. The instrument, proven against the run of record

The sweep runs `analyze_markdown(md, parse_mode="deterministic")` plus
`telemetry.classify_outcome` over cached OCR markdown rebuilt from the D-3
artifacts by DIRECT file path — each artifact JSON carries its own
`input_sha256`, so the index is rebuilt from the files themselves and the
sqlite index is never opened. The analysis cache is never consulted.

Before trusting it, the instrument was checked against the baseline run of
record `2026-08-14T060822.665646-0000-88be9dd3`:

```
total docs 3367
recomputed outcomes [('validated', 2030), ('failed', 1267), ('withheld', 60), ('review', 10)]
DISAGREEMENTS with baseline run 88be9dd3: 0
```

Zero disagreements over 3,367 documents. Every number below is measured on
that instrument.

## MG2. Card 1 — the minus is a class, not a character

`U+2212 MINUS SIGN` is what the Chase-for-Business web export prints;
`U+2013 EN DASH` is what OCR and some producers' font maps put in its
place. Measured on the base tree, the two failure modes are not the same:

* every one of the 13 `AmountFormat`s returned `None` — the field is
  silently dropped;
* `parse_money` and `parse_digit_scrubbed` returned **+500.0** for
  `−500.00` — they matched the digits AFTER the glyph. **A printed debit
  booked as a credit.**

The archive prints it: 47 documents carry a non-ASCII minus welded to a
money token. 44 are unclaimed `failed` (Mercury/fintech — FINTECH-CELL
territory, and that scout's "direction must come from the printed sign"
trap runs through this same grammar). Exactly **3 are claimed, and all 3
are the `withheld` chase_export documents** the brief named.

The fix is one primitive, `normalize_sign_glyphs`, applied at the entry of
every parser in the module, so each `AmountFormat` and each tolerant parser
inherits the class instead of re-enumerating it. It runs BEFORE
`parse_digit_scrubbed`'s guard, which is why no per-bank guard pattern
changed: chase's `_AMOUNT_RE` still spells its sign in ASCII and now admits
the printed glyph. `MINUS_CLASS` is exported for consumers that find money
with a pattern of their own.

One consumer change, in `analysis/chase.py` — the export row finder was
`-?\$\d[\d,]*\.\d{2}`, so on a `−$1,234.56` row it matched from the `$`
onwards and dropped the sign the bank had plainly printed.

End-to-end on a synthetic export, base vs branch:

```
### ON MAIN (base d70efbe) ###
control (ASCII -): amount=    -5.0  direction=debit   recon_ok=True
repro   (U+2212): amount=     5.0  direction=credit  recon_ok=False
REPRODUCED

### ON BRANCH wave3-money-grammar ###
control (ASCII -): amount=    -5.0  direction=debit   recon_ok=True
repro   (U+2212): amount=    -5.0  direction=debit   recon_ok=True
FIXED
```

`analysis/regions.py:25` already hand-rolled `replace("–", "-")` locally —
independent corroboration that the en dash is real, and a candidate to
inherit the shared class instead of keeping its private copy.

## MG3. Card 2 — the money-token shape (amended after review)

`parse_money("34.9")` returned `34.0`: the decimal group is optional, so
the integer part matched alone. `parse_money_tokens("34.9")` was worse —
`[34.0, 9.0]`, two amounts out of one. A plausible wrong number is the
worst failure this module can have.

**THE RULE AS IMPLEMENTED.** The card's one-line name ("one decimal place
is not money") is shorter than the code, and the review was right to make
this precise, because the short form implies a fail-closed `None` that the
implementation does not promise:

> A money token carries either no decimal point at all or **exactly two or
> three** decimals, and is adjacent to **neither a digit nor a dot** on
> either side.

Three consequences, all pinned by fixtures:

1. **These parsers SEARCH, so a refusal is not a `None`.** The search
   resumes and returns the next qualifying token:
   `parse_money("34.9 100.00")` is **`100.0`**, not `None`. `None` comes
   back only when nothing in the whole input qualifies (`"34.9"` alone,
   `"12.5 34.9"`). For a caller handing over a single cell the two are the
   same; for a caller handing over a line they are not.
2. **The refusal class is wider than one decimal.** Dot-adjacent tokens go
   too (`1.2.3`, `12.345.67`), and so does anything with four or more
   decimals — including `0.000668276`, the foreign-exchange factor chase's
   own local grammar already had to defend against.
3. **`parse_digit_scrubbed` never got this rule.** It keeps digits and dots
   and calls `float`, so it still reads `34.9` as **`34.9`** — the true
   value, not a truncation. It was never the defect; its callers bound it
   with `guard`. The asymmetry is deliberate and is now pinned so it cannot
   be "tidied up" by someone assuming the module is uniform.

Mechanically: a money token may not begin part-way through a number
(`(?<![\d.])`) and what follows may not continue it (`(?![.,]?\d)`). Both
are load-bearing — without the leading boundary the trailing one is
defeated, because `34.9` refuses `34` and then matches `9`. The comma is in
the trailing class because the token parser groups with it, so `1,234.5`
cannot fall back to matching `1`.

Refusing exposed a second defect in the same grammar. `.56` — a surveyed
axis the module docstring claims to tolerate — was never actually read:
the search skipped the dot and matched `56`, returning **a hundred times**
the printed amount. The tolerance is now real (`.56` reads 0.56), which is
also what keeps `farmers_merchants` reading its printed `.00` interest.
That caller was found by the full suite rather than by inspection, and it
is the reason the card ships with padding rather than bare refusal.

193 archive documents contain a one-decimal token (103 of them validated),
scotia dominating — and scotia pads at its own call site
(`analysis/scotia.py::_amount_value`), which is why the sweep shows it
unmoved. `bofa._money` anchors with a fullmatch guard, so its 62-hit
documents never passed those tokens through either.

## MG4. Card 3 — the bound belongs at the grammar, never in adb.py

Measured boundary on the base tree: 25 integer digits quantize, **26 raise
`decimal.InvalidOperation`** out of `analysis/adb.py`, which quantizes
every amount to cents in the default 28-digit Decimal context. The
document then dies with a CRASH rather than an honest decline.

`MAX_INTEGER_DIGITS = 13` is measured, not chosen: over the 3,367-document
archive the largest integer part of any well-formed amount is **11
digits**, while **2,143 documents carry bare runs of 14 digits or more**
(longest 54) — barcodes and reference numbers, exactly the F-STRUCTURE
hypothesis. The bound sits above every amount anyone has printed and far
below the crash.

Pattern parsers fail closed to `None`; the raising family raises
`ValueError`, their documented contract for "not money". `adb.py` is
PROTECTED and carries a zero-line diff. The crash boundary itself is pinned
as a regression test, so the two numbers cannot drift into each other
unnoticed.

## MG5. Card 4 — the marker is a token, and measuring it prevented a regression

The rule was "the suffix CONTAINS a D", which is not a rule about markers
at all: `100.00CREDIT` read as **-100.00** because "CREDIT" has a D in it,
and `USD`, `CAD`, `DEBIT` and `DC` all inverted their amounts too.

The obvious fix — match `D` or `DR` exactly — would have been a **mass
regression**, and the archive says so. `OD` is TD Canada's overdraft marker
on a running balance (`371.96OD`; that balance IS overdrawn, so the sign is
right): **596 occurrences across 50 documents, 39 claimed by
`td_canada_native`, 37 of them validated.** Every one of those balance
walks would have inverted. `/` is likewise a separator TD prints inside the
marker cell (`1234.56/D`), not part of the marker.

So the marker set is `{D, DR, OD}` — what the archive prints — plus the
trailing-minus convention. Zero movement on the frozen pre-R-2 equivalence
matrix: every marker shape in `INPUTS` reads exactly as it did before. This
card is a pure latent-defect fix.

## MG7. What the three movers gained — and why they still withhold

Claimed-but-not-validated is not success, so the movers are instrumented
per document rather than counted:

| doc | credits/debits | debit total |
|---|---|---|
| `112431717DA1` | 153/0 to **28/117** | 0.00 to **117,365.14** |
| `5A29258D7626` | 29/0 to **5/24** | 0.00 to **15,393.95** |
| `5C93775BBA87` | 90/0 to **20/68** | 0.00 to **27,082.05** |

Every one was publishing **100% credits and zero debits** — the direction
of the entire ledger was wrong. `5A29258D7626` also had its opening balance
sign corrected (-146.41 to +146.41).

**They remain `withheld_adb`, so the brief's "3 recoverable" should be read
as "3 corrected", not "3 validated".** The residual is an independent and
PRE-EXISTING defect that this cell deliberately did not fix — the export
wraps a long row across two physical lines:

```
Incoming wire transfer
$20,000.00 $22,760.05
```

The amount line carries no description, so `if not description: continue`
drops the row — which is exactly the `sum check off by -20000.00` on
`5A29258D7626`. Verified pre-existing: that row was dropped on the base
tree too. Follow-up card MG-C1 below.

## MG8. Carried findings and cards for Ocean

1. **MG-C1 — the chase export drops wrapped rows.** Described above. It is
   the sole remaining reason all three movers withhold, so MG-C1 and card 1
   together are what would recover the family. Not taken here: it is a
   row-assembly change in a parser, not a money-grammar change, and the
   brief scoped this cell to the grammar.
2. **MG-C2 — 12 call sites swallow a refusal into a silent 0.00.**
   `parse_money(...) or 0.0` (and `abs(... or 0.0)`) appears at
   `capital_one.py:59,61`, `cibc.py:263`, `linkbank.py:72`, `rbc.py:361`,
   `regions.py:219`, `td_us.py:165`, `truist.py:58,59,190`,
   `us_bank.py:236`, `wells.py:263`. A token the grammar refuses is
   published as zero instead of declining the document. This is the exact
   mechanism by which cards 2 and 3 could have turned refusals into silent
   zeros; the sweep proves none fired today, but the idiom is a standing
   fail-open across 10 parsers and deserves a platform card.
3. **CARD 4 CALLERS (out of scope, as briefed).** `parse_money` still reads
   a number out of a whole line when a caller hands it one:
   `analysis/td_can.py:464` passes an entire line (mitigated by `abs()`),
   and `2026-01-31` still reads as `-2026.0` because the ISO separator is
   indistinguishable from the trailing-minus convention at token level.
   `bofa.py:20` looks like a whole-line caller but anchors with its own
   fullmatch guard and is safe; `capital_one.py:201` has been guarded since
   MONEYFIX-1. The fix belongs at the callers, which must pass a cell.
4. **`parse_money_tokens` has no leading-sign rule at all** — `−500.00`
   yields `[500.0]`, exactly as `-500.00` always did. Its only consumer is
   `td_can`, which takes `abs()` of the results, so this is latent. Left
   alone deliberately rather than changed without a consumer that needs it.
5. **THE DETACHED-MARKER TRAP — corrected on review, and now PINNED.**
   The first draft of this finding said a space-separated marker was
   "unattested in the archive". **That was false**, and the correction
   matters more than the original note: a detached `OD`/`DR`/`D` is printed
   **212 times across 23 documents, 6 of them VALIDATED**
   (`DR` 150, `OD` 48, `D` 14). In every attested case the letters are
   DESCRIPTION TEXT, not a marker:

   | document | outcome | printed |
   |---|---|---|
   | `91E80C335091` PNC | validated | `36.00 OD Fee` (an overdraft FEE — positive) |
   | `52F62442E906` PNC | validated | `36.00 OD Fee` |
   | `9A982B45CB60` BMO | validated | `500.00 D 500.00 120,305.25` |
   | Huntington ×4 | failed | `282.12 OD PROTECTION TRANSFER FROM CREDIT CARD` |
   | Beem Credit Union ×5 | failed | `6,649.65  DR` (running balance) |

   So the whitespace boundary on the suffix group is **load-bearing, not
   incidental**: relaxing it to "read the next word as a marker" would
   negate a real fee on documents that validate today. It is now stated in
   `money.py` at `_DEBIT_MARKERS` and pinned by
   `test_a_detached_marker_is_description_text_and_leaves_the_sign_alone`
   and `test_welding_is_what_makes_a_marker_a_marker` — the same letters,
   one space apart, must mean opposite things.
6. **`ANALYSIS_STAGE_VERSION` needs a bump on merge** — 3 documents change
   their analysis output, so their cached payloads are stale. The brief
   reserves the bump to Ocean; `webapp/` is untouched here.
7. **The sign class is exactly two glyphs, and the brief's wider claim is
   corrected.** `MINUS_GLYPHS` is U+2212 and U+2013 — **U+2010 HYPHEN is
   NOT in it**, nor are U+2011 NON-BREAKING HYPHEN or U+FF0D FULLWIDTH
   HYPHEN-MINUS. Measured: each still reads `‐500.00` as **+500.0**. They
   are carried CANDIDATES pending attestation, deliberately not added — a
   sign class is the last place to admit an unattested member, since each
   one silently flips the sign of everything carrying it. U+2014 EM DASH
   stays out permanently: it is punctuation, not a sign.
8. **Attached-dash trailing-minus latent.** `1234-5678` reads as
   **`-1234.0`**, and now `1234–5678` does too, because the dash is
   indistinguishable from the mainframe trailing-minus at token level. This
   reaches only whole-line callers — the same class as finding 3, and
   `td_can.py:464` is mitigated by its `abs()`. **Zero documents moved** in
   the archive sweep. Recorded rather than fixed: telling a trailing sign
   from a separator needs the caller's column, which the grammar does not
   have.
9. **`strip_currency` and `pad_leading_decimal` are exported paths that do
   NOT normalize.** They are string utilities, not parsers, and pass a
   non-ASCII sign straight through (`strip_currency("−$1,234.56")` keeps the
   U+2212). The parsers that DO normalize are, exhaustively: `parse_amount`
   (hence every `AmountFormat`), `parse_money`, `parse_money_tokens`,
   `parse_decimal`, `parse_decimal_mixed_separator`, `parse_grouped_float`,
   `parse_trailing_minus_dropped`, `parse_french_amount`,
   `parse_digit_scrubbed`. A caller that cleans with the helpers and then
   matches on its own must call `normalize_sign_glyphs` first.
10. **`CENTS`/`SIGNED_CENTS` are FULLMATCH patterns — the tail-match
    latent.** `parse_amount` applies them with `re.fullmatch`, which is what
    makes the digit bound bite. Under `re.search` they match the TAIL of an
    over-long run (`"9"*20 + ".67"` yields `9999999999999.67`) and the bound
    is defeated silently. No consumer does that today; recorded because the
    two uses look interchangeable and are not.
11. **Non-finite literals are a carried crash class, low reach.**
    `parse_decimal("Infinity")` returns `Decimal('Infinity')` and
    `parse_grouped_float("inf")` returns `inf` — neither raises, and the
    digit bound does not catch them (`"inf"` has no digits to count).
    `adb._money(Decimal('Infinity'))` then raises `InvalidOperation`, the
    same crash class as card 3 by a different route. Reach is small:
    `parse_money` refuses them (no digits), so only the raising family is
    exposed, and no archive document prints the literal. A `is_finite`
    check at those four entry points would close it.
12. **The equivalence harness now declares divergences.** The frozen pre-R-2
   oracles stay frozen — they are historical record. `assert_equivalent`
   takes a declared divergence set: undeclared drift still fails, AND a
   declaration that no longer diverges fails too, so the list cannot go
   stale. Recommended for any future money-rule change.

# §DECLINES-C — three declined parsers: a month, a font, and a product name

## DC0. Summary

Three ownerships, six structural shapes, 33 declined documents. **21 documents
move `failed` -> `validated`, zero documents move down, and the 61 documents
that were already publishing numbers are byte-identical in every audited
field.** The 12 that stay refused each have a named diagnosis and four of them
are refused on purpose by a rule this cell added.

| cell | shape | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| bluevine | B1 abbreviated month (`Feb. 1, 2026`) | 12 failed | **12 validated** |
| bluevine | B2 fragmented rows — geometry | 2 failed | 2 refused, named |
| relay | R1 private-use sign glyphs | 6 failed | **6 validated** |
| relay | R2 row whose label wrapped | 3 failed | **3 validated** |
| navy_federal | N1 retail product read from the document | 10 failed | 4 withheld (ADB), 6 refused |

Per cell, over the full claimed population of each:

| cell | population | validated | withheld | failed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| bluevine | 14 | 0 -> **12** | 0 -> 0 | 14 -> 2 |
| relay | 26 | 16 -> **25** | 1 -> 1 | 9 -> **0** |
| navy_federal | 54 | 44 -> 44 | 0 -> 4 | 10 -> 6 |

All 21 are instrumented per document, not merely claimed: every published
credit and debit total equals the total the bank prints, the balance walk
reaches the printed closing balance, the ADB validations pass and
`continuity_breaks` is 0. **21 sound, 0 unsound, 3,981 transactions
published.**

`relay` has a second, independent in-document oracle: this platform prints one
`Settled`/`Returned` status word per transaction row, so the printed row count
is checkable against the published one. Over the **whole relay population, all
26 documents, it is exact — 26 match, 0 mismatch, 0 refused** (the nine
recovered ones read 28, 42, 277, 162, 177, 21, 15, 14, 46). A row invented,
dropped or double-counted by the glyph restoration or the wrapped-row rule
would show here even if the arithmetic happened to survive.

## DC1. The instrument

Every figure below comes from replaying the archive markdown through the real
pipeline (`analysis.pipeline.analyze_markdown` in deterministic mode +
`analysis.serialization.report_to_dict` +
`telemetry.record.classify_outcome` + `discovery.runner._failure_reason`),
resolved from the D-3 OCR artifact store in the MAIN checkout **by direct
file path** — the cache key is recomputed with the repo's own
`ocr_settings_key`/`cache_key` and the payload JSON is read from
`webapp_data/artifacts/ocr/<shard>/<key>.json`. The sqlite index was never
read. The ANALYSIS stage is deliberately **not** served from cache: a code
change of mine must never be measured through a payload the previous code
wrote, and `ANALYSIS_STAGE_VERSION` is Ocean's to bump.

Before any production edit the harness was checked against the baseline run of
record `88be9dd3`: over all 94 cohort documents it reproduced the run's
`outcome_class` and `outcome_reason` **exactly, 94/94, 0 disagreements**, with
**0 OCR-cache misses**.

The cohort is derived by content, not by run bookkeeping: the run's row
projection loses `parser_id` on the 1,034 cache-served rows, so the declined
population is taken from `attempted` (which survives) and the validated
population from `parser_id`, unioned. The scout's counts reproduced exactly —
bluevine 14, navy_federal 10, relay 9.

## DC2. bluevine — an abbreviated month is a month (12 documents)

Bluevine prints the same field two ways in the same sentence:

    Statement Period: February 2026 (February 1, 2026 - February 28, 2026)
    Statement Period: February 2026 (Feb. 1, 2026 - Feb. 28, 2026)

The period pattern matched the month with `\w+`, which cannot span the
abbreviating period, so the parser was refused on the **first field it asked
for**. Measured, not assumed: on all 12 the summary block matched and the
transaction rows matched — 70 to 581 rows each — and only the period failed.
The parser then never reached them.

The month is now read as a NAME, from an exact vocabulary of the twelve full
names and their abbreviations with the abbreviating period optional.

**Deliberately not the looser idiom.** `bmo_us_activity.py:70` and
`bmo_ca_business.py:93` use `(Jan|Feb|…)[a-z]*\.?` — a three-letter stem
followed by anything. That form was written first here and a test rejected it:
it reads "Janubry 1, 2026" as January. A statement period is the field every
other date in the document is resolved against, so this reader accepts a month
name or nothing. The test is `test_bluevine_declines_a_month_it_does_not_
recognise`.

The old `datetime.strptime(..., "%B %d, %Y")` also **raised** on an unreadable
month rather than declining — a `parser_exception`, not a decline. The reader
returns None now and the document fails closed.

**Correction (DC10.4): that property was documented before it was true.** The
first version of `_long_date` said "never as an exception" while still calling
`date(...)` unguarded, so an unreadable MONTH declined but an impossible DAY
did not: the period pattern admits a one-or-two-digit day, so `Feb. 30, 2026`
reached `date()` and raised `ValueError` — a crash, in a docstring that
promised a decline. `date()` is now wrapped and the document declines.
Terminally both were non-publishing, so no number was ever at risk; the defect
was that a crash and a decline put the document in different queues, and the
record claimed the better one. Fixture `test_bluevine_declines_a_day_the_month_
does_not_have`.

## DC3. relay — a font that could not print a sign, and a row that wrapped

### R1. Four printed characters arriving in the private-use area (6 documents)

Six of the nine declines embed a subset font whose ToUnicode table leaves four
characters unmapped, so they arrive as private-use codepoints:

| codepoint | printed character | occurrences in the six |
|---|---|---|
| U+E09D | `+` | 207 |
| U+E088 | `-` | 755 |
| U+E081 | `(` | 226 |
| U+E082 | `)` | 220 |

(private-use codepoints shown as <XXXX>; in the document they are invisible)

    Deposits <E09D>$24,969.32
    Withdrawals <E088>$18,168.92
    Expenses <E081>3240<E082> Transfer To Jul 13, 2026 Settled <E088>$300.00

`_ROW_RE` requires `[+-]\$` for the amount, so **not one transaction row
matched** in any of the six — the parser saw a Relay statement with no
transactions.

**The signs are not assumed. They are certified by the document's own
arithmetic.** This parser already required, with `Decimal` equality and no
tolerance anywhere: every row's running balance chains exactly from the printed
opening balance to the printed closing balance; the positive amounts sum
exactly to the printed Deposits total; the negative amounts sum exactly to the
printed Withdrawals total. Over the six documents that is a chain of 28 to 277
links plus two exact totals. A sign read backwards breaks the chain at the
first row it touches. The ablation is pinned by
`test_relay_refuses_a_statement_whose_signs_are_the_wrong_way_round`, which
inverts the glyphs **in the transaction rows only, leaving the printed summary
intact** — see DC10.1 for why that distinction is the whole test, and for the
mutant that proves it load-bearing.

**The two brackets are NOT certified, and an earlier version of this section
claimed they were.** It said they "occur only as a matched pair around an
account's last four digits". Measured across the six documents, that is false:

| document | `U+E081` | `U+E082` | balanced | 4-digit pairs | other pairs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `0d8ac487_Income-July` | 29 | 29 | yes | 19 | 10 |
| `0d8ac487_Income-June` | 44 | 44 | yes | 33 | 11 |
| `1b7c38d5_Operations-May` | 72 | 72 | yes | 62 | 10 |
| `a5314b98_03-2026` | 23 | 20 | **no** | 6 | 16 |
| `a5314b98_05-2026-1` | 30 | 27 | **no** | 9 | 20 |
| `a6deaa10_Relay (Partial)` | 28 | 28 | yes | 18 | 10 |

The counts do not balance in two of six, and every document wraps things that
are not an account's last four: disclosure numerals (`(10)`, `(60)`, `(90)`,
`(3)`), a masked account number (`(XXXXXX-3373)`), and short tokens (`(CD)`,
`(WM)`).

What actually bounds the risk is **reach, not position: no number flows
through these two glyphs.** `(` and `)` appear in no pattern this module reads
a figure with — not the amount, not the balance, not the date, not
`Account Number:\s*([X\d-]+)` — so they can only land in a row's label, which
is description text. A wrong bracket mapping yields a cosmetically wrong
description and cannot move a published figure. The only evidence for `(`/`)`
is that statements from this platform whose font maps correctly print
parentheses in the same construct (`Business Checking (8923) Transfer From`);
that is suggestive, not proof, and it is now recorded as an assumption in both
the code comment and here.

One clarification the correction turned up: the SIGN glyphs do reach one
non-arithmetic field. `U+E088` restores the hyphen in the masked account
number, so `Account Number: XXXXXX<E088>3373` publishes as `XXXXXX-3373`.
That is the certified glyph, so the field is sound — but the neat claim that
"the certified glyphs touch only numbers" is not true either, and is not made.

### R1b. Is the glyph class platform-wide? Measured: no, and the answer is useful

The handoff asked for a measurement, not a guess. Every one of the 3,493
documents in the run of record with cached OCR text was scanned for
codepoints in U+E000–U+F8FF. **66 documents carry them, in three unrelated
families:**

| family | codepoints | documents | folders | what they are |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Relay | U+E081/E082/E088/E09D | 6 | Thread Bank | printed `(`, `)`, `-`, `+` — this cell |
| Mercury | U+EA01/EA02/EA04/EA08 | 30 | Mercury | a subset font, **all 30 unclaimed** |
| symbol/barcode | U+F020–U+F15F | 26 | Unidentified 22, R Bank 2, +4 | **not text loss** |
| singletons | U+E608, U+F0F0, U+F0A0 … | 4 | one each | one glyph each |

The third family was decoded before it was dismissed: subtracting 0xF000 —
the standard PDF symbolic-font offset — yields `` `:O=[$A0J!_"E6 `` and
`QQ1111Q111Q111`, i.e. a barcode/MICR font, not lost words. Those 26 documents
lose nothing.

**Conclusion: there is no platform table to write.** The *phenomenon* recurs,
but each font is its own encoding and only the issuer's own document can
certify a mapping. The mapping therefore lives at the relay reader, and `ocr/`
was not touched. The one adjacent finding worth routing is Mercury: 30
documents, one coherent glyph family, currently `no_parser_matched` — see
DC7.2.

### R2. A row whose label wrapped onto the line above (3 documents)

`_ROW_RE` anchored label, date, status, amount and balance on one line. When a
label wrapped, the row became invisible:

    Business Checking (8923) Transfer From
    Mar 10, 2026 Settled +$375.00 $25,470.00

Each of the three lost **exactly one** row — always the last row of page 1 —
and a statement missing one row fails its own balance walk, so all three were
refused whole. The row tail now matches on its own and takes its label from the
line above.

**Fail closed on attribution, not on arithmetic.** The balance walk would
accept a mislabelled row perfectly happily — the amounts are right, only the
description would be wrong — so the label rule cannot lean on it.

**What the rule is, stated accurately** (an earlier version of this paragraph
implied more than the code does). It is a **blacklist of exactly two furniture
shapes** — the OCR page separator `--- Page N ---` and the platform footer
`Page N of M` — plus the structural fact that a line already consumed as a row
is cleared, so a row can never be another row's label. It is **not** a
positive test that the line above looks like a transaction label. Any other
non-row line directly above a wrapped row is accepted as its label, so a piece
of furniture this pattern does not name would be taken as a description.

The exposure is bounded and worth stating exactly: the wrapped row's own date,
amount and balance are read from the wrapped line itself and still have to
survive the balance walk, so a mislabelling costs a wrong description and
never a wrong figure. Upgrading to a positive label test is recorded as a
residual (DC7.6) rather than guessed at — it needs a characterisation of what
a label looks like across the population, and three documents cannot supply
one. `test_relay_refuses_a_wrapped_row_whose_label_is_page_furniture` pins the
blacklist half.

## DC4. navy_federal — the product, read from the document

`navy_federal` carried `"Business Checking"` as a **structural anchor**, in
four places: the summary regex, the section heading it searched for, the noise
filter, and `account_name`. That silently restricted the parser to the
BUSINESS issue of a statement Navy Federal also prints for retail members. All
ten declines are the retail issue — same grid, same columns, same row order, a
different product word:

| family | products declared | documents |
|---|---|---|
| `614d30ce` | EveryDay Checking + Membership Savings | 4 |
| `85a1317f` | EveryDay Checking + Membership Savings + Money Market Savings | 2 |
| `b71d6d2a` | EveryDay Checking + **e-Checking** + Membership Savings | 4 |

The product is now read from the statement's own `Summary of your deposit
accounts` table, by head noun — this platform names its deposit products
`<qualifier> Checking` and `<qualifier> Savings` — and **accepted only when
the transaction detail confirms it** by printing the same product and account
as a section heading. Two independent printings of the same fact, not one.

That reader was validated before it went into the parser: over all 54 cohort
documents, every checking account it read from the summary table was confirmed
by a matching section heading — **54/54, zero unconfirmed, zero documents
without the table**.

Section extent is now read from the document's own headings too. The old stop
list named the sibling products one issue happens to print (`Mbr Business
Savings`, `Bus Money Mkt Savings`, `Checking Line`) and named **none** of the
products a retail statement carries, so a retail savings section would have
been read as part of the checking one.

Also fixed: an overdrawn balance prints with a trailing minus either detached
(`136.51 -`) or attached (`136.51-`), and only the detached form was read, so
the ledger walk stopped at the first overdrawn day. The file's own
beginning-balance anchor already read the attached form. This is the TDFIX-1
finding one layer down.

### DC4.1 Two accounts, one schema — and a boundary drawn carefully

A statement declaring two DIFFERENT checking products has no single product to
anchor on, and the single-account extraction schema (L-1) cannot say "both".
The four `b71d6d2a` documents are refused.

**The rule is PRODUCT-level and deliberately not ACCOUNT-level, and that
distinction is load-bearing.** Measuring the cohort found something the scout's
note did not anticipate: **three currently-VALIDATED documents already declare
several accounts under one product** —

    58ba2f73_april   Business Checking × 3   (7200649320, 7217670327, 7217965081)
    58ba2f73_march   Business Checking × 2
    81a8298f_APRIL   Business Checking × 2

— and the parser publishes the first of them as if it were the statement. An
account-level rule would have refused those three, which is truth-set movement
and a stop-the-line event. This cell therefore changed nothing about them: with
one checking product declared, the anchor is well-defined and the existing
account selection is untouched, byte-identically. The pre-existing L-1 exposure
those three represent is reported, not changed — DC7.1.

### DC4.2 The result, and why it is 0 new validated

| | documents | disposition |
|---|---|---|
| already validated | 44 | **44, byte-identical in every audited field** |
| now readable, ADB withheld | 4 | honest refusal with a named diagnosis |
| refused: two checking products (L-1) | 4 | by the rule above |
| refused: zero activity | 1 | A-prime is Gustavo-pending — DC5 |
| refused: consumer date-ownership layout | 1 | needs the geometry rung — DC5 |

The four that now read are refused by the platform's own ADB gate on
`posting_dates_cover_source` — the check that catches a parser folding posting
dates together, so end-of-day balances land on the wrong days. **This is the
gate working, and the correct outcome.** The parser's own guards pass on all
four (credits and debits match the printed totals exactly, the final running
balance equals the printed ending balance), which is precisely why a
date-attribution defect needs a check that looks at dates.

Diagnosed one further level, because the two causes rank differently:

| document | missing posting dates | cause |
|---|---|---|
| `614d30ce_april` | `2026-03-15` only | the beginning-balance day — a **false** failure, DC7.3 |
| `614d30ce_june` | `2026-06-02`, `2026-06-14` | real mid-period mis-attribution |
| `85a1317f_march` | `2026-03-11`, `2026-03-19` | real mid-period mis-attribution |
| `85a1317f_may` | `2026-04-25`, `2026-05-24` | mixed |

**No attempt was made to widen the line-order heuristic to fix the real ones.**
In the retail layout the date and description follow the money for debits as
well as credits, where the business layout puts them before; the existing
reader guesses ownership from direction, and the gate has now proved that guess
wrong on documents where it does produce output. Guessing harder would risk
mis-dating documents that currently validate. This is a geometry problem and it
is named as one.

|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | bluevine | geometry: fragmented rows | date, description and amount interleaved across lines with no recoverable reading order — `03/07/26` / `$9,500.00` / `03/15/26 … $-200.00` / `$-2,500.00`. Which amount belongs to which date is not decidable from the text. |

## DC6. Non-interference

Argued structurally, then measured.

**Structurally:** a parser can only reach a document its detector claims, and
`git diff d70efbe..HEAD` touches no detection surface in any of the three files
— no `DETECTION_MARKERS`, no `required(...)`, no `detection_text`, no
`make_detector` call changed. The relay glyph restoration is applied INSIDE
`parse_relay_statement`, after `detect()` has already run, so it cannot change
what relay claims either. The set of documents whose outcome can change is
therefore exactly the 94 measured in DC0.

**Measured:** a stratified probe of 500 documents outside the three
cells, drawn round-robin across folder labels so no large folder (Chase 613,
Bank of America 405) can dominate — **67 distinct folder labels**,
23,463 transactions replayed. Because the base tree's CODE is identical to
the tree that produced the run of record (only docs commits separate
`99b9b33` from base `d70efbe`), the run of record IS the before-state.

    documents probed                    500
    agree with the run of record        498
    disagree                            2
    claimed or attempted by my parsers  0

Both disagreements are instrument artifacts, not movements, and neither
involves these parsers. The instrument starts from the CACHED OCR TEXT, so it
does not run the preflight or OCR stages: `BMO/08a2c390_bmo voided check.pdf`
was deferred to visual OCR in the run and has no cached text at all, and
`Desjardins/7da28d6e_avril2026.pdf` is rejected by preflight as `invalid_pdf`,
a class reached before any text exists. Both are `failed` in the run and
`failed`/absent here; neither was ever analysed.

## DC7. Carried findings and questions for Ocean

**DC7.1 — `navy_federal` publishes one of several checking accounts, today,
on three validated documents.** `58ba2f73_april` declares three Business
Checking accounts and the platform publishes the first one's balances, ADB and
ledger as the statement's. `58ba2f73_march` and `81a8298f_APRIL` declare two.
This is pre-existing, merged, and validated; it is the L-1 gap made concrete.
This cell did not change it — refusing them is truth-set movement — but Ocean
should know the 2,030 validated tier contains three documents where "the
account" is a choice the parser made silently. Recommend: a review flag rather
than a refusal, decided at platform level, not in this parser.

**DC7.2 — Mercury: 30 documents, one glyph family, all unclaimed.** The census
found U+EA01/EA02/EA04/EA08 across 30 Mercury documents, every one currently
`no_parser_matched`. That is the same defect class as R1 — a subset font whose
ToUnicode table is incomplete — and it is the largest single block of it in the
archive. It belongs to the Mercury/fintech cell in this batch, and the census
JSON naming all 66 affected documents is available. Whoever takes it should
know the mapping must be certified by the issuer's own arithmetic, as R1's was,
not inferred by eye.

**DC7.3 — a false `posting_dates_cover_source` failure, in a shared module.**
`614d30ce_april` is blocked only by the beginning-balance day. The statement
prints

    2.26
    03-15
    Beginning Balance

on three separate lines, and `_NOT_A_POSTING_ROW` in `analysis/dates.py` tests
one line at a time, so the bare `03-15` is counted as a source posting date
that no transaction can ever cover. Where the same platform prints
`05-01 Beginning Balance` on one line the guard catches it correctly, which is
why the 44 business documents are unaffected. This is the same class as the
`_SUMMARY_TOTAL_ROW` fix already in that file, one line-split further, and its
direction of effect is the same safe one: it can only REMOVE dates from the
source set, so the check can go from failing to passing, never the reverse.
`analysis/dates.py` is outside this cell's ownership and was not touched.
Recommend routing to whoever owns the shared date grammar this batch.

**DC7.4 — four documents moved `failed` -> `withheld` with no validated gain.**
Ocean's instrument will show them. The claim is that this is an improvement in
honesty, not a regression: they move from "no parser could read this document"
to "the platform read it and refuses to publish an ADB it cannot trust", with a
diagnosis W3-2 can rank (`posting_date_coverage`). If Ocean prefers no class
movement without a validated gain, reverting is one commit — but the navy
federal hardcode removal is R-1 class debt and its removal is the point of the
card.

**DC7.6 — RESIDUAL: relay's wrapped-row label rule is a two-item furniture
blacklist, not a positive label test.** Raised by adversarial review (finding
B) and recorded rather than fixed. Today a wrapped row takes the line above as
its label unless that line is the OCR page separator or the platform footer;
any other unnamed furniture would become a description. Cost is bounded to a
wrong description — the row's date, amount and balance come from the wrapped
line and still face the balance walk — so this is a quality residual, not a
correctness one. A positive test needs a characterisation of what a label
looks like across the whole relay population; the three documents in this cell
cannot supply it, and inventing one from three samples is how a blacklist
becomes a wrong whitelist. Recommend it rides with whoever next has relay
volume.

**DC7.5 — the scout's `navy_federal` estimate was 9 recoverable; the measured
answer is 0 validated.** The gap is not a missing capability, it is four
documents the ADB gate refuses and five refused on rules the handoff itself
directed. Recorded so the estimate is not carried forward.

## DC10. Amendments from adversarial review

Ocean's verdict was **SHIP conditional**. The code held — the reviewer built a
mutant with relay's entire balance-walk certification deleted and confirmed
the shipped parser still refuses a rows-only sign inversion — but **two of the
evidence items did not**, and both were mine. Recorded in full because a cell
whose thesis is "measured, not assumed" has to hold its own prose to that.

**DC10.1 — the vacuous pin (required, fixed).** The sign ablation rewrote
every `+$`/`-$` in the document, the printed SUMMARY included. The summary
pattern requires a literal `+` before Deposits and `-` before Withdrawals, so
the parser returned None at the summary regex **before reading a single row**.
The test therefore passed for the wrong reason, and would have passed against
a tree with the entire certification deleted — it proved nothing, while
sitting under a docstring calling itself "the load-bearing one".

Rewritten to invert the ROW glyphs only (`Settled +$` / `Settled -$`), leaving
the summary intact, plus two asserts that the summary survived so the test
cannot silently go vacuous again. Verified against the reviewer's mutant,
reproduced independently here:

    inversion                                       shipped       mutant
    rows-only inversion (the NEW ablation)             None    STATEMENT
    whole-document inversion (the OLD ablation)        None         None

    NEW ablation kills the mutant : True
    OLD ablation kills the mutant : False
    shipped still reads the honest statement: True

The mutant is built by deleting the balance walk, the closing-balance check
and the two exact total checks from a compiled-in-memory copy of `relay.py`;
nothing was written to the worktree.

**DC10.2 — the bracket claim was false (required, corrected).** DC3/R1 and
`relay.py` both asserted the bracket glyphs were "proven by position — only a
matched pair around an account's last four digits". Measurement refutes it:
unbalanced open/close counts in two of six documents, 10–20 non-conforming
pairs per document. Both records now state the truth — an **uncertified
assumption**, bounded by reach rather than position, because no number flows
through `(`/`)`. Full table and reasoning in DC3/R1.

**DC10.3 — the navy_federal second-print check was a substring test
(hardening, applied — but NOT as specified, and that matters).**
`f"{product} - {account}" in markdown` is satisfied by prose that merely
mentions the pair, which defeats the point of demanding a second printing.
The finding is correct and the check is now position-anchored.

**The prescribed remedy could not ship, and the cohort is why.** The condition
asked for the existing whole-line `_SECTION_HEADING_RE`, described as a
one-token change with no behaviour change. Applied literally it **regressed
three currently-validated documents** — caught by re-sweeping all 94 cohort
documents after the amendment rather than trusting the description:

    Unidentified/1db08d32_Mode March 2026 Bank Statement.pdf   validated -> failed
    Unidentified/4a83173e_may_2026_monthly_statement.pdf       validated -> failed
    Unidentified/73b975d3_June2026MonthlyStatement.pdf         validated -> failed

In those three the text extractor merges the section caption onto the end of
the grid's column-header line, so the caption is never a whole line:

    Date Transaction Detail Amount($) Balance($) Business Checking - 7137039603
    Date Transaction Detail Amount($) Balance($) Business Checking - 7196281617 Checking
    Business Checking - 7216974365 (Continued from previous page)

The shipped rule anchors on the two positions a caption actually occupies —
**line start, or immediately after the grid column header** — and leaves what
FOLLOWS it open, because a continuation marker or a stray column word is
downstream of the caption and varies. What may PRECEDE it is the whole test,
and a sentence cannot. That is strictly stronger than the substring test it
replaces and does not refuse a document the platform reads today.

Fixtures both ways:
`test_navy_federal_ignores_a_prose_mention_of_the_heading` (refused) and
`test_navy_federal_accepts_a_caption_merged_into_the_column_header`
(accepted). Cohort re-swept after the change: 94/94 unchanged, zero
audited-field drift.

Recorded plainly because it is the second time in this cell that a
confidently-described claim did not survive measurement — the first was mine
(DC10.2), this one was the review's. The lesson is the same either way: the
94-document re-sweep is cheap and the description of a change is not evidence
about it.

**DC10.4 — bluevine crashed on an impossible date (hardening, applied).** The
docstring promised "never as an exception"; `Feb. 30` raised. `date()` is now
guarded and the document declines. Detail in DC2.

**DC10.5 — the wrapped-row rule was overstated (corrected).** Finding B: it is
a two-item furniture blacklist, not a positive label test. DC3/R2 now says so;
the upgrade is residual DC7.6.

Two of the five are corrections to claims rather than to code, which is the
part worth carrying forward: the parsers were right and the write-up was not,
and only a reviewer who ran the mutant could tell the difference.

# §HUNT-CELL — the Huntington folder: 54 documents, two issuers, and a bank that prints its own answer four times

## H0. Summary

The folder holds **54 distinct documents and two issuers**. Fifty are
Huntington National Bank's sectioned business deposit statement; four are
Burke & Herbert Bank of Moorefield, WV, filed here because the account
holder's address is in Huntington, **WV** and several card rows were made at a
Huntington Bank ATM. Every one of the 54 was `failed / no_parser_matched` in
the run of record; no registration reached the 0.5 claim threshold and
the highest near-miss over the 54 was 0.25.

| id | family | documents | outcome on this branch |
|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | Huntington sectioned deposit statement | 38 | **33 validated**, 5 withheld (see H6.1) |
| Q | the same layout, printed incomplete | 8 | `parser_declined`, each with named evidence |
| A2 | the same layout carrying a SECOND account | 4 | `parser_declined` — L-1, fail closed |
| B | Burke & Herbert mainframe layout | 3 | **3 review**, ADB computed, every oracle met (H6.2) |
| C | Burke & Herbert insufficient-funds notice | 1 | `no_parser_matched` — not a statement |

**33 documents move `failed` → `validated`, 4,520 transactions are published
across them, and all 33 instrument sound with zero unsound.** Two further
groups — 5 + 3 documents — are complete, correct parses held back by two
PRE-EXISTING defects in modules this cell does not own; both are measured
counterfactually below and carded, not patched.

Two new registrations, `huntington` and `burke_herbert`. Registry 53 → 55.

## H1. The instrument, and what it was checked against first

Every figure below comes from replaying the archive markdown through the real
pipeline (`analyze_markdown` + `telemetry.record.classify_outcome` +
`discovery.runner._failure_reason`), with the OCR text resolved from the D-3
artifact store **by direct file path**; the sqlite index was never opened.

Before any production edit the harness was checked against the run of record
`88be9dd3`: over all 54 documents it reproduced the run's `parser_id`,
`outcome_class` and `outcome_reason` **exactly, 54/54, 0 disagreements**, with
**zero OCR-cache misses**.

The scout's partition was verified and two numbers corrected: the defective
group is **8 documents, not 5** (H4), so the recoverable Huntington family is
**38, not 41**; and the folder holds a second issuer the scout read as one
family (H5).

The scout's headline of 41 is nonetheless the right target, reached a
different way: **38 Huntington** (33 shipped, plus the 5 of H6.1 behind the
`regions` card) **plus 3 Burke & Herbert** (behind the page-declaration card)
= 41. What is NOT reachable is any of the 8 short-print documents: no card
recovers a service charge the bank never dated.

## H2. What the layout gives you, which is unusually much

One physical line carries the whole account summary as label/figure pairs.
Activity follows as named, direction-bearing sections — `Deposits (+)`,
`Other Credits (+)`, `Checks (-)`, `Other Debits (-)` — each repeated verbatim
when it continues after a page break. Fees are itemised in
`Service Charge Detail`, totalled in `Service Charge Summary`, and the period
closes with `Balance Activity`: the bank's own end-of-day balance for every day
it posted anything.

So the bank prints its own answer four times, and the parser publishes only
what all four agree on:

1. the summary identity — `beginning + credits - debits - service charges`;
2. the per-direction subtotals, which the printed sections must add up to;
3. the service-charge total, which the itemised fees must net to;
4. **`Balance Activity`, reproduced day by day from the published ledger.**

Check 4 is the one that matters and the one no aggregate can make. The sums
cannot see a misdated row; the daily walk fails on the day the date is wrong.
Since `analysis/adb.py` requires `ledger_reconciles_to_closing` at zero
tolerance and `posting_dates_cover_source`, and since Average Daily Balance is
the platform's headline figure, a layout whose dates are unproven is a layout
whose ADB is unproven. A statement that prints no `Balance Activity` is
therefore refused rather than published on its sums (H4).

Stated plainly and against interest: **check 1 is redundant.** Given checks 3
and 4 it follows algebraically, no document can isolate it, and the mutation
run reports it as unkillable. It is kept as the one direct statement of the
bank's own identity and the code says so, rather than a fixture being invented
to make it look load-bearing.

### H2.1 Two conventions of the print, read rather than guessed

**A negative is a TRAILING minus** — `$2,693.10-`. It is this issuer's only
negative marker and it appears on the summary's opening and closing figures,
on the service-charge-cycle averages and in every cell of `Balance Activity`.
Seven documents in the folder open or close overdrawn (six Huntington, one
Burke & Herbert) and twelve print at least one negative daily balance. Read as
a magnitude they still balance — against a sign-flipped closing balance — so
self-consistency proves nothing and the cross-month chain is what does. Three
pairs in this folder print the minus on BOTH sides, closing balance and the
next statement's opening balance:

| account | closes | opens, next statement |
|---|---|---|
| `...2676` | `$2,693.10-` (April) | `$2,693.10-` (May) |
| `...3152` | `$1,184.20-` (April) | `$1,184.20-` (May) |
| `...5891` | `$1,388.26-` (March) | `$1,388.26-` (April) |

**A record correction, and it cuts against the marker rather than for it.** An
earlier draft of this section offered a fourth pair — May 3152 closing at
−2,318.04 into June 3152 — as a fifth line of evidence. It is not one: May
3152 prints its closing balance as `$2,318.04` with **no** minus, while June
3152 opens `$2,318.04-` with one. The issuer is not perfectly consistent, so
the glyph alone is not the authority; the summary identity is, and a document
that omits the minus fails that identity and is refused rather than published
sign-flipped. Ocean's review caught the bad example.

**`Service Charge Detail` prints two money columns** — `Service Charge (-)` and
`Waives and Discounts (+)` — and the flattened text keeps no trace of which
column a figure stood in: a charge and a waiver are both
`date amount description`, and the waiver rows are not even a separate block
(one appears mid-block on `414771fa_..._2026-03-01_...`, before the block ends
and a second one begins).

A first design split them at the point where the printed dates stop ascending,
on the argument that the columns are read top-to-bottom in turn. **It was
rejected on measurement**: the regression only exists when the first waiver
predates the last charge, and on **five** of this folder's own documents it
does not, so a waiver was booked as a charge and the fee total came out by
twice its amount. Re-measured for the record after review — the earlier draft
said four, and the case against the rejected design is stronger than that:
applied to the 30 documents that itemise fees, it gets 25 right and **5 wrong**
(`09d4938d_February statement _1` +72.00, `09d4938d_Huntington December
statement Account 8098` +72.00, `09d4938d_november huntington statement Account
8098` +72.00, `414771fa_..._2026-04-01_...` +60.00,
`414771fa_..._2026-05-01_...` +60.00). What settles it
is that the document states both column totals separately in
`Service Charge Summary`, so the boundary is the position at which the rows
before it sum to the stated charges and the rows after it sum to the stated
waivers. If no position satisfies both, or more than one does, the split is not
determined by the document and the parser does not guess it. That block's own
identity (`charges - waivers == the stated total`) is checked first, so a
misread of the arbiter cannot license a mis-split.

`Net Service Charges` is printed between the two column totals and is in
neither: adding it would count the previous month's charges twice. A fixture
pins that.

## H3. A2 — the second account, refused at parse and not at detection

Four documents present a `Business Overdraft Protection Account` beside the
deposit account: its own summary (`Beginning Balance / Payments (-) /
Advances (+) / Interest Expense (+) / Ending Balance`), its own activity
sections and its own `Daily Balance` table. Two accounts, two balance chains,
one statement.

`Statement` carries one account (L-1), so publishing this document would mean
publishing one of its two accounts and dropping the other silently — the exact
failure the schema limit exists to prevent. Refused.

It is refused **at parse, not by an excluding marker**, and that is deliberate:
the document IS a Huntington statement of this layout, and reporting it as a
bank nobody has seen would put it in the most expensive queue. It reports as
`parser_declined` — a layout we recognise and decline — which is what
§DISPATCH-REPORTING built that split for. No outcome class moves: both are
`failed`.

**Volume for Gustavo's architecture item: 4 documents, one account family
(`e9475306_*`), deposit + line-of-credit on one statement.**

## H4. Q — eight documents whose own printed detail is short

Eight documents (`df4e5937_*`, accounts 3152 and 5891) print a summary that
accounts for money the document never itemises. Every one of them declares its
own page count and carries every page it declares, so nothing was lost in
handling: the bank printed them this way.

All eight state a `Total Service Charges (-)` and print **no**
`Service Charge Detail` block, so that money has no date and no row; and all
eight print **no** `Balance Activity`, so nothing in the document dates the
ledger. Three are short in the transaction sections as well:

| document | stated but not itemised | section shortfall |
|---|---|---|
| `df4e5937_March 3152` | service charges 80.50 | — |
| `df4e5937_April 3152` | service charges 189.50 | — |
| `df4e5937_May 3152` | service charges 95.00 | — |
| `df4e5937_JUNE 3152` | service charges 8.50 | — |
| `df4e5937_March 5891` | service charges 468.50 | — |
| `df4e5937_April 5891` | service charges 288.50 | debits 291.80 printed vs 791.80 stated (short 500.00) |
| `df4e5937_May 5891` | service charges 72.00 | debits 17,528.66 printed vs 23,378.66 stated (short 5,850.00) |
| `df4e5937_JUNE 5891` | service charges 110.50 | debits 15,660.30 printed vs 16,660.28 stated (short 999.98) |

A service charge with no printed date cannot be published without inventing
one, and an invented date corrupts the daily ledger and therefore the ADB —
the one number this platform is most careful about. Fail closed, eight
documents, named.

## H5. B — Burke & Herbert, and the folder label that was wrong

Four documents are not Huntington's. The issuer is Burke & Herbert Bank; the
statements print `burkeandherbertbank.com`, a Moorefield WV return address,
and a fixed-pitch mainframe `ACTIVITY IN DATE ORDER` grid. "Huntington" is on
them because the holder's address is `HUNTINGTON WV 25701` and because rows
read `ATM W/D … HUNTINGTON BAN 5704 ROUTE 60 EAST`. **R4-3's counterparty
hazard, arriving in a folder label instead of in a marker** — worth carrying
forward, because folder labels are the discovery run's bank attribution.

The text layer flattens each page's entire activity region onto ONE physical
line — banner, every row, and each row's continuation text, run together. No
columns survive. What does survive is that **every row prints its own running
balance**, so the read is checked row by row: opening balance plus the first
row's amount equals the first row's printed balance, and so on to the last,
which must equal the printed `ENDING BALANCE`.

That chain closes on **215 of 215 rows across the three statements, with zero
breaks**, at the first attempt. The bank also prints the **COUNT** beside each
direction's total (`2 DEPOSITS/CREDITS 26,245.24`), so the ledger is checked
against its own row counts in both directions as well as its money — 3/3
documents, both directions, exact. The cross-month chain closes too (Feb→Mar
ends 15,302.22 and Mar→Apr opens on it; Apr ends 7.53 and May opens on it), and
on `6768-2026-Mar` the computed ADB is **9,113.00** against the bank's printed
`AVERAGE LEDGER BALANCE 9,113.00`.

The fourth document is a `NOTICE OF ITEMS WITH INSUFFICIENT FUNDS`: no period,
no summary, no ledger. It is not claimed. The informal-document registration
class (`formal_statement=False`) is Gustavo-pending and this cell did not open
one — recorded, not built.

`resolve_year` is imported from `analysis/dates.py` rather than reimplemented.
The first draft copied it into both parsers and
`tests/test_no_parser_helper_clones.py` caught it, which is exactly what that
guard is for.

## H6. Two complete parses, held back by defects this cell does not own

Both are measured counterfactually. **Neither fix is shipped**: the modules
belong to no card in this handoff, and a cell that quietly edits a shared
module is how a wave loses its byte-identity argument.

### H6.1 `repair_regions_summary` fires on another bank's statement (+5)

`analysis/regions.py:243` gates the Regions summary repair on
`"REGIONS" in markdown.upper() and "SUMMARY" in markdown.upper()`. Five
Huntington statements pay a bill to `REGIONS BANK` and print a
`Service Charge Summary`, so the repair fires on them and rewrites
`beginning_balance`, `ending_balance`, `stated_total_credits`,
`stated_total_debits`, `stated_service_charge` and `stated_average_balance`
from labels (`Beginning Balance`, `Checks`, `Ending Balance`) that Huntington
also prints. On `09d4938d_February statement _1` it replaces a correctly-read
`Debits (-)` of 23,968.60 with 12,096.40; reconciliation then fails, ADB is
withheld, and the document lands `withheld_adb`.

This is R4-3 applied to a REPAIR rather than to a detection marker: the bank's
name appears in other banks' statements as a counterparty. The five are, precisely, the five folder documents whose text contains the
word REGIONS: `09d4938d_February statement _1`,
`09d4938d_Huntington December statement  Account 8098`,
`09d4938d_Huntington January Staement   8098 acct`,
`09d4938d_March Statement _1` and
`09d4938d_november huntington statement  Account 8098`.

**Counterfactual, with the repair neutralised in memory and nothing else
changed: all five validate, all five instrument SOUND.** The platform failed
closed rather than publishing wrong numbers, which is the system working; but
the repair can corrupt a correct parse of any issuer, and its blast radius is
larger than this folder.

### H6.2 an unlabelled image page reads as a missing page (+3)

The three Burke statements land `review / integrity_flags` on
`missing_declared_statement_page`. The check
(`analysis/pipeline.py:306`) requires every page label `1..N` to be printed.
This layout's final declared page is a **deposit-image sheet** that prints no
page-number footer, so label `N` is never found:

| document | declares | labels printed | PDF pages |
|---|---|---|---|
| `6768-2026-Mar` | 6 | 1–5 | 8 |
| `6768-2026-Apr` | 8 | 1–7 | 10 |
| `6768-2026-May` | 6 | 1–5 | 8 |

The page is present. On `6768-2026-Mar` it is physical page 7 and lists
`2/13 $18,245.24`, `2/23 $8,000.00`, `2/13 $1,525.00`, `2/20 $1,200.00` —
which are exactly the two DEPOSIT and two WITHDRAWAL rows of the published
ledger, so the "missing" page independently corroborates the parse.

**Counterfactual, treating the last declared page as present and changing
nothing else: all three validate, all three instrument SOUND, both printed
count checks TRUE on all three.**

## H7. Scope, semantics and the sweep

**Nothing shared was touched.** The branch is two new parser modules, two
registry rows, one conformance fixture each and tests. `webapp/`, `ocr/`,
`pipeline.py`, `reconcile.py`, `metrics.py`, `adb.py`, `count_semantics.py`,
`money.py`, `tables.py` and `dates.py` all carry a **zero-line diff** against
`d70efbe`. So the only way any other document's outcome can move is if one of
the two new registrations claims it — which makes the sweep below a complete
argument rather than a sample.

**Zero cross-claims.** The conformance cross-product is now 55 × 54 = **2,970**
