## H8b. Amendments from adversarial review

Ocean's review returned SHIP with conditions. All eight of the cell's claims
reproduced independently; what the review found were three defects in the
record and two in the code, and one of the code defects had been hiding a
finding.

**D1 (the blocker) — the module docstring specified the design that was
REJECTED.** `analysis/huntington.py` described the date-regression boundary as
though it were the shipped rule. The code has always used the totals-pinned
unique cut; the docstring did not, and the rule it described is measurably
wrong on five of this folder's own documents. Rewritten to state the shipped
rule (the unique cut where the prefix sums to the printed charges AND the
suffix to the printed waivers, refusing on zero or multiple cuts), with the
rejected design and its measured failure kept as the reason. This is the worst
kind of comment defect — one that would teach the next reader the wrong rule —
and it was invisible to every test, because tests exercise code and not prose.

**D7 — a printed zero read as an absent figure.** `stated_service_charge` was
built with an `or` chain, so a printed `Total Service Charges (-) 0.00` fell
through to the fallback and published `None`. "The bank stated the charge was
nothing" and "the bank stated nothing" are different claims. Two documents were
affected — `3222c646_Weismantel Nov 25` and `3222c646_Weismantel feb 26` — and
both now publish `0.00`. Explicit `is not None` check, extracted into
`_stated_service_charge` with the reasoning attached, and fixtured.

**D9 — an oracle cited as evidence but never published.** §H5 offered the
agreement between the computed ADB and Burke's printed `AVERAGE LEDGER BALANCE`
as corroboration, while the parser never set `stated_average_balance` — so the
platform's own advisory stated-vs-computed check could not fire on it. Now
published, and **the check surfaced something the cell had not seen**:

| document | printed | computed | agrees |
|---|---|---|---|
| `6768-2026-Mar` | 9,113.00 | 9,113.00 | yes |
| `6768-2026-Apr` | 4,122.56 | 4,122.56 | yes |
| `6768-2026-May` | 1,267.21 | 1,267.22 | **no — by one cent** |

The third document's printed average differs from the reconstructed one by
$0.01. The check is advisory and is not in `adb.ok`'s required set, so no
outcome moves and the ledger is unaffected — the balance chain still closes on
215/215 rows. It is a rounding-basis difference in the bank's own figure, and
it is recorded rather than tuned away. Publishing the field is what made it
visible at all, which is the argument for publishing it.

Not published for `huntington`, deliberately and unchanged: that layout prints
its averages under the footnote "the above balances correspond to the service
charge cycle for this account", which is not the statement period.

**D6** — the dead `_SECOND_ACCOUNT` constant and its stale comment (which
described `Balance Activity`, not the constant it sat above) are deleted.

**Record corrections: D2** seven overdrawn, not ten (six Huntington + one
Burke). **D3** the second cross-month example was not evidence — May 3152
prints no minus on its closing balance — struck and replaced with the three
genuine both-sides pairs, and the inconsistency recorded as a point against the
glyph rather than for it. **D12** the rejected design fails on five documents,
not four. **D5** the unswept 192 are now broken down in full. **D4** the
conformance module's own docstring carried an inherited off-by-one (`52` and
`54 × 53`) and now reads 55 and `55 × 54 = 2,970`. The guard-set proof reads
897, not the 852 measured on an intermediate tree.

**Zero outcome movement from any of this:** re-measured over the folder after
the two code fixes — 33 validated / 5 withheld / 3 review / 12 declined / 1
unmatched, 4,520 transactions, 33 sound / 0 unsound, identical to the
pre-review measurement.

### Two further carried findings from the review

12. **D8 — the fee-boundary residual, and a free oracle sitting unused.** The
    shipped split is located by the printed column totals alone. Where several
    fee rows share a date AND their amounts allow more than one cut, the
    parser refuses (uniqueness is required) — correct but blunt, because the
    document carries a second, independent signal that nothing consults: this
    issuer NAMES its waiver rows (`24-HOUR GRACE ... FEE WAIVER`,
    `TOTAL RELATIONSHIP SERVICE FEE WAIVE`). Measured over every fee row this
    cell publishes, the description signal and the totals-pinned split agree
    **157 of 157, zero disagreements** — and **25 of the 30 documents** with
    itemised fees have fee rows sharing a date, so this is the common shape
    rather than an exotic one. Consulting the descriptions as a corroborating
    check (never as the locator) would let the parser refuse a genuinely
    ambiguous split with evidence, and would catch a totals-pinned cut that is
    unique but wrong. Not done here: it is a widening, and the cell's rule is
    to publish only what the printed totals pin.
13. **D10 — the second-account guard keys on a heading.**
    `_LINE_OF_CREDIT_RE` matches the printed heading
    `Business Overdraft Protection Account Account:`. That is the heading this
    issuer uses for the product it sells today; another second-account product
    under a different heading would not be caught, and the deposit account
    would be published alone. The four surveyed documents all print this
    heading, and the failure mode is bounded by the fact that a second
    account's rows are not inside the deposit account's sections, so its money
    does not enter the ledger — the summary checks would have to pass by
    coincidence. Recorded because the guard's scope is narrower than its
    purpose.

## FT2. Mercury — the columns that print once per day, and the column that lies

`analysis/mercury.py`. 31 documents, 2,696 postings, one template across seven
account holders and two sponsor banks.

**Two columns print once per DAY, not once per row.** `End of Day Balance` is
exactly what it says: the last posting of a calendar day carries the balance,
every earlier posting of that day carries none. The Date column behaves the
same way, page breaks included — Mercury splits a day's postings over two pages
and does not reprint the date. A reader that expects both on every row either
drops the rows that lack them or hands the day's balance to the wrong posting.
Rows without a balance publish `running_balance=None`, which is the state
`reconcile` already accumulates across, and the day is inherited from the row
above.

**The Type column is not a direction column**, and this is the trap the cell
was warned about. Measured over all 2,696 postings:

| Type cell | rows | against the printed sign |
|---|---|---|
| a masked card number | 639 | no direction word at all; **27 are credits** (refunds) |
| `Credit Account Payment` | 120 | says "Credit", every one a **debit** |
| `Credit Cashback Deposit` | 118 | says "Credit", every one a **credit** |
| `Intl. Transaction Fee` | 155 | a fee — and **4 of them are credits** |
| `Wire` / `Wire Payment` | 28 | the same instrument in both directions |

**Direction comes from the sign printed on the amount, and from nothing else.**

**The column boundary is one glyph.** Mercury sets the Type column behind a
small icon from its own webfont, and that font maps its icons into the Unicode
Private Use Area. A PUA codepoint means nothing on its own — which is the
point: it is read as INK, not as a symbol, and it is the one mark of the
Description | Type boundary that survives PDF flattening. **2,696 of 2,696
posting rows carry exactly one, no row carries two, and no occurrence falls
anywhere outside the posting grid.** Four glyphs appear; the three that are not
the card icon agree with the printed sign on all 2,057 of their rows and the
card icon does not on 27 of its 639, so the icon is used as a BOUNDARY and
never as evidence about direction.

**The PUA glyphs are NOT the signs — a correction to intelligence relayed
mid-cell.** Ocean passed on a DECLINES-C finding that a platform can encode
`+`/`-`/`()` as private-use codepoints, that no cross-platform translation
table is possible, and that a reader mapping them must certify the mapping
against the document's arithmetic. Measured over all 31 Mercury statements and
their 3,453 printed amounts, the character immediately before a `$` is:

| what precedes the amount | count |
|---|---|
| `MINUS SIGN` U+2212 | 1,202 |
| `EN DASH` U+2013 | 687 |
| `HYPHEN-MINUS` U+002D | 13 |
| nothing at all (the credits) | 1,551 |
| **a PUA codepoint** | **0** |
| parenthesised negatives `(1,234.56)` | **0** |

Mercury's signs are ordinary Unicode dashes. Its PUA glyphs are a different
thing entirely: all 2,696 occurrences are followed by TEXT and never by an
amount, because they are the Type-column icon. And nothing matched Mercury
before this cell for the simplest reason — no Mercury parser existed; the
run's near-miss vector for these documents tops out at `chase_export:0.167`
and its `parser_declined` count for Mercury is 0.

The three ablations Ocean asked for are in the suite, aimed at what is
actually printed:

* **permuting the "in" and "out" icons** between two rows produces a
  BYTE-IDENTICAL payload — the strongest available statement that direction is
  never taken from the glyph, and the test that fails the day someone wires it
  in;
* **a PUA codepoint that appears nowhere in this archive** divides the columns
  exactly as Mercury's own does, so no mapping is assumed and no table is
  consulted;
* **dropping the minus from one debit** — the only change, row shape intact —
  leaves the grid readable and publishes NOTHING: the walk breaks and
  `average_daily_balance` is `None`, i.e. `withheld_adb`, while the intact
  document validates through the same path. That is the arithmetic certifying
  the sign, and it is what makes reading three different minus glyphs safe.

**Three glyphs for one minus.** The summary block prints `-$40,577.11` on 13
statements and `−$40,577.11` (U+2212) on 14 — the other 4 print no sign because
the figure is `$0.00`. The posting rows use U+2013 687 times and U+2212 1,202
times. Same generator, same issuer, consecutive months. The layout engine picks
a dash by WIDTH, not by meaning, and a reader that knows only ASCII hyphen
sign-flips whichever rows the typesetter set with another. `money.MINUS_GLYPHS`
is that finding, and all three are pinned.

**A month word in a merchant name does not open a row.** The Date cell holds a
day of *this* statement's period; a token resolving outside it stays part of
the description and the row continues the day above. The first draft consumed
the token and dropped it from the description even when it rejected it as a
date — an edit to what the bank printed — and a test caught it.

**A printed zero-activity period is a statement.** One savings statement prints
an opening and closing balance of `$0.00`, both totals `$0.00`, an empty grid
and a `Total $0.00` closing row. Admitted on the four negatives Ocean ruled for
Chase (A-prime) and applied in §SCOTIA-REBUILD F9, in the terms Mercury prints:
the grid must have been EMPTY rather than unread, both stated totals zero, and
the two balances printed and equal. Three ablations are pinned — rows printed
and none read, activity stated with no rows printed, and balances that moved
with nothing to move them — and each refuses.

## FT3. Found — the pending grid, and the fee that is already counted

`analysis/found_lead.py`. 15 documents, 2,474 settled postings.

**A pending item is not a posting.** The month-to-date document prints a
`Pending transactions` grid above the settled one and marks every row of it
unsettled by printing `--` in BOTH the Date and the Balance column. The issuer
states the rule in the same document: *"pending transactions are visible in
your account activity but not included as part of the total account balance"*.
28 such rows appear across the three documents; booking them would inflate the
ledger against the bank's own totals. They are excluded on the two printed
marks together, and the section heading is then required to agree — a row that
claims to be pending outside the pending grid means this reader has lost its
place. Both halves are pinned, and so is the half-nil row.

**The Fees line is a memo inside the debit total.** `beginning + credits -
debits` reproduces the printed ending balance **exactly on all 15**, with the
printed `Fees` figure already contained in `Purchases & other debits`.
Published as `stated_service_charge` for reporting and deliberately not
deducted a second time.

**The period comes from inside the balance labels.** Found prints its period
twice — once in a flattened header block (`February 1 to February 28, 2026`,
year on the end date only) and once inside the label of each summary balance
(`Beginning balance on February 1, 2026`), where each boundary carries its own
year. The statement is built from the labels; the header block is a free second
opinion and is what the registered integrity check reads.

**The account number is recovered by its GROUPING.** The header block flattens
into three label lines followed by three value lines, so no label stands beside
its value. Routing is `NNN NNN NNN` and the account is `NNNN NNNN NNNN` — two
different printed groupings, which is what tells them apart. `tables.
unique_line` then requires the value to be identical on every page: two
different values under one pattern is either a pattern catching something else
or more than one account in the PDF, and neither is a choice to make by taking
the first.

## FT4. The document that declines to be a statement

Found's month-to-date view carries one sentence the closed statement does not:

> The information in this document is not a bank statement and therefore should
> not be relied upon as a bank statement.

It appears on **3 of the 15** Found documents and on **none of the 12** closed
statements. That is not a partial-period judgement of ours; it is the
document's own declaration, and the registry already has the mechanism —
`chase_export` is `formal_statement=False` because a transaction export is not
a statement. `found_lead_activity` is registered the same way, with the
issuer's words as its note. The figures are still published: each of the three
carries a computed ADB, and `not_a_formal_statement` is the ONLY integrity flag
any of them raises.

**The boundary is the printed TITLE, and that is a correction.** This cell
first split the two registrations on a flat uppercased substring of the
disclaimer clause. Ocean's adversarial review proved that leaks in BOTH
directions, and the second one is unsafe:

* a closed statement that merely QUOTES the clause — a disclosure note, a
  quoted policy — was wrongly demoted to review; and
* the clause **split across a line wrap**, which is how the PDF actually breaks
  flowed body text, made a real month-to-date document invisible to the
  substring test: `found_lead` claimed it as `formal_statement=True` and the
  platform published it **`validated/approved` with no flag at all** — asserting
  a partial-period view was a closed bank statement, on a document that says
  otherwise in words it happened to wrap.

The title cannot wrap: it is a short generated line reprinted at the top of
every page. So `Account Statement` is now REQUIRED on `found_lead` with
`Activity (Month to Date)` EXCLUDING, and the reverse title REQUIRED on
`found_lead_activity`; the disclaimer stays as corroboration on the
month-to-date registration. The closed-statement registration therefore scores
a hard **0.0** on a month-to-date document before any other marker runs,
whatever its disclaimer looks like. Both leak directions are pinned, the
wrapped-clause fixture exactly as the reviewer built it, and a third pins that
a Found document printing NEITHER title is claimed by neither and fails closed.
No `supersedes` edge is needed and none is added — they are disjoint by
construction, and the conformance cross-product is what holds that.

The two registrations share this module and this reader, because the document
class changes how the platform REPORTS the result and not how the grid is
read.

## FT5. Brex — two columns in the summary, and a dash that means zero

`analysis/brex.py`. 6 documents, 157 postings.

**The summary is a two-column grid.** Every row prints `This Period` and
`Year-to-Date` side by side, so each figure appears twice with different
values, and a reader that takes "the money on the line" gets the year's number
for the month's statement. The printed column header `This Period Year-to-Date`
is what fixes which cell is which, and it is a REQUIRED marker: without it
there is no way to know, so the document is not this layout.

**A nil cell is a dash.** Brex prints `-` where a figure is zero — on
`Fees & Charges` in all six documents, and on `Beginning Account Balance` for
an account's first statement. Reading it as "absent" costs the statement its
opening balance, and `analysis.adb._resolve_opening` then derives the opening
from the closing balance, which makes `ledger_reconciles_to_closing` an
identity against itself. **That is the reconciliation-tautology class this
program has already closed once** (the scotia finding in batch 2), and it is
why the dash reads as zero here. The reading is corroborated by the documents
rather than assumed: on every statement that prints it, the printed
`beginning + additions + subtractions` reproduces the printed ending balance
exactly with the dash valued at zero, and on the `Fees & Charges` row the value
is independently known to be zero on all six.

**Two direction-declaring grids and no balance column.** Deposits and
withdrawals are printed as separate sections, each with its own column header
(`Date From Method Amount` / `Date To Method Amount`) and its own printed
total. The column header — not the section heading — is what re-declares the
grid after a page break, because Brex reprints the header and not the heading.
Direction still comes from the sign; the grid is an independent second
declaration, and a row whose sign disagrees with its grid is REPORTED as a
contradiction rather than resolved by preferring one of them. Zero such rows in
the six.

**A `Deposited checks` appendix re-prints deposits the grid already booked.**
One document ends with a headed section, no column header, listing two check
deposits a second time in a different phrasing and a different date format
(`02/25 Check from Rakuten $81.92` against the grid's `2/25 Rakuten Check`).
Booking them doubles $756.92 against the bank's own total; stepping over them
is the silent-drop defect this cell refuses everywhere else. Ocean's review
found that this parser was doing the second — a dated posting outside an open
grid was skipped here, where `mercury.py` and `found_lead.py` refuse. Now the
heading is recognised and **every appendix row is checked against the ledger**:
a row the grid never booked means a posting was dropped, and the document is
refused rather than published short. A dated posting outside both the grids and
the appendix is refused outright, which is the sibling convention.

**A long counterparty name wraps.** The date and the name occupy one physical
line and the Method and Amount land on the next. A row therefore opens at a
date and stays open until an amount closes it; a second date arriving while a
row is still open would attach this row's money to that row's counterparty, so
it refuses.

## FT6. No silent drops — and the rule caught this cell's own defects

All three parsers share one rule, stated once here because it is the cell's
main structural contribution:

> **A line carrying money inside an open grid is never stepped over.**

A dropped row is invisible to every arithmetic check downstream — the rows that
remain still sum to their own total, still walk to the closing balance, and
still reconcile — so a reader that quietly skips what it cannot parse produces
a document that passes every gate and is wrong. Where a line inside an open
grid ends in a money token and cannot be read as a posting, the document is
REFUSED. Page furniture (which carries no trailing money) closes the grid
normally, and the next page's column header reopens it. The converse is refused
too: a posting row found OUTSIDE an open grid means the reader lost its place.

The rule earned its place immediately. **Three defects in this cell's own code
were caught by its own tests and by self-review**, and a fourth item listed
here in the first draft was NOT a defect fix — Ocean's review caught the
overclaim, and it is corrected below:

1. A Mercury posting row with no Type mark closed the grid and was silently
   dropped, because nothing followed it to trigger the refusal.
2. A rejected date token was consumed and dropped from the description, so the
   published description was not what the bank printed.
3. `13/45/26` and `13/45` match Found's and Brex's date shapes perfectly and
   are not dates. Both were converted with a helper that RAISES, which escapes
   `parse` as a `ParserCrashError` in deterministic mode — the defect class
   `date_tokens.iso_or_none` exists to prevent and the one discovery hit on 17
   documents. Both now refuse.
4. **CORRECTED — the row-split change was a clarification, not a fix.** The
   first draft of this record claimed Mercury had been splitting rows at "the
   last money on the line" and that the mark-split repaired it. It did not:
   measured over nine ambiguous shapes, the earlier pattern (non-greedy body,
   `\s+` separator, mandatory mark check) produced the IDENTICAL split on
   every one — its `\s+` and the mark requirement already forced the correct
   reading. The mark-split makes the column boundary structural rather than
   emergent, which is worth having, but it fixed nothing and the fixture that
   claimed to pin the repair passes against the old pattern too. Its docstring
   now says so.

   **And the mark-split introduced two defects of its own**, both found by
   asking Ocean's question — does this really differ from what it replaced? —
   and both now fixed and pinned by fixtures that DO discriminate:

   * a row whose Description cell is EMPTY prints the mark straight after the
     date; the pattern demanded a non-space character there, so the engine
     backtracked and swallowed the DATE into the description, costing the row
     its posting day and moving an end-of-day balance onto the wrong date;
   * a row printing TWO icons left the first one **raw inside the published
     description** — a font-private codepoint in a financial field. The glyph
     is column furniture in every position and is now scrubbed in every
     position.

## FT7. The Rho document — L-1, fail closed, recorded

`Brex/a4a4064f_Jan Statement.pdf` is not Brex. It is a **Rho** (Under
Technologies Inc, DBA Rho Technologies, over Webster Bank) deposit statement,
and it holds **two accounts in one PDF**: two `Deposit Account Statement`
blocks, two account numbers (`******6928`, `******2073`), two summaries
(`Ending Balance $8,538.60` and `$0.00`) over one period.

That is the L-1 boundary — the extraction schema is single-account — and this
cell does not cross it. Nothing claims the document, it stays
`failed/no_parser_matched`, and the layout is recorded here so whoever takes
L-1 has a real specimen. Publishing the first account's figures as "the
statement" would be a wrong answer that reconciles, which is the failure mode
the platform exists to prevent.

## FT8. Carried findings and questions for Ocean

1. **THE ONE DECISION FOR OCEAN — `found_lead_activity` and
   `formal_statement`.** As shipped, Found's 3 month-to-date documents publish
   their figures and land in `review`, on the strength of the issuer's own
   printed sentence. They are instrumented sound: all three close their balance
   walk with zero breaks, reproduce both printed totals exactly, and pass every
   ADB validation. If Ocean rules that a month-to-date view with a complete
   printed summary and a stated period is a formal statement, the change is
   deleting three lines from the `_OVERRIDES` entry and the cell becomes
   **52 validated / 0 review**; no parse output moves either way. It is put
   here rather than decided because it is a reporting judgement about a
   document class, and `formal_statement=False` costs every document of that
   class its automatic approval.
2. **`ANALYSIS_STAGE_VERSION` needs a bump on merge, and this cell did not make
   it.** 52 documents change their analysis output, so every cached payload for
   them is stale; `webapp/artifact_cache.py` documents that a code change
   altering analysis output must bump the version in the same commit. The brief
   reserves the bump to Ocean, so `webapp/` is untouched here — flagged so it
   is not missed. Nothing outside `analysis/` was modified at all.
3. **`count_semantics` — all four registrations are correctly UNSURVEYED.**
   `analysis/count_semantics.py` is untouched, and none of the three issuers
   prints a per-direction instance count anywhere in the 52 documents
   (measured: 0). `stated_credit_count` and `stated_debit_count` are therefore
   `None` throughout, the stated-count check cannot fire, and a NEW
   registration absent from the semantics table emits nothing — the structural
   default, and correct. Deriving counts from the ledger would manufacture the
   oracle the platform checks itself against.
4. **The Mercury Type column is published inside the description, not as a
   field.** The schema has no column for it, so the published description is
   the printed row with the icon replaced by the space the columns already put
   there — `Mercury Credit Credit Account Payment` reads oddly and is exactly
   what the bank printed. A `Transaction.type` field is a schema change and not
   this cell's to make; recorded because a reader of the output will notice.
5. **A zero-amount posting would be published as a credit.** `direction` is
   `debit if amount < 0 else credit`, so a `$0.00` row lands on the credit
   side. Measured: zero such rows in the 2,696. It cannot affect any published
   figure (coverage is amount-based and none of these issuers prints a count),
   but it is the one place where the sign rule has no answer — and the icon
   glyph, which would distinguish them, is deliberately not consulted because
   it is wrong on 639 rows.
6. **FOLLOW-UP CARD — the Brex sign-vs-grid check re-parses the document.**
   `brex.printed_total_contradictions` calls `_postings` a second time to
   recover the per-row contradictions, because `IntegrityCheck` receives the
   `Statement` and the markdown but not the parser's working. It is correct and
   costs one extra parse on 6 documents. The general fix — letting a parser
   hand findings forward to its own integrity check — would benefit every
   registration that wants to report something it noticed while reading, and it
   is the same seam RC8.2's silent-row-drop counter needed.
7. **The archive is not the pinned corpus** (RC8.3, carried). Every census in
   this record covers the 3,506-document archive; the gate is what covers the
   other 109, and it is GREEN. No document of any of these three layouts exists
   in the pinned corpus, so the four registrations' only corpus-side coverage
   is `tests/test_parser_conformance.py` and `tests/test_fintech_layouts.py`.
8. **CORRECTION TO RELAYED INTELLIGENCE — Mercury does not encode signs as
   PUA.** The DECLINES-C finding is real and its method is the right one, but
   its premise does not transfer to Mercury: 0 of 3,453 amounts carry a PUA
   sign, there are 0 parenthesised negatives, and all 2,696 PUA occurrences sit
   at the Type-column boundary followed by text. Recorded here because a
   correction that lives only in a commit message is a correction that gets
   re-made. The METHOD was adopted in full — certify by the document's own
   arithmetic, assume no mapping, ablate — and the resulting tests are stronger
   for being aimed at the real shape (FT2).
9. **RESIDUAL — the Type|Amount boundary inside a row is still "last money".**
   The mark fixes the Description|Type boundary structurally, but within the
   tail that follows it the amount is still found as the money token that lets
   the rest of the line match. A Type cell containing money would therefore be
   mis-split. The surveyed Type vocabulary is words and masked card numbers
   only — 0 of 2,696 contain money — so it is unreachable today; recorded
   because the outer boundary's fix does not extend inward.
10. **RESIDUAL — the month-word date guard is a NARROWING, not a decision.**
   It rejects a leading month token that resolves outside the statement
   period. A merchant name opening with a month word that lands INSIDE the
   period ("May 15 Holdings" on a May statement) is still read as the date and
   would re-date the row. The balance walk and `posting_dates_cover_source`
   are what would catch it. The code comment claimed more than that until
   Ocean's review; it now states the real scope.
11. **`found_lead_activity`'s bank label names a document class, not a bank.**
   `by_bank_label("Lead Bank (Found) Month-to-Date Activity")` resolves to it,
   which is only reachable for a document no parser claimed whose LLM
   extraction named that exact string — effectively never. Giving both
   registrations the same label would instead make `by_bank_label` resolve
   deterministically to the lower `(band, id)`, which is `found_lead`, and is
   equally defensible. Recorded rather than churned.

## FT9. Proofs

All of these run on the merge commit itself, `42c4826` — re-run in full after Ocean's review conditions were applied, since those changed
production code in all three parsers.
# §UNID-PACK-A — three registrations out of the Unidentified folder: a balance that is the only oracle, a minus that is not ASCII, and a member statement that is several accounts

## UA0. Summary

Three new registrations, no shared ownership, sequenced independently.
**35 of the 45 archive documents in the three families move `failed` →
`validated`, zero documents move down, and every already-claimed document in
the archive is byte-identical.** The remaining 10 fail closed, each named
below with its diagnosis.

| family | archive docs | validated | fail closed |
|---|---|---|---|
| `woodforest` | 20 | **15** | 3 withheld + 2 declined |
| `wealthsimple` | 18 | **16** | 1 declined + 1 unclaimed void cheque |
| `symitar` | 7 | **4** | 3 declined (L-1) |

All 35 are instrumented per document rather than merely claimed: every stated
total the bank prints equals the published ledger, the balance walk closes on
the printed closing balance, and `continuity_breaks` is 0. **4,631
transactions** are published across the 35.

The expected result in the brief was ~41 claimed. It is 35, and the six-document
gap is not a defect in the readers — it is two facts about the documents that
the scout's prototype did not measure, both recorded in UA6:

* two Woodforest statements post the account's opening deposit **one day
  before the period the bank itself prints**, and the platform's ADB engine
  excludes out-of-period transactions;
* the Symitar family is **7 documents, not 8**, and three of them carry two
  genuinely ACTIVE deposit accounts, which the single-account extraction
  schema cannot represent (L-1).

## UA1. The instrument

Every figure below comes from replaying the archive markdown through the real
pipeline (`analyze_markdown` + `telemetry.record.classify_outcome` +
`discovery.runner._failure_reason`), resolved from the D-3 OCR artifact store
in the main checkout **by direct file path** — the sqlite index was never
opened. All 3,506 enumerated rows resolve to an artifact; there were zero
cache misses.

Before any production edit the harness was checked against the run of record
`88be9dd3`: over the 42 distinct CIBC-folder documents it reproduced the run's
`outcome_class` **42/42, 0 disagreements**. Those rows are cache-served and
carry no `parser_id`, so parser identity was enriched from the earlier runs as
the brief directs (2,093 distinct hashes carry a known `parser_id` across the
24 recorded runs).

### The scout's numbers, corrected by measurement

| family | scout | measured |
|---|---|---|
| Woodforest | 20 docs / 17 rec | 20 docs / **15** validated |
| Wealthsimple | 17 docs / 16 rec (+3 in the CIBC folder) | 18 distinct / **16** validated |
| Symitar CU | 8 docs / 8 rec | **7** docs / **4** validated |

**The three "parserless-validated" documents in the CIBC folder are not
Wealthsimple statements.** They are genuine `CIBC Account Statement`s that
print `INVESTMENT Wealthsimple Investments Inc.` as a payee, and they are
claimed and validated by the `cibc` registration — they showed no `parser_id`
in the run of record only because those rows were cache-served. They needed no
migration; what they needed was for the new registration not to steal them,
which is why `wealthsimple` requires the product line and the grid header and
not the issuer word. All 42 distinct CIBC-folder documents are byte-identical.

## UA2. `woodforest` — the running balance is the only sign oracle

The document prints a `Summary of Accounts` row that states the period's whole
arithmetic —

    BALANCE FORWARD - TOTAL DEBITS + TOTAL CREDITS = CLOSING BALANCE

— and it holds on all 17 documents whose summary block reads.

The posting grid heads `Date Credits Debits Balance Description`. Credits and
Debits are two ADJACENT columns and the text layer destroys which of the two a
magnitude stood in: every posting arrives as one bare number between the date
and the running balance. The description is not an oracle either — `POS DB`
and `POS CR` prefix some rows and not others, and plenty of rows carry
neither.

What the bank prints on every row is the balance AFTER the posting, so
direction is the movement between two printed balances and magnitude is the
printed cell — the standard `analysis/scotia.py` established and
`analysis/cibc.py` applies to the same problem. A row whose printed magnitude
contradicts that movement keeps a debit reading and the document then fails
the platform's ledger checks; the sign is never invented to make the
arithmetic close. The walk is seeded from `BALANCE FORWARD`, because this
layout prints no opening row inside the grid.

Measured before a line of production code was written, over all 20: the reader
reproduces **every one of the bank's own printed totals exactly** — credits,
debits and the closing balance — on all 17 readable documents, with zero rows
whose magnitude disagrees with the balance movement.

**A date opens a row only where the grid can print one.** The rule is the date
token followed by BOTH money cells in their printed order; a description does
not print two money cells that way, so `POS DB INVOICE 03-04 REF 000000001014568`
stays one row. Pinned.

### The fail-closed five

* **`e96144ab_Royalty2/3/4` — scrambled reading order (3).** These emit the
  cells of each row out of column order — description, balance, date, amount,
  and not even consistently — which cannot be reassembled from a linear text
  stream without the geometry the text layer threw away. Royalty3 and Royalty4
  decline outright (their summary block does not read); Royalty2's summary
  reads but all 16 rows the grid yields contradict the balance movement, so it
  is refused at `withheld_adb`. It is deliberately NOT declined by a
  "how many rows agree" threshold: that would be a tuned constant, and the
  platform's own oracles already refuse the document. The parser publishes what
  it reads and the ledger checks say no — the division of labour `cibc` uses.
* **`c183e584_Feb` and `fad3db75_document` — an opening deposit posted before
  the period (2).** Both are mid-cycle account openings: `BALANCE FORWARD` is
  0.00 and the first posting is dated the day BEFORE the printed
  `Statement Period` (02-10 for a Feb 11–28 statement; 01-23 for a Jan 24–31
  one). The bank's own `TOTAL CREDITS` includes it, and the bank's own Daily
  Closing Balance Summary prints a balance for that day. `analysis/adb.py`
  excludes out-of-period transactions, so the ledger cannot reconcile and both
  are withheld. Widening `period_start` to cover the row would invent a period
  the document does not state, so it was not done. See UA6.1.

Result: **15/15 validated documents instrument sound**, 1,794 transactions.

### What was measured and deliberately NOT published

`stated_average_balance` and `days_in_period` ARE published — both are printed
in the document's own `Account Summary` block. The bank's average and the
platform's ADB differ by a systematic sub-dollar amount on 13 of 15 documents
(and by 60.08 on one), which `analysis/adb.py` already has a designed warning
for; it is not a required check, so nothing is withheld by it.

`stated_daily_balances` is NOT published, and that was a measurement rather
than a preference. The Daily Closing Balance Summary is PARTIAL on most
documents (19 of 28 days, 23 of 30, …) — it prints only days with activity —
and on `fad3db75_document` it carries a date OUTSIDE the printed period, which
`adb.py` treats as an invalid snapshot. Anchoring on it also does not close the
sub-dollar gap: reproducing the bank's average from its own table succeeds on
exactly the two documents whose table is complete. Publishing it would add
risk and buy nothing.

## UA3. `wealthsimple` — a printed minus that is not ASCII, and a row that wraps

`Chequing monthly statement`, one account, `DATE POSTED DATE DESCRIPTION
AMOUNT (CAD) BALANCE (CAD)`.

**The sign glyph.** A withdrawal is set `–$403.00` with **U+2013 EN DASH**. The
family prints **no ASCII minus in its money at all**: a census of the whole
family finds 2,469 occurrences of U+2013 and every single one stands
immediately before an amount cell. The sign is therefore read as an explicit
class of printed sign glyphs (U+2013, U+2212, U+2014 and ASCII `-`) standing
immediately before the amount's currency symbol — the position is what makes
it this cell's sign rather than punctuation belonging to the description, and
the family prints dashes inside descriptions and addresses (`Co-op`,
`209 - 31 Rodenbush Drive`) that must not be read as signs. Both are pinned.
`analysis/money.py` is growing a shared sign-glyph class in a parallel cell
(MONEY-GRAMMAR); this reader deliberately does not depend on it. **Flagged for
Ocean's merge — see UA6.3.**

**The row closes on its Balance cell.** A row opens on the two printed dates
and ends at the amount/balance pair, which is its last column. Reading it that
way is what lets a long description wrap onto a later physical line — one
archive row does, and a line-at-a-time reader silently dropped it and broke the
walk — while the page-2 legal boilerplate printed after the final row is never
swallowed into it. A first version that closed rows only on the next date
opener made every document in the family fail; the balance-cell rule fixed all
18 at once.

**The date.** The layout prints two, and the document itself says which is
authoritative: *"Posted date is when the transaction is processed and
finalized. Use this for accounting purposes."* The posted date is published.
On two documents the two columns differ on 191 and 183 rows, so this is a real
choice and not a formality.

**The summary block prints its two labels before their two figures**
(`Your March summary MAR 1 BALANCE / MAR 31 BALANCE / $497.27 / $380.58`), so
the pairing is positional. Each label carries its own date, which is what lets
the parser CHECK the pairing against the printed period instead of assuming
it; a document whose labels do not match is declined. No totals and no counts
are printed, so every stated total and count stays `None`.

### `analysis/dates.py` — a dated balance label is not a posting row

Two documents were withheld for a reason untrue of them. `source_posting_dates`
read the summary's `AUG 31 BALANCE` as a posting row, so
`posting_dates_cover_source` failed on an activity day the statement never had.
The heuristic's own docstring says balance labels are excluded — but this
layout prints the label with the DATE as the label's own qualifier, so none of
the compound wordings in `_NOT_A_POSTING_ROW` ("closing balance", "opening
balance") ever forms. It bit only the two documents whose last day happens to
carry no posting.

The narrowing is structure-keyed — the whole remainder after the date is the
bare word, and there is no money on the line — and carries the same
direction-of-effect argument FIXUPS-1's `_SUMMARY_TOTAL_ROW` does: it can only
REMOVE dates from `source_posting_dates`, and the check is
`source_dates - parsed_dates`, so a document can go from failing to passing and
never the reverse. **Censused over all 3,380 distinct archive documents, the
shape occurs in exactly 17 — every one of them this family's, none claimed by
any other parser.**

Worth recording plainly: on this layout the check is now **vacuous, not
load-bearing**. Every posting row prints TWO dates, which the heuristic reads
as a balance grid rather than a posting, so it finds no source dates at all.
The label was the only date it ever saw, and it was the wrong one. Pinned.

Result: **16/16 validated documents instrument sound**, 2,486 transactions,
zero continuity breaks.

### The two that fail closed

* **`June_2025.pdf` — zero activity.** It prints the grid header, an opening
  and closing balance of $0.00, and no rows. It declines. Admitting it is the
  platform's zero-activity rule (ruled on for Chase as A-prime, applied in
  §SCOTIA-REBUILD S3.4) and is Ocean's to extend, not this parser's to assume —
  the same call §RBCCIBC RC8.5 made for the RBC zero-activity statement.
* **`void_cheque(1).pdf`** is a void cheque, not a statement:
  `no_parser_matched`.

## UA4. `symitar` — one PDF, several of a member's accounts

The document is a MEMBER statement: an `ACCOUNT SUMMARY` naming every account
the member holds, then one section per account, re-opened with `(Continued)`
after each page break. The parser's whole job is deciding which section is a
ledger this schema can carry, and three distinctions do it.

**A loan facility is not a deposit ledger.** The member's credit products are
printed in the same document under a different grid — `Date Amount Fees
Interest Principal Balance Description`, with its own payment and interest
columns. A section is read only when it prints the deposit grid. This matters
concretely: a first census that counted any dated money pair as a posting
found "4 active accounts" on every `fad663aa` document and would have blocked
all three; three of those four are loans.

**A dormant sibling is not a second ledger.** Members hold share/membership
accounts that print `No Transactions This Period` beside a beginning balance
equal to their ending balance. Failing the document closed because such an
account exists would refuse a perfectly readable statement, so dormant deposit
siblings are skipped.

**A second ACTIVE deposit account is a document this schema cannot carry.**
Three `5a75e912` documents hold a Free Business Checking account AND a Money
Market account that posts a real dividend deposit. Two deposit ledgers cannot
be represented (L-1), so those three are declined rather than published under
one account's name.

**The per-account oracle**, and both issues are read:

* the six-figure equation row — `Beginning Balance + Credits/Deposits +
  Dividends - Debits/Withdrawals = Ending Balance`, with YTD Dividends printed
  sixth — which states the account's whole arithmetic and holds on every
  document that prints it; and
* where none is printed, the account's own entry in the document's
  `ACCOUNT SUMMARY`, which states its ending balance.

Where the equation row and the grid's own opening row disagree, the document
contradicts itself and is declined. Dividends are credited to the account and
post as their own rows, so the stated credit total is the two credit columns
together — measured, not assumed.

Amount and balance are printed BEFORE the description in both issues and the
amount carries its own printed sign, so here the running balance is a
cross-check rather than the sign oracle it has to be on Woodforest.

Result: **4/4 validated documents instrument sound**, 351 transactions.

| document | accounts | active deposit | outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| `5a75e912_jan26` | 2 deposit | 2 (checking 207 rows, money market 1) | declined, L-1 |
| `5a75e912_feb26` | 2 deposit | 2 (135 / 1) | declined, L-1 |
| `5a75e912_april26` | 2 deposit | 2 (184 / 1) | declined, L-1 |
| `5a75e912_march26` | 2 deposit | 1 (181 rows; sibling dormant) | **validated** |
| `fad663aa_Apr 2026` | 3 deposit + 3 loan | 1 (64 rows) | **validated** |
| `fad663aa_May 2026` | 3 deposit + 3 loan | 1 (59 rows) | **validated** |
| `fad663aa_June 2026` | 3 deposit + 3 loan | 1 (47 rows) | **validated** |

## UA5. Scope, semantics and the wider probe

**Zero cross-claims.** The registry goes 53 → 56 and the conformance
cross-product is now 56 × 55 = 3,080 negative assertions, all passing. Two of
the three new fixtures exist specifically to pin a counterparty trap that is
real in this archive rather than hypothetical:

* another issuer's statement naming **Woodforest** in a payee line (there are
  two such documents in the archive, one in the Chase folder and one claimed
  by `navy_federal`, both already validated by their own parsers);
* a **CIBC** statement naming `INVESTMENT Wealthsimple Investments Inc.` as a
  payee (three such documents, all in the CIBC folder).

Neither reaches the new registration, because in both cases the institution
word is only one of three required markers and the other two are the
document's own printed column headers.

**The probe is the whole archive, not a sample.** The brief asks for a
stratified non-target probe of at least 400 documents; the before/after sweep
below covers all **3,380 distinct documents across all 68 folder labels**,
which is a superset of any stratified sample. Across it, the three new
registrations claim **exactly 44 documents — woodforest 20, wealthsimple 17,
symitar 7 — and not one document outside their own families.** No other
parser's claim set changes anywhere.

**`count_semantics` — nothing to review.** `analysis/count_semantics.py` is
untouched and no new registration emits a stated count: Woodforest prints two
totals with no instance count beside either, Wealthsimple prints no totals at
all, and Symitar's equation row prints figures rather than counts. All three
ids are therefore correctly UNSURVEYED and the stated-count check cannot fire
on them. Deriving counts from the ledger would manufacture the oracle the
platform checks the ledger against.

**Currency is set explicitly on all three** — `USD` for Woodforest and
Symitar, `CAD` for Wealthsimple, whose activity grid states it in both money
column headings. None of the three inherits the schema default, so none
repeats the `rbc` `currency="USD"` defect recorded in §RBCCIBC RC8.1.

## UA6. Carried findings and questions for Ocean

1. **FOLLOW-UP CARD — a mid-cycle opening deposit posted before the printed
   period.** Two Woodforest statements (`c183e584_Feb`, `fad3db75_document`)
   are fully readable — every printed total matches the published ledger
   exactly — and are withheld only because their single opening deposit is
   dated the day BEFORE the `Statement Period` the bank prints, while
   `analysis/adb.py` requires `transactions_within_period`. The document is
   internally consistent: the bank's own `TOTAL CREDITS` includes the row and
   its own daily balance table prints a balance for that day. This cell did
   NOT widen the period to cover the row — that would invent a period the
   document does not state — and did not move the row to a boundary day, which
   `adb.py` explicitly refuses to do. Whether the ADB engine should admit a
   pre-period opening posting when `BALANCE FORWARD` is 0.00 is a platform
   policy question and Ocean's to rule on, exactly as the zero-activity rule
   was. Two documents turn on it.
2. **The Symitar family is 7 documents, not 8, and 3 are L-1 blocked.** The
   brief's "8/8" is not reachable, and the family size is now measured over
   the whole archive rather than sampled: `symitar` claims exactly 7 documents
   in 3,380. Three of them carry two genuinely active deposit accounts (a
   checking account and a money market that posts a real dividend), which the
   single-account extraction schema cannot represent. They are declined, not
   mis-published. They are also a small, well-understood test case for L-1
   whenever it is scheduled: the sections, their per-account oracles and their
   boundaries are already parsed by `analysis/symitar.py`, so the remaining
   work is schema and packaging rather than reading.
3. **MERGE OVERLAP — the shared sign-glyph class.** `analysis/wealthsimple.py`
   defines its own `_SIGN_GLYPHS` (U+2013, U+2212, U+2014, ASCII `-`) and
   reads it positionally, immediately before the amount's currency symbol. The
   MONEY-GRAMMAR cell is landing a shared class for the same problem in
   `analysis/money.py`. The brief said not to depend on it and this reader does
   not, so the two are independent and cannot conflict at merge — but they ARE
   duplicate knowledge, and once MONEY-GRAMMAR is merged this parser should be
   moved onto the shared class in a follow-up that proves byte-identity over
   the 16 documents. Flagged so it is a deliberate decision rather than a
   forgotten duplicate.
4. **`analysis/dates.py` is shared, and this cell narrowed it.** The change is
   structure-keyed and can only shrink `source_posting_dates` — so
   `posting_dates_cover_source` can go from failing to passing and never the
   reverse. The shape it excludes was censused over all 3,380 distinct archive
   documents and occurs in exactly 17, every one of them Wealthsimple's, and
   the full sweep confirms no document outside the three families changed by a
   byte. It is nonetheless a shared module and the second cell in a row to
   narrow this one heuristic (FIXUPS-1 `8ec039e` was the first), which is
   itself worth noticing: the guard is tuned to be quiet and each new layout
   finds a new false positive in it. A layout-declared
   `SOURCE_POSTING_DATES_BEGIN` block already exists as the authoritative

   per row.** On the Wealthsimple grid the heuristic sees two date tokens on
   every posting line and classifies them as a balance grid, so after the
   narrowing it finds NO source dates at all and the check passes trivially.

   identity, not by this check. Recorded because a check that is quiet for a
   good reason and a check that is quiet because it cannot see anything look

6. **The detect-sweep budget is now the binding constraint on registry
   growth.** `test_detect_sweep_stays_affordable_for_the_discovery_run` FAILED
   on this cell's first corpus-marked run — the three new registrations each

# §CITI3-CELL — three registrations, and a folder label that was not evidence

## C0. Summary

Three new registrations on one ownership. **41 of the 45 documents in the
three archive folders move `failed` -> `validated`**, zero documents move
down, and no document outside the three families changes in any way.

| card | family | documents | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | Shopify Balance ledger (`shopify_balance`) | 16 | 16 failed | **16 validated** |
| B | CitiBusiness CHECKING ACTIVITY (`citibusiness`) | 14 | 14 failed | **14 validated** |
| C | Zions Bancorporation Statement of Accounts (`zions`) | 13 | 13 failed | **11 validated**, 2 withheld |
| — | not statements of these layouts | 2 | 2 failed | 2 fail closed, named |

All 41 are instrumented per document rather than merely claimed: the summary
identity closes, every stated TOTAL the bank prints equals the published
ledger, every printed COUNT equals the published count, and — on the two
families that print a running balance — the balance walk closes on every one
of 3,840 rows. **4,901 transactions** are published across the 41.

The scout's counts reproduced exactly (16 / 14 / 13, and rec 0 for the other
two), and **one of its identifications was wrong** — see C3.

## C1. The instrument, and what it was allowed to touch

Every figure below comes from replaying the archive markdown through the real
pipeline (`analyze_markdown` + `telemetry.record.classify_outcome` +
`discovery.runner._failure_reason`) on this branch, resolved from the D-3 OCR
artifact store **by direct file path** — the sqlite index was never opened.
Zero OCR cache misses across all 45 documents: 44 are served from the digital
partition and one is a cached NEGATIVE (a scan the digital tranche deferred).

Base of record: `d70efbe`. Before/after is measured against a clean export of
that tree (`git archive d70efbe`), not against memory.

## C2. Card A — the Shopify Balance ledger, and a folder label that was not evidence

The archive files these 16 under **Fifth Third Bank**, because the statement's
own disclosure says the money is held at "Evolve Bank & Trust and Fifth Third
Bank, Members FDIC". That is a folder label and a custodian, not an issuer:
nothing in the document is a Fifth Third statement. The registration is
written against the layout's own furniture — the `Shopify Balance` masthead,
the `Statement summary` block, `Transaction history`, and the grid's own
column header — and two negative fixtures pin the point: naming the partner
banks is neither necessary (a document without them is still claimed) nor
sufficient (a document with only them is not).

A third negative fixture pins the other direction: `SHOPIFY*` merchant rows
appear in other banks' ledgers throughout the archive, and a mention of the
word is not a Shopify statement.

**The layout destroys nothing.** Both date columns print in full, so no year
is inferred; the amount carries its own sign; a balance closes every row. The
work was in three places: bounding the grid so page furniture never lands in
a description, cutting rows at the printed date PAIR (a long description wraps
and its money cells arrive on the next physical line), and the account
question below.

### More than one account on one PDF

Twelve of the sixteen carry a **second account block**: its own masthead, its
own account number, and a summary printing `$0.00` for all four figures under
`No transactions during this period.`. The platform's schema holds one account
(L-1), so this could have been 4 claimed and 12 refused.

It is 16, and the argument is arithmetic rather than convenient. A block
printing zero opening, zero deposits, zero withdrawals, zero closing and no
rows contributes nothing to any published figure — consolidating it with the
funded account would change no number this platform emits. So publishing the
funded account alone is **exact**, not partial. That inertness is therefore
*asserted*, not assumed: `_inert` tests all four printed figures AND the row
count, and a document with two funded blocks returns None. Two fixtures pin
it, including the near-miss — a second block with a non-zero opening balance
but no rows still fails closed.

The `Totals` row the grid closes with reprints the period's net movement and
closing balance, so it is registered as an **integrity check** rather than
consumed silently, on the pattern `bmo` already uses for its second summary.

Result: **16/16 validated, 2,855 transactions**, balance walk closing on all
2,855.

### The shared date guard, narrowed once

Two of the sixteen were withheld at `withheld_adb` on
`posting_dates_cover_source`, and the document was right: the statement's last
posting was three weeks before the phantom "activity day". The cause is the
`Totals` row again. Where its label and column captions fill the line, the
bank's own date for that total prints ALONE on the line below, and the
money-proximity test in `analysis.dates.source_posting_dates` finds the
total's figures on the next line and counts it as a posting date. This is the
defect class `8ec039e` already fixed one line higher up.

The narrowing suppresses a bare date line only where the previous line
**opens** with `Total`/`Totals` and prints no money. It fires on **16 lines in
16 documents (0.5%) of the 3,400-document archive, all of them this one
wrapped row, all in this family**.

**Where that precision actually comes from — a correction to this cell's first
account of itself.** The anchor is not a structural guarantee; it is an
archive-measured property, and on its own it isolates almost nothing: **1,355
documents (39.9%) print a moneyless line opening with "Total", 2,333 such
lines in all**. What makes the rule precise is ADJACENCY — it is consulted
only from the bare-date branch, i.e. only when the very next line is nothing
but a date token. Anchor and adjacency together give the 16.

The anchor still earns its place, on the other axis. Unanchored, the same
adjacency test also swallows genuine posting dates: **41 further lines across
15 documents and 4 folder labels** (Bank of America, Citizens Bank, PNC Bank,
Unidentified), which are only **4 distinct printed shapes** — a merchant
called "Total Quality Logistics", the column headers `... FEES TOTAL*` and
`Date Description Total Items ...`, and a PNC sentence beginning "Note: The
total charge...". An earlier draft of this section reported that counterfactual
as "57 lines across 5 folder labels"; that number added the 16 lines the
shipped rule correctly catches to the 41 it prevents, and counted this
family's own folder as a fifth label. The qualitative argument is unchanged —
the anchor prevents real false suppressions — but the magnitude is 41 lines /
15 documents / 4 shapes / 4 labels.

**The known falsifier, stated rather than implied.** Because the rule cannot
be proven from structure, there is a shape it gets wrong: a posting row whose
DESCRIPTION opens with the word and prints no amount on its own line, directly
above a lone date (`Total Wine & More` / `06/09` / the amounts). Its date is
suppressed. No document in the surveyed archive prints it, and it is pinned as
a test so the boundary is visible.

What keeps that tolerable is the direction of effect, which matches the
existing `_SUMMARY_TOTAL_ROW` rule: it can only remove dates from
`source_posting_dates`, so a document can go from failing to passing but never
the reverse. The cost of being wrong is a coverage check quieter than it
should be, never a false validation.

These pins live in `tests/test_adb.py`, beside the other `source_posting_dates`
tests, rather than only in this cell's file: the rule belongs to a shared
module, and retiring one parser's tests must not silently drop its only
coverage.

**Recorded, not celebrated (C7.1).** Every posting row of this grid prints TWO
dates, and `_is_posting_row` classes any line with more than one date token as
a balance grid. So the coverage heuristic sees *nothing* on this layout: the
wrapped `Totals` line was the only line it could see, which is why suppressing
it was enough. A test pins that emptiness so the limitation is visible in the
suite rather than only in this paragraph. What holds this family honest is the
balance walk.

## C3. Card C — the scout named a division, and the family has two

The scout reported the Zions folder as "Zions Statement of Accounts (13,
rec 13): brands itself NSBank (Nevada State) — marker on the printed
branding." The first half is right and **the marker advice is wrong**.

Nine of the thirteen carry `WWW.NSBANK.COM`. The other four carry
`WWW.AMEGYBANK.COM`, `Amegy Bank - The "A" Bank` and `Amegy Bank of Texas`.
Both are divisions of **Zions Bancorporation, N.A.** printing one mainframe
layout under different trade names, and a marker on either brand would have
left the other four unclaimed — precisely the failure `rbc_french` had, where
a marker written for one product meant the registration saw none of the other.
The string "Nevada State Bank" appears in **none of the thirteen**; only the
URL does.

What all thirteen print is the corporate footer `A division of Zions
Bancorporation, N.A.`, the title `Statement of Accounts`, the
`SUMMARY OF ACCOUNT BALANCE(S)` block and the grid's own column legend. That
is the registration. Fixtures pin that both brands are claimed, that neither
trade name is required, and that the footer alone is not enough.

### The oracles, and the two that are traps

The layout is the most generous in this cell, and the module uses all of it:

* the summary grid's amounts and **instance counts**, read positionally
  against the printed column legend — never against a product name, because
  this bank renamed `BUSINESS GROWTH CHECKING` to `BUSINESS ELEVATE CHECKING`
  inside the archive's own date range and both spellings appear;
* `DEPOSITS/CREDITS` and `CHARGES/DEBITS`, whose rows print the sign their
  section implies. Measured: 162 deposit rows all positive, 899 charge rows
  all trailing-minus, **zero disagreements**. A row that disagreed with its
  own section would fail the document closed;
* `Number Of Days This Statement Period`, checked against the span the
  statement's own two dates describe. The period opens the day AFTER
  `Last Statement`, and the bank's day count is what proves that reading —
  32 for a Feb-27-to-Mar-31 statement, and it agrees on all 13;
* the `DAILY BALANCE` block, published as `stated_daily_balances`.

Two printed figures are deliberately NOT read.

**`CHECKS PROCESSED` is a register, not a section of postings.** Its cheques
have already posted in `CHARGES/DEBITS` — verified by count on every document
— so reading it would publish every cheque twice. This is the
double-publication class already closed once for BofA.

**`Total Items` is not the transaction count.** Measured across the family it
exceeds the summary's own counts by between 0 and 12, with no constant offset,
so it is not used as an oracle. What it does count is not established here
(C7.3).

Because the layout splits money out across TWO printed columns, the debit
TOTAL is the sum of both — and the debit COUNT covers the same two columns.
A count narrower than its own total is the defect §FIXUPS-1 corrected on
`first_community`, and the scopes are aligned here by construction.

Result: **11/13 validated, 1,061 transactions**, and the first family in this
cell whose printed counts are assigned: all 13 documents state a per-direction
count and all 26 equal the published count.

### `count_semantics` — surveyed at registration, and measured quiet

A new registration defaults to `UNSURVEYED`, which would leave these 26
printed counts assigned but never compared. They are surveyed instead, both
directions **comparable**, because the two sides are the same set by
construction: the printed count heads the very column whose rows the parser
publishes, and the parser refuses a row whose sign contradicts its section.
The debit direction is a two-category sum with the same shape as the
`wilson_muir` promotion already in the table, and carries that entry's
existing `multi_category_sum_proven_complete` scope label; the credit
direction carries the existing `whole_direction`. Neither introduces a new
label — an earlier draft coined `whole_direction_column` for the credit side,
which was a synonym for a concept the table had already named.

The equality pin in `tests/test_count_semantics.py` is what forced this to be
a deliberate edit rather than a silent one. Measured after wiring: **13/13
agree, 0 disagreements, 0 count-related integrity flags, and no outcome
moves** — the check is now load-bearing on a population where it previously
could not fire.

### The two that fail closed, and why they are not this parser's defect

`7b66e22e_..._7412-2025-11-28` and `e28d7ad3_..._0340-2026-04-30` are withheld
at `withheld_adb` on `posting_dates_cover_source`. **They are not claimed as
successes.** Both are false positives of the shared heuristic, and neither
phantom date comes from anything this parser reads:

* `...7412-2025-11-28`: the line `11/01 $0.00` — a single-column cell of the
  DAILY BALANCE block belonging to the **inert savings account**. It is missed
  by the two rules that filter the funded account's daily-balance grid: the
  section title is preceded by the layout's printed dotted rule, so
  `_DAILY_BALANCE_SECTION_START` (anchored, no leading dots) does not match
  it, and this block has only ONE cell on the line where the funded account's
  has three, so the "more than one date token" rule does not catch it either.
* `...0340-2026-04-30`: the continuation-page header
  `April 30, 2026 EARTH POWER A/C AND HEAT INC 5802990340`, which repeats the
  statement date. It occurs four times in that document.

Both were verified against the documents rather than assumed: neither has any
row on the date in question (zero occurrences of `04/30 04/30` and
`11/01 11/01` in any posting section), the ledger's last activity is 04/28 and
11/28, and the bank's own printed daily balances end at exactly the published
closing balances. Every other instrument on both documents is sound.

Fixing either needs a change to `analysis/dates.py` with a much wider blast
radius than card A's, and one of them — widening
`_DAILY_BALANCE_SECTION_START` — is **actively unsafe** without also
hardening `_DAILY_BALANCE_SECTION_END`, because a too-narrow END would let the
skip-mode swallow genuine posting rows on some other bank's layout and turn a
correctly-withheld document into a validated one. That is a false-validation
risk, so it was left undone rather than half-done. Carried as C7.2.

## C4. Card B — one printed grid, two flattenings, and a quoted amount

No CitiBusiness parser existed. The five printed columns are Date,
Description, Debits, Credits, Balance, and the text layer destroys the two
that decide direction: an amount arrives as a bare figure with no trace of
which money column it stood in.

**Direction is read from the arithmetic the bank printed**, the same way
`cibc` reads its three-column grid: the movement between two printed balances
IS the signed amount. A row whose printed magnitude disagrees with that
movement fails the document closed rather than being signed by guesswork, and
a fixture pins that a row whose description reads `ELECTRONIC CREDIT` is
published as a debit when the balances say so — the wording is not the column.

The family arrives in **two flattenings** of the same grid. One trails both
money cells at the end of the row; the other prints them immediately after the
transaction type and the rest of the description after them. The module reads
the invariant rather than either arrangement — after the Date column a row
prints exactly two cells, amount then balance, and the Description column is
whatever is printed around them — and both are pinned, and pinned to publish
the same ledger.

### What is a printed cell, and what is only quoted

Four rows across the family gave four money cells instead of two. Each is a
government EDI remittance advice quoting the payment amount twice inside the
description: `RMR*IV*DMSAHD-2605*AI*508497.83*508497.83*0.`. This is the
"tariff quoted inside a description" class from §RBCCIBC card A, in a
different alphabet. A printed cell stands in a column, so it begins a
whitespace-delimited token; a figure welded into a reference does not. With
that rule **all 985 rows of all 14 documents carry exactly two cells**.

### The average balance that belongs to another period

Every statement of this family prints `Average Daily Collected Balance` — and
it is not this period's. It sits inside a `SERVICE CHARGE SUMMARY` block whose
own printed span is the PREVIOUS analysis period: the April statement's block
reads `FROM MARCH 1, 2026 THRU MARCH 31, 2026`, the June statement's reads
`FROM APRIL 29, 2026 THRU MAY 31, 2026`. It is on all 14. Reading it into
`stated_average_balance` would report another period's average as this one's,
so it is never read, and a test pins the block's printed period against the
statement's so the trap is documented where someone would fall into it.

`Relationship Summary: Checking` reprints the ledger's closing balance at the
top of page 1 and is registered as an integrity check.

Result: **14/14 validated, 985 transactions.** The 14 are 13 distinct
statements: `e93c186f_April2026 2.pdf` and `e93c186f_April2026 BS.pdf` are
different PDF bytes whose admissible text is identical, so they are two
documents in the run's denominator and one statement in the world.

The 15th document in the folder is not a Citibank statement at all and stays
`no_parser_matched` — see C5.

## C5. The two documents that are not statements of these layouts

| document | what it is | disposition |
|---|---|---|
| `Citibank/4c5fd2c9_AxBusChk-July202026.pdf` | a browser print of the **American Express** Business Checking dashboard — page "1 of 5" of a 2-page capture, no statement period, no summary, and the "Available balance"/"Current balance" labels printed with no figures beside them | `no_parser_matched` |
| `Zions Bank/e28d7ad3_EP GROSS SALES JAN 2025 TO JUNE 2026_...pdf` | a scanned sales report, not a bank statement; the deterministic preflight returned no text and the result is a cached NEGATIVE in the digital partition | `failed` (deferred scan) |

Both match the scout's rec 0. Neither is recoverable by anything in this cell.

## C6. Scope, and the wider population

**Zero cross-claims.** The conformance cross-product is now 56 x 55 = 3,080
negative assertions and passes.

**The complete non-interference argument, by construction.** `resolve()` keeps
only registrations scoring at or above the claim threshold, so a new
registration can change another document only by CLAIMING it — or by making it
ambiguous, which is the same event. The sweep therefore records the whole
claim SET, not the winner, for every readable document in the archive under
both trees.

**Shared-module changes, censused rather than sampled.** `analysis/dates.py`
is the only shared file whose behaviour changed; its census is in C2.
`analysis/date_tokens.py` gains `iso_unique_in_period` — a new function with
no pre-existing caller, promoted because `citibusiness` and `zions` had
written the same helper byte-for-byte and
`tests/test_no_parser_helper_clones.py` caught it. That guard finding is
recorded here because it is the guard working, not a nuisance: the fix is a
leaf module that imports no parser, and the three families were re-instrumented
after it to prove the promotion behaviour-neutral.

Nothing outside `analysis/shopify_balance.py`, `analysis/citibusiness.py`,
`analysis/zions.py`, `analysis/dates.py`, `analysis/date_tokens.py`,
`analysis/count_semantics.py` and `analysis/parser_registry_entries.py` was
modified. `webapp/`, `ocr/`, `pipeline.py`, `reconcile.py`, `metrics.py` and
`adb.py` carry a zero-line diff against `d70efbe`.

**`ANALYSIS_STAGE_VERSION` needs a bump on merge and this cell did not make
it.** 41 documents change their analysis output, so every cached payload for
them is stale. The brief reserves the bump to Ocean, so `webapp/` is
untouched here — flagged so it is not missed.

## C7. Carried findings for Ocean

1. **The page-coverage heuristic is blind to a two-date posting grid.**
   `_is_posting_row` treats any line with more than one date token as a
   balance grid, so on the Shopify layout — where every posting row prints
   `Posted Date` and `Transaction Date` — `source_posting_dates` returns the
   empty set and `posting_dates_cover_source` is vacuously true on all 16.
   The check is not failing; it is not running. Pinned by a test. Widening it
   to read two-date grids would touch every registration and is not this
   cell's call.

2. **FOLLOW-UP CARD — two more false positives of the same heuristic, with
   the evidence attached.** They cost 2 Zions documents (C3). (a) A section
   title preceded by the layout's printed dotted rule is not matched by
   `_DAILY_BALANCE_SECTION_START`, whose pattern is anchored with no leading
   dots — but widening START without hardening
   `_DAILY_BALANCE_SECTION_END` (currently a short keyword list) risks the
   skip-mode swallowing genuine posting rows elsewhere, which would turn a
   correctly-withheld document into a validated one. (b) A continuation-page
   header that repeats the statement date reads as a posting row; extending
   the existing money-proximity lookahead to all lines does NOT fix it
   (measured — one of the four headers has a genuine posting row two lines
   below), so it needs a page-header notion the module does not have.

3. **`Total Items` on the Zions layout is unexplained.** It exceeds the sum of
   the summary's own three counts by 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 4, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 12
   across the thirteen. Not used, and worth knowing before anyone treats it as
   a count oracle.

4. **`shopify_balance` publishes the schema's default `currency="USD"`.** The
   layout prints no currency code anywhere. The evidence that these are US
   accounts is circumstantial but consistent (US addresses, `Members FDIC`,
   US partner banks), and the published value is correct for all 16. It is
   noted because Shopify Balance also exists outside the US, and the honest
   fix is to read a printed code — which this layout does not print — rather
   than to assert one. Same shape as RC8.1, without the live defect.

5. **The Zions bank label is the legal entity, not the division.** All 13
   publish `bank="Zions Bancorporation"`. The document's own branding is a
   division (Nevada State Bank / Amegy Bank) and there is no uniform printed
   spelling of it — nine print only a URL. Publishing the entity is what the
   documents actually evidence; if Ocean wants the division surfaced,
   `account_name` already carries the product and a second field would be the
   place, not a brand-name lookup table.

6. **A zero-amount CitiBusiness row is published as a debit.** One row in the
   family prints `0.00` with an unchanged balance. Direction follows the repo
   convention (`amount > 0` is a credit, else debit); it moves no total, and
   this layout prints no counts, so no oracle constrains it. Recorded because
   the convention is doing the choosing, not the document.

7. **`cibc._en_date` is a near-clone of the promoted
   `date_tokens.iso_unique_in_period`.** It resolves a bare `Mon D` token
   against the period in exactly the same way; only the month lookup differs,
   which is why the clone guard does not catch it. Folding it in would be a
   small cleanup, but it would move `cibc`'s code under a cell that has not
   re-proven the RBC/CIBC cohort, so it was left alone.
