      4133.75 + -337150.0 != 3983.75
```

A money pattern with no LEFT digit boundary reads a reference number's tail
as a thousands group: `...1337 150,00` matches `\d{1,3}( \d{3})*,\d{2}` as
`337 150,00`. A $337,150.00 debit invented out of a document number. With
`(?<!\d)` on the token — the digit-bound lesson the wave already learned in
§MONEY-GRAMMAR — **12 of 16 reconcile.**

### U4.3 The remaining 4 were a genuine ambiguity, and the document resolves it

```
04 07 'C/ACHAT 00105958482 PETRO-CANADA 13 100,00 2 399,30'
      2499.30 + -13100.0 != 2399.30
```

`PETRO-CANADA 13 100,00` is a $13,100.00 purchase if `13` is a thousands
group and a $100.00 purchase at store 13 if it is part of the merchant's
name. Both readings are well-formed French money and no grammar separates
them. **The bank's own printed running balance does:** 2499.30 − 100.00 =
2399.30. So the candidates are the token and each of its suffixes at a group
boundary, the movement the printed balances demand selects among them, and a
row that no reading fits refuses the document rather than publishing a guess.

**Correction, from Ocean's adversarial review (closure 1).** This section
first claimed "the readings are distinct numbers, so at most one can ever
fit". That is false, and the code asserted it: a group of zeroes makes two
readings the SAME number — `000 100,00` is 100.00 whether the leading group
is thousands or description — so two candidates fit, the `!= 1` guard fired,
and a row whose amount was never ambiguous was refused. Candidates are now
deduplicated **by value**, keeping the longest (the whole money cell); a
genuine ambiguity still yields two DIFFERENT numbers and still refuses unless
the balance picks one. Measured over the family: **0 of 2,905 rows need the
dedupe**, so this is a latent-correctness fix and moves nothing in the
archive — all 21 payloads are byte-identical across it. The zero-group shape
is now a fixture, and `_amount_from_chain` is unit-tested directly on all
four of its cases.

**How often the resolver is actually load-bearing.** Of the 2,905 published
rows, 604 carry a space-grouped amount that offers more than one distinct
reading, and on **6** of them the reading the balance selects is a suffix —
i.e. six rows in the family would be published with a wrong four- or
five-figure amount without it. Ocean's reviewer independently found the same
six.

This is not amount-from-balance. The printed amount is still read and still
has to match; that is what keeps the chain a check rather than a tautology
(a balance-derived amount would satisfy `previous + amount == balance` even
across a dropped row). **All 16 reconcile.**

### U4.4 The `MM JJ` collision, and where it actually bites

UB5 described the date pair colliding with a space-thousands amount. The
collision is real but not inside a single figure — a `\b`-bounded
`\d{2} \d{2}` cannot match inside `9 999,99`. It bites at the **seam between
two figures**: `... 2M7FINANCIALSOL 640,00 20 490,64 04 10 DPA ...` contains
`00 20`, a well-formed date pair lying across an amount and the balance
beside it. UB5's anchor is the fix and is what shipped: a row start requires
a **following capital**, because a real date pair is followed by the
description's first word and a false one by more digits.

### U4.5 The oracle, and what it is worth

The fee table prints a count AND a total for each direction — four figures,
none of them derived from anything this reader computes. All four are
checked; three-out-of-four is a refusal, and each is proven load-bearing by
ablation. On top of a zero-break balance chain, that is two independent
oracles per document.

And, unasked-for again, a third: the 16 are **three accounts in consecutive
monthly runs**, each period's closing balance opening the next, with no
discontinuity anywhere —

```
04-378-26   Jan..Jun 2026        2853.79 -> 1760.96 -> 1966.86 -> 4113.92 -> 1030.18 -> 3466.14 -> 993.00
66-576-21   Oct 2025..Mar 2026  -1372.08 -> -3771.99 -> -1757.53 -> -4723.81 -> -904.15 -> -1984.20 -> 29.93
02-145-29   Mar..Jun 2026        1503.80 -> 34624.43 -> 13314.79 -> 18224.66 -> 2952.30
```

### U4.6 What the registration asserts, and what it refuses to

`id = releve_facturation` names the printed furniture, not an issuer.
`Registration.bank = "Releve de Compte Statement Template"` names the
template, for the reason `community_section`'s label names a platform — and
it carries **no institution word and no folder-label substring**, because
`discovery.evidence.registered_bank_tokens` normalises it and matches folder
names by containment in either direction. A label containing "Unidentified"
would have reported the `Unidentified/` folder as a bank we support; that was
checked against all 69 folder labels before the label was chosen.

`Statement.bank` is `None` on every document. `currency` is `"CAD"`, read
from the product line `COMPTE : COMPTE COURANT CANADIEN` — the document's own
name for the account and the only currency evidence on the page, since the
column headers print a bare `($)`. A product line this reader cannot read is
a refusal, not a fallback to the schema default of `"USD"` (U7.2).

## U6. The two regex guards — which one is load-bearing (D1)

The first version of this section reported both guards as load-bearing, on
mutation counts taken before the dedupe of closure 1 existed. Ocean's review
called that out and it is wrong. Re-measured over the 16 real documents, on
the shipped tree:

```
both guards present              : 16 / 16 documents reconcile
without the money left boundary  : 16 / 16      <- defence-in-depth
without the following-capital    :  0 / 16      <- load-bearing
without either                   :  0 / 16
```

**`(?=[A-Z])` is the guard that carries the family.** Without the
following-capital anchor a row start is found inside the seam between two
figures and not one of the sixteen survives.

**`(?<!\d)` is defence-in-depth**, and only became so when
`_amount_from_chain` shipped: the resolver recovers the right figure from a
token the missing boundary misread, so removing the boundary now changes no
outcome. It is kept because preventing a wrong figure from reaching the
resolver is better than recovering from one, and because the resolver's
refusal branch is the only thing standing behind it.

That created a real gap, which Ocean's framing predicts and this cell closed:
after the dedupe, **the whole cell suite passed with the boundary removed** —
a guard nothing would notice being deleted. It now has its own unit test
against the pattern rather than against a downstream outcome.

Mutation, re-run on the shipped tree (38 cell tests):

```
remove (?<!\d) from the money token   :  1 of 38 fail   (its own pattern test)
remove (?=[A-Z]) from the row anchor  : 23 of 38 fail
```

The historical claim in U4.2 stands and is a different statement: in the
PRE-resolver prototype, the missing boundary is what made 10 of the 16 look
chain-broken.

this cell's file. **Ruling wanted.**

**U7.2 — `Statement.currency` defaults to `"USD"`, which is an assertion.**
For a schema field with a non-null default, "we did not read this" and "we

and declines a document whose product line it cannot read. Only that one
wording is archive-evidenced (16 of 16), so no `AMERICAIN` branch was

## S0. Summary

`analysis/first_farmers.py` already read this template, for one issuer, under
one product name. It is not that bank's layout: it is a **core processor's**,
and the archive prints it under **five** issuers in two printed issues — a
sectioned ledger and a running-balance one — over the same summary strip and
the same period line.

So it is registered once, on the **template's own furniture**, with the
**issuer read out of each document**, and the issuer-specific reader that came
first now supersedes it. That is §JHA-CELL's pattern applied one template over,
and this cell is the second instance of it rather than a new idea.

**39 documents print the template; 10 move `failed` → `validated`; nothing
moves down.** The card was scoped digital-first and that is how it paid: 9 of
the 10 are digital, and of the 15 scanned documents this reader could have
reached, 14 keep refusing — correctly, and each is named in S6.

| | before (run `d5c75ff6`) | after |
|---|---|---|
| validated | 6 | **16** |
| failed | 33 | **23** |
| withheld | 0 | 0 |
| review | 0 | 0 |

All 10 are instrumented per document rather than merely claimed: both printed
counts equal the published counts, both printed totals equal the published
totals, the summary's own identity closes, and the printed `DAILY BALANCE`
grid agrees with the walked ledger on every day, in both directions.
**625 transactions** published across the 10.

The 7 documents of the running-balance issue are **7/7 byte-identical**, and
the pinned corpus holds one of them.

## S1. The instrument

Every figure below comes from replaying the archive markdown through the real
pipeline (`analyze_markdown(parse_mode="deterministic", sheets=...)` +
`telemetry.record.classify_outcome`), resolved from the D-3 OCR artifact store
**by direct file path** — the sqlite index was never opened, and the archive
and the caches were never written to.

Population re-derived from the artifact STORE rather than from the run's rows,
which is §JHA J11.5's lesson taken as a starting condition instead of as a
correction: every one of the 6,773 OCR artifacts was read, its payload
envelope's own `input_sha256` taken as the document identity, and the longest
offline text kept. **3,396 distinct documents have offline text**, of which
3,367 are in the run of record `d5c75ff6` (3,380 distinct shas; the 13 without
are the `deferred_visual_ocr` documents) and **29 are in the store but outside
the run**. Base commit `ba13ec3`.

## S2. The cohort, characterized before any code was written

The scout's decisive signature was the period line

    TOTAL DAYS IN STATEMENT PERIOD mm/dd/yy THROUGH mm/dd/yy: N

and the measurement confirms it exactly:

| probe | documents, store-wide |
|---|---|
| the period line, with its dates | **39** |
| `LAST STATEMENT` **and** `THIS STATEMENT` | 152 |
| `AVG AVAILABLE BALANCE` | 39 |
| `TOTAL DAYS IN STATEMENT PERIOD`, label only | 61 |

The period line alone hits 39 documents and **every one is this platform: zero
near misses**. It is nonetheless registered as a CONJUNCTION with the two
summary-balance labels, because a single phrase is a claim about this archive
and a conjunction is a claim about the template — and because the
two-required-marker invariant (R4-3) exists for exactly that reason. Composed,
the pair reaches the same 39: nothing added, nothing lost. The period
statistic is registered as CORROBORATING rather than as a third requirement:
it is coextensive with the period line on this archive, and an issuer that
suppresses a statistic still prints the template.

Of the 39: **6 already claimed** (`first_farmers`, all validated), **1 claimed
and declined by `first_farmers` itself**, and **32 `failed`, every one
`no_parser_matched` with an EMPTY `attempted`.** Nothing had ever claimed them.

Printed issues: 32 sectioned, 7 running-balance. Classification: 21 scanned,
17 digital, 1 mixed. **Every document prints exactly ONE account**, so this
template costs nothing to L-1 — which is the one thing that makes it cheaper
than the first core-processor template, where L-1 cost 7 documents. Two scanned
documents read their masked account number two ways across pages (a different
number of `X`s, and in one of them a misread digit), which is OCR variance in
the mask rather than a second account; both refuse for other reasons and
neither publishes.

## S3. Reading the issuer out of the document

**This section is the post-review form of the read.** The first version was
defeated four ways by the adversarial review, and the record of what it got
wrong is in S11; what follows describes what the branch actually does.

| issuer evidence | coverage of the 39 |
|---|---|
| a name in the platform's INSTITUTION SLOT (below) | **14**, in 2 distinct spellings |
| a labelled domain (the §JHA rule) | 7 — all of them the running-balance issue |
| the wrapped-field arrangement, deliberately not read | 8 |
| anything at all, on the remaining 10 | **none** |

`Statement.bank` is `str | None` and the honest-unknown-issuer ruling of
2026-08-14 applies: 25 of the 39 publish no name. The arithmetic does not
depend on it, so an unnamed issuer costs a label rather than a document —
**9 of the 10 newly validated documents publish `bank=None`**, and the tenth
is `ADE55A5BADF4DE8C`.

**The institution slot.** The name is not "the text at the top of the page":
proximity is not a role, and the review published a program manager's banner
by putting one above a contact block. The slot is the field the template
itself reserves, bounded on BOTH sides by the template:

```
UNITED COMMUNITY (204) 000 00016 02 PAGE: 1
SOUTHSTATE BANK, N.A. 101 00031 O1 PAGE: 1
^ left edge: the line opens   ^ codes    ^ right edge: the platform's own field
```

Five guards, and it is worth being exact about which does the work, because
the first version of this section was wrong about that:

* the **scope** — only the masthead is read. This archive's ledgers print
  `amazon.com` and two other banks' names as counterparties, and §JHA's
  reviewer got `walmart.com` published as an issuer when a comparable scope
  slipped;
* the **contact block** corroborates, and **this is the guard that actually
  fires**: it is what declines all 25 unnamed documents. Measured, not assumed
  — the label rule below fires on ZERO archive documents;
* the **institution slot** binds the name to the ROLE. A banner with no
  routing codes and no `PAGE:` field after it is not in the slot;
* the **label rule** — ANY colon-terminated opening field is furniture, with no
  bound on its length and no exclusion of digits or hyphens. The review escaped
  all three of those bounds in the earlier form, one of them with
  `Return-Service-Requested`, which this template really does print in that
  slot as `Return Service Requested`. It reaches no archive document because
  the contact-block guard declines them first; it is there for the layout that
  carries a contact block AND opens on a label, which the review built;
* the **furniture rule** — a candidate made only of words this template prints
  as its own headings is the template talking about itself, so
  `STATEMENT OF ACCOUNT` in the slot yields nothing. The list is the
  TEMPLATE's vocabulary, not a list of banks: it names no institution, and a
  bank whose name contains one of those words still publishes, because the
  test is that EVERY word matches.

The **digit rule** ends the name where the routing codes begin, and a
standalone `&` is a name word — without it `FIRST FARMERS BANK & TRUST`
publishes as `FIRST FARMERS BANK`, which is not a shorter version of that name
but a different institution's.

**The read is ATTESTATION-SCOPED, and that costs two archive documents their
label.** The archive prints a second arrangement in which the header field
wraps and the rest of the first line is the issuer's address:

```
UNITED COMMUNITY (10( POB0X 2537
000 00010 02 PAGE: 1 ACCOUNT: XXXXXXXXXXX3311
```

The branch does not read it. There the template bounds the name on the left
only, and the archive's documents of that arrangement separate cleanly just
because OCR happened to put a digit in the first address token; the same rule
on `FIRST EXAMPLE BANK PO BOX 2537` publishes `FIRST EXAMPLE BANK PO BOX`.
A wrong name is worse than no name, so 8 documents — including the publisher
`E069F856CA1BECEC`, which an earlier form of this cell named — go unnamed.

Published as printed. Nothing is transformed, expanded or title-cased: turning
a printed masthead into a bank's legal name would be an invention.

**The boundary of the read, stated rather than left implicit.** A name printed
INSIDE the institution slot is published, whoever it belongs to. If a program
manager's name is what the document prints between the left edge of the page
and the routing codes, that is what the document says the institution is, and
separating a program manager from a bank there would take a list of
institutions — the hardcode this registration exists to avoid. Pinned as
`test_a_name_the_document_prints_in_the_institution_field_is_published`.

## S4. What a document has to prove, and what the archive did to it

Five printed figures and one printed grid, all of them, exactly. They are
independent printings of one period, so a dropped row, a duplicated row or a
mis-read amount breaks at least two:

1. the row count in each direction equals the printed count;
2. the row total in each direction equals the printed total;
3. `opening + credits - debits == closing`, the summary's own identity, checked
   in the parser where it is cheap and local (§JHA J9.8's card, taken up here);
4. every day in the printed `DAILY BALANCE` grid equals the walked end-of-day
   balance, **and** every day the ledger posts on appears in the grid.

A **sixth** printing is not used as a gate and is therefore free evidence: the
bank prints its own `AVERAGE BALANCE`, published as `stated_average_balance`,
and the platform's computed ADB is compared against it downstream. Over the 10:

```
computed ADB == printed AVERAGE BALANCE exactly : 7
                                differs by 0.01 : 2   (rounding convention)
                              differs by 524.14 : 1
```

The tenth is an account **opened during the period**: the opening balance is
`.00`, the first deposit lands on day 5, and the bank averages from the day the
account was funded while the platform averages over the period it printed. Our
figure is arithmetically right for the printed period; the disagreement is
visible precisely BECAUSE the bank's figure is published, and it is the same
initialization-event class Gustavo approved narrowly for another issuer. The
document validates either way; nothing here depends on the resolution.

## S5. Look-alike glyphs, refused rather than absorbed

The card named one document carrying a Cyrillic `U+0415` inside `DATE`.
Measured, **8 of the 39 carry Cyrillic look-alikes** — 7 in a column header,
one in the transaction descriptions and cheque serials of the same document.
And the scanned issues carry a second, commoner substitution: a leading zero
read as a lower-case letter inside the DATE column.

Both are guarded structurally rather than repaired, and the guard is two
things, each load-bearing:

* every date and money token is matched with an explicit ASCII digit class.
  `\d` is Unicode-aware in Python and admits digits from other scripts, and a
  money grammar that reads a look-alike as a digit publishes a figure the bank
  never printed;
* every token must begin at a boundary that is not a letter, a digit, a dot or
  a slash. Without it a corrupted date matches ONE CHARACTER IN, as a
  single-digit month, and the row is published on a day the bank never printed.
  This is not hypothetical: the scout's prototype did exactly that on one
  archive document, absorbing a corrupted date in the deposit grid while
  dropping the identically-corrupted row in the debit section — the same
  corruption read two ways in one document.

With the boundary the corrupted row is invisible instead, and the count check
refuses the document. That is the honest outcome for a scan we cannot read,
and it is why the scanned population stays refused.

| `9AACD0850F64A893` | 26c/23d | 27c/24d | one credit and one debit, both dated `o2/11` |
| `9FD4C16EA7364D5F` | 12c/78d | 18c/101d | counts, both directions |
| `DCF3A85ECE6CB67F` | 8c/54d | 15c/87d | counts, both directions |

Two of these are worth naming apart. `95246AAF1A2D7F59` reads **416 credits
and 85 debits, exactly as printed, and still refuses**: one amount was scanned
wrong by 640.00 and only the TOTAL can see it. That is the case a count check
is structurally blind to, and it is why the totals are gates rather than
corroboration. `9AACD0850F64A893` is the whole scanned class in one document:
two rows carry a corrupted date where the bank printed a valid one, and both
are invisible to a grammar that will not start a date inside a token.

**The 15th scanned document publishes.** `ADE55A5BADF4DE8C` is 20 pages,
434 credits and 101 debits, and it satisfies every printing this template
carries:

```
printed 434 CREDITS 223,094.68        read 434 credits, 223,094.68
printed 101 DEBITS  214,299.18        read 101 debits,  214,299.18
printed LAST STATEMENT   55,763.38    + 223,094.68 - 214,299.18
printed THIS STATEMENT   64,558.88    = 64,558.88            identity closes
printed DAILY BALANCE, 21 days        every day equals the walked balance,
                                      and the ledger posts on no other day
printed AVERAGE BALANCE  35,931.75    computed ADB 35,931.75
printed MINIMUM BALANCE   8,344.23    the grid's lowest day, 06/05  8,344.23
```

**Seven printings, of which FIVE are independent and two are derived.** The
distinction matters and the first version of this section did not draw it:

* independent — both counts, both totals, and the `DAILY BALANCE` grid. Each
  is a separate thing the bank printed about the period;
* derived — the summary identity is a function of the four summary figures
  already checked, and the printed `AVERAGE BALANCE` is a function of the grid
  already matched. They corroborate the SUMMARY's internal consistency; they
  add no independent evidence about the ledger. (`MINIMUM BALANCE` agreeing
  with the grid's lowest day is a third derived one.)

**And the gate set has a blind spot, named here rather than left to be
found.** Move value between two rows that share a date AND a direction, and
every one of the five independent printings still holds: the counts do not
change, the totals do not change, and no end-of-day balance moves. The review
demonstrated it with a two-byte edit, and
`test_the_gates_are_blind_to_a_same_day_same_direction_redistribution` now pins
it as a known limit.

**This does not weaken the publication, and the reason is specific.** A
same-day same-direction redistribution that preserves both sums is the
signature of a FORGERY. OCR corruption is not compensating: it drops a row or
mangles a digit, which breaks a count or a total — and does, on all 14 of the
archive's refusing scans, including the one where a single amount is wrong by
640.00 with both counts exactly right. No printing this template carries can
separate a forged ledger from an honest one, and claiming otherwise would be
the overstatement this record exists to avoid.

The card's expectation was that the scanned
population refuses; the measurement is that 14 of 15 do, and the one that does
not is corroborated seven ways. It is put to Ocean as a measurement rather than
smuggled in as a rounding of the card (S9.1).

## S7. Non-interference, measured over the whole store

Detection is the entire risk surface for a document outside the cohort — a new
registration can only change another document's dispatch by claiming it — so
the sweep is total: **all 3,396 documents with offline text, before and
after.**

Two different things are measured here and the first version of this section
ran them together. **Detection** says who CLAIMS a document; **dispatch** says
what the document RESOLVES to, which is not the same, because a registration
that detects a document and then declines it leaves it `unclaimed`. The table
below is the dispatch one — `pr.resolve` over the markdown the pipeline itself
builds, page separators included, which is also what makes it comparable with
S0.

```
DISPATCH OUTCOME transitions
   2477  claimed   -> claimed
    909  unclaimed -> unclaimed
     10  unclaimed -> claimed

ambiguous, after : 0      ambiguous, before : 0
```

```
DETECTION, the other measurement
core_processor_sectioned detects     : 39
the measured template cohort         : 39
   detected but OUTSIDE the cohort   : 0
   in the cohort but NOT detected    : 0
claimant set changed                 : 39, and no other document
winning parser changed               : 0
near-miss vector, one required marker: 113 documents at score 0.125
```

**32 documents are newly DETECTED and 10 newly CLAIMED.** The other 22 are
detected, attempted and declined — they are the refusals of S6, and their
`attempted` vector now reads `('core_processor_sectioned',)` where before this
cell it was empty. That is the visible form of a fail-closed refusal and it is
the intended outcome, not a shortfall.

The 7 documents whose claimant set grew are the running-balance issue, and
their WINNER did not change: `first_farmers` outranks the new registration on
every one.

The before-side of the dispatch table is derived rather than re-swept, and the
licence for that is the detection sweep above: `resolve` is a pure function of
the claimant set and the supersedes graph, so a document whose claimant set is
byte-identical before and after cannot change outcome. Only the 39 changed
claimants; the other 3,357 are carried across unchanged, and the 39 are taken
from the base run document by document.

Sibling population, replayed through the real pipeline:

```
first_farmers payloads byte-identical : 7 / 7
payload changed 0    moved UP 0    moved DOWN 0
```

Detect-sweep cost, measured the §JHA J11.3 way (300 sampled archive documents,
one process, best of three):

```
68 other registrations        21.113s
core_processor_sectioned       0.169s   share 0.8%   0.565 ms/document
projected over 3,396 documents 1.92s
```

The normalization is registry data (`detection_text`, one upper-casing per
document rather than one per marker), the period line is a compiled pattern
and the other two markers are substring probes.

## S8. The supersedes edge, proven rather than asserted

The edge is mandatory and the counterfactual says so in one line. With
`first_farmers.supersedes` emptied and nothing else changed:

```
433B622CF3C07FE5  ambiguous  candidates=['core_processor_sectioned','first_farmers']
4FD3B1A8A71D58BA  ambiguous  candidates=['core_processor_sectioned','first_farmers']
58CB0DCC7460A445  ambiguous  candidates=['core_processor_sectioned','first_farmers']
8035EE1A5453C75D  ambiguous  candidates=['core_processor_sectioned','first_farmers']
8F755C593D63C6C5  ambiguous  candidates=['core_processor_sectioned','first_farmers']
9CCB4FB2BB2F8F27  ambiguous  candidates=['core_processor_sectioned','first_farmers']
B60DDD2DBC06A151  ambiguous  candidates=['core_processor_sectioned','first_farmers']
```

Six of those seven are validated today. Without the edge all seven resolve
`ambiguous` and go to review — a six-document regression from a registration
that publishes ten.

The edge is safe in the STRONG sense rather than the observed one:
`first_farmers` identifies its issuer by a tele-banking domain and a product
name that the general reader does not consult at all, so the general reader can
never shadow it and it can never reach an issuer it was not registered for. And
the general reader declines the running-balance issue at `parse`, so the edge
cannot strand a document either.

## S9. Carried findings and questions for Ocean

**S9.1 — the card said the 15 scanned members must keep refusing; 14 do, and
the 15th is the one the card also named as a publisher.** The handoff states
both things (§Evidence bullets 5 and 7), and the measurement resolves them the
only way the evidence allows: `ADE55A5BADF4DE8C` clears all five printed gates,
the two-directional grid walk, and the bank's own printed average to the cent.
**Ruling wanted:** publish it (this branch), or hold the whole scanned
classification back and lose it.

**S9.2 — the ledger's last section runs to the end of the document.** The
`DAILY BALANCE` grid is the last section the template prints, and nothing marks
where it stops, so the disclosures below it are inside its block. No archive
document prints a dated amount there — measured over all 39 — but one that did
would add a phantom grid day and the document would REFUSE. Fail-closed, and
carded rather than patched, because every candidate boundary measured here (the
column header, a line anchor) also lost real sections on the scanned issues.

**S9.3 — the section split is case-sensitive, and it is load-bearing on the
SUMMARY path, not the ledger path.** The first version of this entry claimed
the case-sensitive scan was what kept lower-case prose out of the ledger. It is
not. `parse` looks its blocks up by the template's exact UPPER-CASE names, so a
scan that matched `deposits` would file the prose under a key nothing reads and
no row would come of it — that key lookup is the ledger's guard, and
`test_on_the_ledger_path_the_exact_uppercase_key_is_what_holds_prose_out`
proves it by taking the case-sensitivity away and watching the ledger not move.

Where case-sensitivity IS load-bearing is `_summary_region`, which cuts the
summary strip at the first section heading after the account heading: a
lower-case section word in prose printed between the two ends the region before
the strip begins, and the document publishes nothing. Thirteen of the 39 print
such prose (the funds-availability notice says `deposits`; the interest
disclosure says `average daily balance`). Both guards are now pinned, each
where it actually acts.

**S9.4 — `count_semantics` is deliberately not extended.** This registration
gates on the printed counts, so a `comparable` entry would make the
stated-count check a tautology on it — the same disclosure §JHA J9.1 made for
three other ids. The table's default is UNSURVEYED and therefore silent, which
is the correct outcome and needs no entry. Recorded so the absence is a
decision.

**S9.5 — one issuer's digital statements are unreadable without geometry.**
Seven documents (S6, second group) print their summary strip in column order,
so the labels and the figures they belong to are on different lines. Their
ledgers are perfectly readable; only the summary is lost. A real customer for
the geometry rung, and the largest single block of remaining value on this
template.

**S9.6 — `stated_daily_balances` is now populated by this reader.** The printed
grid is published as source evidence, which is what the field is for. It is
also an ADB input, so it is named here rather than left to be discovered: the
10 documents' ADB figures in S4 are computed WITH it.

**S9.7 — the account-opening average.** One publisher's printed
`AVERAGE BALANCE` divides by the days since the account was funded rather than
by the printed period. Same class as the Woodforest initialization-event card,
one document, no gate depends on it.

**S9.9 — the recall follow-up: 22 documents print the period LABEL and not the
line.** Measured over the store, outside the 39: 22 documents print
`Total days in statement period` WITHOUT the `mm/dd/yy THROUGH mm/dd/yy` dates
this registration requires — the period is printed as a bare day count. 19 are
`failed`, 3 are `validated` by other means; 18 digital, 4 scanned. **20 of the
22 also print both summary-balance labels** and 15 print at least one of this
template's exact upper-case section headings (12 `DAILY BALANCE`, 2 with
`CHECKS`, 1 `CHECKS` alone). They sit in four folders — Enterprise Bank &
Trust 8, City Bank 5, El Dorado Savings Bank 5, Unidentified 3, plus 1 — so
they are a related PRINTED VARIANT of this platform rather than a different
platform.

This cell did not widen to them, deliberately: the dated period line is what
makes the current marker pair exact at 39/39 with zero near misses, and the
undated variant would need its own period grammar and its own measurement.
**Carded as the recall follow-up for this template — the largest named block
of remaining value on it, ahead of the 7 geometry documents in S9.5.**

**S9.8 — the detect budget is spent, on base.** The affordability test fails
at 68 registrations before this cell exists (348 ms against a 250 ms bound,
load-controlled). This branch adds 12 ms of that. It is named here because
§JHA recorded the budget as HELD at 68 and this is the entry that says it no
longer is — the structural fix belongs to the DETECT-BUDGET cell, not to a
parser card, and no card should raise the constant to get itself green.

### U6b. The ASCII fast path

`_fold` is a per-character Python loop and a registry sweep runs it over
every discovery document. NFKD is the identity on ASCII and no ASCII
character combines, so the fold there is exactly `.upper()`, and
`str.isascii` — a C-level flag check — is what says so. Applied AFTER the
sign and mojibake normalizations, which are the only steps that could
introduce a non-ASCII character. Equivalence is pinned as a test and was
measured identical on all 196 probe documents.

## U10. Closures from Ocean's adversarial review (verdict: SHIP)

The reviewer attacked the split resolver directly and it held — six live
suffix-rows in 2,905, every failure a refusal — and re-derived `desjardins`
6/6 and the 110 byte-identical on their own sweep. Five closures were
required and all five are in this branch. Closure 1 is in U4.3, closure 5's
D1 is in U6; the rest are here.

**D2 — a zero-movement row's direction is the balance's, not the column's,
and the docstring said otherwise.** `_transactions` derives direction from
`new_balance >= balance`, so a zero-amount row is always a CREDIT, while
`_oracle_disagrees` claimed to count "the column the row was printed in" —
the rule `reconcile` and `count_semantics` actually use. Worse, the test
named for the property only exercised the credit case and so passed for the
wrong reason.

Fixed by stating the rule as implemented rather than by inventing a column:
`DÉBIT ($)` and `CRÉDIT ($)` are two columns on the page and one string in
flattened text, so the column is not recoverable, and **deriving the zero
row's direction from the fee table was considered and rejected** — assigning
the row to whichever side the printed counts need would let the count check
supply the value it then verifies, which is the tautology
`count_semantics` exists to disclose. The consequence is now named: where the
bank counted such a row as a DEBIT, both printed counts disagree and **the
document is refused**. Fail-closed, and pinned in BOTH fee-table directions
(the credit case publishes, the debit case refuses). Measured: **0 of the
2,905 rows in this family carry a zero amount**, so nothing is lost today.

**D3 — six of the 16 will read as `label_unmatched` in the folder-agreement
rollup, and that is correct.** They sit in `Desjardins/`; the parser is
`releve_facturation` and `Statement.bank` is `None`, so neither candidate
label matches the folder and `folder_agreement` returns `label_unmatched`.
The other ten are in `Unidentified/`, which is in the function's own exempt
set, and land in `unlabelled_folder`. The U3 table originally claimed all 21
were exempt; that was wrong and is corrected above.

**This bucket must not be "fixed".** The obvious way to make six
disagreements disappear is to name the registration after the folder it is
filed under — which is precisely what §U4.1's evidence forbids, and what
`tests/test_parser_detection_markers.py` exists to prevent. The rollup is
reporting a true fact: six statements are filed under a bank name that
appears nowhere in them. A `label_unmatched` entry here is the honest
outcome, not a regression, and it should be read the way §J9.5 asks the
`community_section` entries to be read.

**D4 — the five `community_section` movers publish `currency='USD'` with no
printed evidence.** They take the schema default (`analysis/schema.py`:
`currency: str = "USD"`), because for a non-null default "we did not read
this" and "we read USD" are the same value. That is the exact assertion card
2 refuses to make one file away: `releve_facturation` publishes CAD only from
the printed product line and declines a document whose product line it cannot
read. The asymmetry is recorded rather than resolved — it is pre-existing on
all 110 documents of that template, not this cell's to change, and the fix is
a platform decision about whether `currency` should be nullable. **Joins the
currency-evidence platform card**, alongside the `rbc` `currency='USD'`
ceremony already on Gustavo's reserved list; it is the same class of question.

**D5 — a note for the next editor of the masthead scope**, written into
`_masthead_lines`. The masthead is the top of the document, which is also
where the OCR layer's `<!-- source: <filename> ... -->` comment sits, and
`_ISSUER_RE` would read a domain out of a filename like
`Visit bankname.com statement.pdf`. Nothing is wrong today: every production
path reaches a parser through `analyze_markdown`, which applies
`admissible_text` at its single parse seam (W3 FILENAME-BOUNDARY). The point
of the note is that this function's safety is guaranteed ELSEWHERE, so a
direct call with raw markdown is outside it, and widening either the scope or
the label widens that exposure.

**Records corrected.** The detector profile is restated in U8 with both
measurements rather than only this cell's. The mutation denominators are 38,
not 30. The D1 narrative is rewritten in U6.
FAILED tests/test_parser_parity.py::test_detect_sweep_stays_affordable_for_the_discovery_run
1 failed, 13 passed, 3894 deselected in 1871.08s          exit 1
```

Three of these tests exist only because the first pass of this check found the
mutant surviving — the uniqueness rule, the case-sensitive section split and
the zero-count rule were covered only by their neighbours until the mutation
run said so. **And the mutation check is not sufficient on its own: it kills
mutants of the code that exists, and every one of the issuer defects in
S11 was a hole in the code's SHAPE, which no mutant of that shape can find.
The adversarial review found all five. That is the lesson worth carrying, not
the 22.**

## S11. Amendments from adversarial review

Verdict SHIP, with three closures. The review reproduced +10/0, ambiguous 0/0,
the supersedes counterfactual line for line, and all 29 refusals including the
640.00 total-only case. What it also did was defeat the issuer read five ways
and catch four claims in this record that were wrong.

**S11.1 — the issuer read published a non-issuer five ways, and is now
structurally scoped.** Every construction below carries the platform's contact
block, so corroboration could not be what refused them, and every one is now
fixtured in `tests/test_core_processor_sectioned.py`:

| the review's construction | why the old read published it | what refuses it now |
|---|---|---|
| a program manager's banner above a contact block | proximity was read as a role | the INSTITUTION SLOT: no routing codes, no `PAGE:` field, no name |
| a label over 31 characters | the LABEL rule was length-bounded | the bound is gone — any colon-terminated opening field is furniture |
| a label carrying a digit | the rule's class excluded digits | the class is `[^:]*` |
| `Return-Service-Requested:` | the class excluded hyphens | same — and this template really prints that phrase in that slot |
| `FIRST NATIONAL BANK` over `OF EXAMPLETOWN` | the name was taken from one line | a continuation line under the slot refuses the whole read |
| `STATEMENT OF ACCOUNT` in the slot | nothing said furniture is not a name | the FURNITURE rule: every word is template vocabulary |
| `FIRST FARMERS BANK & TRUST` | a standalone `&` ended the name | `&` is a name word |

The deepest change is the last one in the list of guards rather than the
table: the read is now **attestation-scoped**. It reads only the arrangement in
which the template bounds the name on BOTH sides, and it declines the wrapped-
field arrangement that the archive prints 8 times — because those 8 separate
cleanly only by an OCR accident, and the same rule on a plainer address
publishes `FIRST EXAMPLE BANK PO BOX`. **The cost is measured: named issuers
fall from 23 to 14, and one of the ten publishers (`E069F856CA1BECEC`) loses
the label the pre-review branch gave it. No document's figures change.**

# §SCANC — the four-way partitioned summary, and why the counts are the check

## SC0. Summary

A core processor's statement template whose summary does not merely total the
period, it **partitions** it:

```
  PREVIOUS BALANCE      b0
+ N CREDITS       C          rows the bank counted as deposits
- M DEBITS        D          rows the bank counted as withdrawals
- SERVICE CHARGES S          rows the bank did NOT count
+ INTEREST PAID   I          rows the bank did NOT count
  ENDING BALANCE  b1         and b0 + C - D - S + I == b1
```

with two-column `Date Amount Description` grids under `Deposits and Other
Credits` / `Checks` / `Other Debits`, and a `Balance By Date` grid that walks
the period day by day. What the reader must reproduce is SIX printed
figures - a count, a total and an uncounted lump on each side - plus the daily
walk, and it publishes nothing unless every one of them holds.

**The balance identity is a fail-fast, not a seventh constraint.** Ocean's
review is right and the earlier wording here was double-counting. Once the
partition holds on both sides the captured rows come to `C + I` and `D + S`,
and once the walk holds the running balance carries `b0` to `b1` over exactly
those rows - so `b0 + C - D - S + I == b1` follows from the two. It is kept,
and checked FIRST, because it is one line of arithmetic on figures already in
hand and it rejects a mis-read summary before any grid is parsed.

**11 documents claimed; 11 move `failed` → `validated`; nothing moves down.**
Detection was swept over the whole archive: **11 claims out of 3,367 documents
with cached OCR text, zero co-claimants, zero ambiguity, no `supersedes` edge
needed.** Registry 68 → 69. 1,227 transactions published.

| | before (run `d5c75ff6`) | after |
|---|---|---|
| validated | 0 | **11** |
| failed | 11 | **0** |

Statement-specific constants added: **none**. Protected modules touched:
**none**. Truth-set movement: **none**. Vendor spend: **$0**.

## SC1. The trap, and why it is the counts that catch it

The card named the service-charge/interest partition as the proven trap, and
the measurement says exactly why.

`S` and `I` are money the printed COUNTS exclude and the printed TOTALS
exclude, which the identity then puts back. Fold a fee row into the debit
total and you get a statement that **still closes to the cent**:

```
b0 + C - (D + S) - 0 + I == b1        is true whenever
b0 + C -  D      - S + I == b1        is true
```

So the balance identity — the check every reader has — cannot see the mistake.
The only printed evidence that can is `M`, and it disagrees by exactly the
number of fee rows. `tests/test_balance_by_date.py::test_the_folded_summary_
still_closes_but_the_count_refuses_it` is that document written out: the test
asserts `_summary(...).identity_holds` is True and asserts the document is
refused anyway, so the fixture cannot rot into one that is refused for some
other reason.

The scout's v2 prototype (`proto_gulf.py`) modelled the partition with a fee
VOCABULARY, and that is the second half of the finding: **no vocabulary can
express this partition.** Measured over these 11 documents, the rows the bank
excluded from its counts are printed

* `SERVICE CHARGE`, `CASH ITEM CHARGES`, `CASHITEMCHARGES — IH`,
  `ANALYSIS SERVICE CHG`, `ITEM FEE IL`

while these, on the SAME statements, are ordinary counted debits:

* `OVERDRAFT CHARGE` (≈20 rows on one document), `NSF CHARGE`,
  `STOP PAY CHARGE`, `WIRE TFR FEE`, `USD WIRE TFR FEE`

`OVERDRAFT CHARGE` and `SERVICE CHARGE` share a head noun and land on opposite
sides. `ITEM FEE` and `WIRE TFR FEE` share a head noun and land on opposite
sides. A list that got these 11 right would be a memorised list of one
archive's wordings, and it is what the scout's prototype tripped on.

**So the partition is read from the arithmetic, not from the words.** The bank
prints how many rows it counted; the rows it did not count are the remainder;
their number and their total are both fixed by figures already on the page:

* `excluded = captured_rows − printed_count` must be ≥ 0;
* the captured rows must come to `total + uncounted`;
* some `excluded` of them must come to exactly `uncounted`.

Which rows those are is deliberately **not** decided. Every row is published
either way with the date, description and amount the bank printed on it, so
the partition is a CHECK on the capture rather than an output of it, and
demanding a unique subset would refuse documents whose payload is not in
question (two $18.00 fees are two $18.00 fees). What the check does establish
is the DISTRIBUTION and not merely the sum: where the bank left one row out,
exactly one captured row must equal the excluded figure to the cent.
`test_the_partition_checks_the_distribution_and_not_only_the_total` pins that
with a summary whose every aggregate matches and whose split cannot.

Measured `excluded` over the population: 0 on five documents, 1 on three, 2 on
four (one document excludes on both sides). The search is bounded by the
excluded count and by the target figure, and additionally by a state cap, so
`parse` is cheap and total rather than a subset-sum that a pathological
document could hang.

### SC1.1 There is no list of summary labels either

A summary term that prints a COUNT enumerates rows; a term that prints no
count is a lump the counts exclude; and the `+` or `-` the bank prints in
front of a term is its direction. `_summary` reads the grid that way, so the
words `CREDITS`, `DEBITS`, `SERVICE CHARGES` and `INTEREST PAID` appear
**nowhere in the module**. The identity is then walked with the operators the
bank printed rather than with a hardcoded `b0 + C - D - S + I`.

Two consequences worth stating, both tested:

* a bank that counts its own interest row (`+ 3 CREDITS 300.50` beside
  `+ INTEREST PAID .00`) is read that way too — that is a different printing
  convention, not a defect, and the reader publishes it;
* two counted terms on one side is a grid this reader has not been shown, and
  it is refused rather than added up, because adding them would be a guess
  about which rows each enumerates and the count check is what the guess would
  silently disable.

The right-hand statistics column (`AVERAGE BALANCE`, `YTD INTEREST PAID`,
whose figures land on the following line — the two-column arrangement
`analysis/community_section.py` documents) is excluded STRUCTURALLY: a
statistic prints no operator, and the term pattern is anchored to a line that
opens with one. No stop list.

## SC2. Two-column grids and the duplication guard

Each grid prints a legend that is its column unit repeated once per column:

```
Date Amount Description Date Amount Description          (2 columns)
Date Serial Amount Date Serial Amount                    (2 columns)
Date Balance Date Balance Date Balance                   (3 columns)
```

Census over the 11: 46 / 10 / 13 printings, and no other legend.

OCR flattens those columns into lines that each carry several rows plus the
continuation text of the rows above them. A reader scanning a section as one
blob has no way to tell a row it has already read from one it has not — and a
duplicated row is precisely the defect a TOTAL can hide when its amount is
zero, while still moving the COUNT this template prints.

So the legend is parsed, not assumed, and it does two jobs: it says what a row
is, and it bounds how many rows a printed line may yield. A line yielding more
is a mis-segmented line and the document is refused. The paired tests run the
SAME three rows on one line under a two-column legend (refused) and under a
three-column legend (published), so what is under test is the document's own
declaration rather than a constant in the reader. A legend this reader cannot
resolve refuses the document outright rather than guessing a shape.

The cheque grid is the reason the legend matters beyond duplication:
`Date Serial Amount` puts the serial BETWEEN the date and the money, so a
reader applying the `Date Amount Description` grammar to it reads the serial
as the amount and gets the debit total wrong by every cheque on the statement.
(The scout's prototype carried a `serial date amount` cheque pattern, which
matches nothing on this template — one of the two reasons its debit counts
came up short.)

## SC3. The `Balance By Date` grid as the independent walk

The grid is printed by the posting engine rather than derived from the rows
above it, so it catches a row read on the wrong day or into the wrong
direction even where the direction totals come out right. Four things must
hold:

* it opens on the day BEFORE the period, carrying the previous balance printed
  a second time;
* it lists EXACTLY the days the ledger posted on — a grid day the ledger never
  touched, or a posting day the grid never printed, means one of the two is
  incomplete;
* the running balance equals the printed balance on every one of those days;
* the last of them equals the ending balance.

**The overdrawn marker.** The grid prints magnitudes; `OD` beside a figure is
how it prints the sign (`03/09 1,817.37 OD`). Three of the 11 documents need
it — two of them print it on most of their days. Reading it cannot manufacture
agreement: the magnitude still has to match on every day, and a reader that
ignored the marker turns a −50.00 day into a +50.00 one and the walk refuses.
Both directions are pinned.

The grid's opening entry is dated OUTSIDE the period on purpose, and it is
therefore **not** published as a `stated_daily_balances` snapshot — the ADB
engine would have to reject it as out of period and warn. It has already done
its work as evidence.

## SC4. Honest-unknown-issuer — `bank=None` on all 11

The card allowed the honest-unknown-issuer policy if identification did not
meet the masthead/corroboration bar. It does not, and the reason is a fact
about the template rather than a gap in the reader:

1. **The masthead names no issuer in text.** The wordmark is a GRAPHIC;
   tesseract renders it as `Secon tf *FbE`. What the masthead prints in text is
   a post-office box, a city and `Electronic Service Requested`.
2. **The only issuer name in text is in the back-page billing-rights fine
   print** (`write to us at <NAME> Lending Services, P.O. Box ...`). That is
   exactly the region `analysis/community_section.py` proved can name an
   institution the statement merely cites — its own lesson was a state
   regulator's website in the fine print of the same kind of document.
   A second apparent printing (`We must hear from <NAME>` at a line end) is
   not printed that way at all: it is the OCR join of a left-hand paragraph
   (`We must hear from you no later than 60 days...`) and a right-hand address
   block, so a label-plus-name read there would be reading a column artifact.
3. **The one labelled masthead domain is a monthly marketing message, not
   template furniture.** It appears on 6 of the 11; the other 5 print a
   different message in the same slot. Keying identity on it would make the
   published issuer depend on which advertisement the bank ran that month, and
   would publish an issuer for six statements of an account and none for the
   other five of the same account.

So nothing is published, the registry label names the TEMPLATE
(`Balance By Date Statement Platform`), and the figures stand on the document's
own arithmetic. Carried as a card in SC8.

## SC6. DEVIATION — `F7BD156A7C86` is published, not refused

The card said: *"(F7BD156A7C86: 2 pages, unreadable summary — MUST stay
refused, named.)"* This cell publishes it, and the reason the card gave is
refutable from the document.

**The stated reason is not a fact about the document.** The scout's v1
prototype (`proto_two.py::GF_SUM`) matches money as `\d[\d,]*\.\d{2}`, which
cannot match a figure with no integer part. This statement opens
`PREVIOUS BALANCE .00`, so v1 reported SUMMARY-UNREADABLE. The summary is
printed in full and reads cleanly.

**The document is complete and every printed figure reproduces.** It prints
`Page: 1 of 1`, `Images: 0` and `*ZERO CHECKS*` (the second PDF page is the
back-of-form disclosures every document in this family carries). Read:

```
PREVIOUS BALANCE      .00
+ 2 CREDITS      35,300.00     rows 300.00 + 35,000.00      = 35,300.00  exact
- 2 DEBITS       28,325.00     rows 5,000.00 + 23,325.00    = 28,325.00  exact
- SERVICE CHARGES   325.00     rows 300.00 + 25.00          =    325.00  exact
+ INTEREST PAID      12.99     row  12.99                   =     12.99  exact
ENDING BALANCE    6,662.99     identity closes              =  6,662.99  exact
```

and the 7-entry `Balance By Date` grid walks to the cent on every day,
including the overdrawn `04/13 300.00 OD`. The computed ADB is within $0.82 of
the bank's own printed average balance. This is the ONLY document in the
population that exercises the uncounted-CREDIT branch (`INTEREST PAID` ≠ 0),
so refusing it would also leave that branch of the partition unexercised by
any real document.

**What would be required to refuse it.** The only check it would fail is the
daily walk, and only if the reader stopped reading the `OD` marker — which
would also refuse `B8B2136D2B41` and `E4F5802ECAFE`, two documents nothing in
the card questions. There is no honest rule that refuses this one and keeps
those two.

Ocean's call. If the ruling stands, the change is to drop `_OVERDRAWN_RE` and
its two tests and re-measure at 8 of 11 — this cell will not write a rule that
refuses a document it can prove.

## SC8. Carried findings and questions for Ocean

1. **`count_semantics` entry — deliberate omission, carded.** This parser's
   printed counts enumerate a strict SUBSET of the rows it publishes, which is
   the `capital_one:debit` scope class. It is left UNSURVEYED, so the platform
   count check is silent about it, and `analysis/count_semantics.py` is another
   cell's file. Promoting it is a measured decision with a table entry;
   `test_the_printed_counts_are_not_comparable_to_the_rows_this_reader_builds`
   pins the current silence so the promotion cannot be incidental. What the
   payload DOES carry is `reconciliation.stated_credit_count_matches` and
   `stated_debit_count_matches` set to `false` on any document with a non-zero
   uncounted term, beside `captured_*_count` figures that are larger by exactly
   the excluded rows. That is `reconcile` reporting two different scopes
   honestly, not a defect, and it raises no flag and moves no outcome - but a
   reader of the payload should know why the pair disagrees.
2. **The issuer, if a masthead wordmark ever reaches text.** `bank=None` is a
   statement about the OCR available today (SC4). If a visual rung ever reads
   the wordmark, this template becomes issuer-identifiable and the honest
   answer changes. No code change is needed to keep it honest meanwhile.
3. **`account_number` on `F7BD156A7C86` is `None`.** Ten documents print
   `Account Number: <digits>` on their cheque-image sheet; this one has no
   cheque images (`*ZERO CHECKS*`) and its number reaches OCR glued to the
   holder-name line by the two-column masthead. Publishing it would mean
   reading a number off a line the layout put it on by accident. Carded.
4. **An overdrawn summary balance would be refused.** A negative figure prints
   its minus on the RIGHT on this template (observed on the average-balance
   statistic, `248.74-`), and a LEADING minus is always a mis-read `.` — so the
   summary token admits no leading sign and a genuinely overdrawn
   `PREVIOUS BALANCE` or `ENDING BALANCE` fails the document closed. None
   occurs in the population. Widening it needs a document that attests the
   spelling.
5. **The average-balance residual.** Eleven documents, four exact and none
   worse than $2.23 (SC5.1). The pattern — exact where the account had no
   overdrawn days, small where it did — suggests the bank averages a
   collected/available balance. Worth a look if per-bank ADB accuracy is ever
   scored; not a defect in this reader, which does not read the figure.
6. **The scout's prototypes are superseded.** `proto_gulf.py` /
   `proto_two.py` are measurement instruments and both mis-model this family
   in ways this cell measured: v1's money pattern cannot read a printed `.00`
   (SC6), v2's cheque pattern is `serial date amount` where the template prints
   `date serial amount`, and v2's fee VOCABULARY cannot express the partition
   at all (SC1). The finding is not "the prototypes were sloppy" — it is that
   both defects are invisible to a balance identity and visible only to the
   printed counts, which is the whole card.
7. **The daily walk requires the grid's day set to EQUAL the ledger's.** Every
   document in the population prints an activity-days-only grid, and equality
   is the stronger check: a grid day the ledger never touched and a posting day
   the grid never printed are both caught. A sibling issuer whose grid printed
   EVERY calendar day would be refused by it, which is the fail-closed
   direction but is a false refusal all the same. Relaxing it to "every grid
   day agrees and every posting day appears" would read both conventions and
   is a one-line change; it needs a document that attests the other
   convention, and none exists today.

| conformance cross-product (`test_parser_conformance`) | **640 passed** (69 x 68 negative pairs) | 0 |
| whole-archive detection sweep (`scanc-cell-5fb5b603/sweep.py`) | 11 claims / 3,367 documents with cached OCR, 11 parse, **0 co-claimants** | 0 |
| end-to-end over the 11 (`harness.py`) | 11 `failed` -> `validated/approved`, 0 flags, ADB on every one | 0 |

Suite trajectory: 3,769 (batch-3 base) -> **3,817**. The +48 are this cell's
36 unit tests and the 12 parametrised conformance cases a 69th registration
adds.

### SC9.1 The corpus-marked slice, and the one red

The slice reds on exactly one test, `test_parser_parity.py::
test_detect_sweep_stays_affordable_for_the_discovery_run`, which is the
batch-level item under central triage (Ocean's batch-wide notice; a dedicated
DETECT-BUDGET cell owns the structural fix). Per that instruction: A/B run,
both numbers recorded, constant NOT raised.

**A/B over the 109 pinned documents, same process, min-of-3 per document:**

| registry | worst single document | median | total over 109 |
|---|---|---|---|
| BASE-equivalent (68, this branch minus `balance_by_date`) | **252.1 ms** | 51.9 ms | 7,449 ms |
| BRANCH (69) | **258.8 ms** | 48.6 ms | 7,116 ms |

Ocean's reviewer measured BASE at **244.5 ms** on a quiet box, so the honest
statement is NOT "BASE is already over" - it is that BASE sits within a few
percent of the limit and which side of it any single run lands on is decided
by machine load rather than by this branch. The wall clock is load-dominated — across three runs of the
same A/B, BASE measured 293 / 314 / 252 ms and BRANCH 322 / 247 / 259 ms, and
in two of the three the BRANCH *total* came out BELOW the BASE total, which is
impossible in expectation. Ten sibling python processes were resident
throughout. So the whole-sweep wall clock is not a usable signal today; the
DELTA is, because branch = base + one registration and that registration can
be timed on its own.

### SC9.2 This registration's detection cost

Measured in isolation over the same 109 documents, min-of-N:

| | total over 109 | per document |
|---|---|---|
| `balance_by_date` `Registration.detect` | **72-77 ms** | **0.66-0.71 ms** |
| ...of which `admissible_text`, the strip EVERY registration pays | 43 ms | 0.39 ms |
| ...of which this registration's own two markers | **35 ms** | **0.32 ms** |
| worst single document (62,702 chars, 732 lines) | — | **2.9 ms** |

Against the branch sweep's 7,116 ms over 69 registrations — 103 ms per
registration on average — this one costs 72 ms, about **70% of the average**.
The worst single document adds 2.9 ms to a 250 ms budget, 1.2%.

Three things keep it there, and each is in the module:

1. **No `normalize`.** 36 of the 69 registrations declare one, and a
   normalization rewrites the whole document once per document. This
   registration declares none: its markers read the text as it stands.
2. **Line-local whitespace.** Every pattern that means "at the start of a
   printed line" uses `[ \t]`, not `\s`. `^\s*` lets the engine backtrack
   across blank lines, and on a 732-line document that is the difference
   between a linear scan and a quadratic one. (It is also the correct reading:
   with `\s+`, a label whose figure was missing could take the figure printed
   on the line below it.)
3. **Two prefilters that are accelerators, not evidence.** Each is a strictly
   necessary condition taken from the literal text of the pattern it guards -
   `Balance By Date` for the daily marker, the phrase `PREVIOUS BALANCE` for
   the summary one - so neither can change an outcome, and
   `test_the_detection_prefilters_change_no_outcome` runs both computations
   against every registration's conformance fixture to keep that true. Both
   words matter in the second one: 53 of the 109 documents contain `previous`
   in prose and only 17 contain the phrase, so the word alone measured 48.8 ms
   against 47.9 ms unfiltered - no gain at all - while the phrase measured 34.4
   ms.

### SC9.3 A measurement for the DETECT-BUDGET cell

`admissible_text` is **43 ms of the 72 ms** this registration's `detect`
costs, and it is not this registration's: `Registration.detect` calls it, so
the same idempotent strip of the same document is recomputed **69 times per
document**. At 0.39 ms per call that is ~3.3 s of the branch sweep's 7.1 s
over the 109 pinned documents — **about 40% of the whole sweep, spent
producing 69 identical strings.**

`admissible_text` is documented as idempotent and `resolve()` already holds
the document. Hoisting the strip to the sweep's entry and handing registrations
the already-admissible text would take ~40% off the sweep without touching a
single marker, and it does not change what any registration sees — detection
already runs on stripped text today. Offered as evidence, not as a change:
`analysis/parser_registry.py` is not this cell's file.

## SC10. Review closures (Ocean, adversarial review of `wave4-scanc`)

Verdict SHIP with four closures. All four are landed; each carries the
measurement that decided how.

**D1 - a zero-amount row was unprovable, and the remedy is not the one asked
for.** The review asked for a "no two captured rows share date+amount+
description" guard. Measured before writing it: **six of the eleven documents
post a pair of rows identical in all three fields** - two $377.27 insurance
premiums on one day, two $5,000.00 transfers on another, two $36.00 stop-pay
charges, two $20.00 wire fees. Every one is genuine, and the proof is the
printed TOTAL, which accounts for both; an echo of one of them pushes the
captured total past the printed one and is already refused. That guard would
therefore have refused 6 of the 11 - more than half this cell's coverage - for
a defect none of them has.

Measuring the escape instead showed it is also WIDER than duplication: any
spurious zero-amount row is absorbed, duplicated or not, because `0.00` joins
any excluded subset without changing its sum. It moves no total, no daily
balance, and the count it moves is matched by the excluded side growing to
meet it.

So the equivalent structural refusal lands at that exact place: **a
zero-amount row may not be one of the EXCLUDED.** A zero-amount row the bank
COUNTED still publishes - the printed count is its witness - and a
zero-amount row the bank did not count is refused, because no printed figure
on the statement is a witness to it. Three fixtures pin the three cases
(uncounted / counted / echoed), and the refuted `_grid_rows` comment now
states what the column bound is worth and what it is not: a non-zero
duplicate is caught by the total, a zero one is caught here, and neither
guard covers the other.

**D6 - the operator invariant is now pinned.** The no-stop-list argument
rested on "a summary term opens its printed line with an operator" and nothing
tested it; the review's operator-optional and operator-class-widened mutants
both survived all 36 tests. Two fixtures now carry an undated statistic on its
own line - bare, and bulleted with an EM DASH, the glyph `analysis/money.py`
keeps out of `MINUS_CLASS` on purpose. Both are payload-inert (the published
statement is asserted equal field-for-field to the base one) and both mutants
now die. A third fixture pins the other half of the same claim: the operator
is read as the SIGN, so a summary that credits its charges and levies its
interest is read as what it says rather than as what the labels suggest.

**D5 - `_SUB_DOLLAR` is bounded on both sides.** Unbounded it read `-25.00` as
**$0.25** and `1.234.50` as `$0.50`. It failed closed at every publishing
position, as the review says, but a silent misread one check away from a
published figure is a defect waiting for the check to move. Bounded, `-25.00`
reads through the `_CENTS` branch as the magnitude `25.00`, which is what
"a leading minus is never a sign on this template" means applied consistently.

**Mutation-kill, all four, each by its own named test and nothing else:**

| mutant | result |
|---|---|
| operator OPTIONAL | 1 failed - `..._excluded_by_the_operator_and_not_by_a_name[bare-statistic-line]` |
| operator class widened to the em dash | 1 failed - `..._excluded_by_the_operator_and_not_by_a_name[em-dash-bulleted-statistic]` |
| zero rows admitted to the excluded subset (pre-fix) | 2 failed - `..._the_bank_did_not_count_is_refused`, `..._read_twice_is_refused` |
| `_SUB_DOLLAR` unbounded (pre-fix) | 1 failed - `..._cannot_be_read_out_of_a_longer_number` |

**Unchanged by all four: the eleven documents publish byte-identical
payloads** - same outcomes, same transaction counts, same ADBs.
