## MGD10. Carried findings for Ocean

**The private-opinions ledger, ranked by blast radius rather than by the order
they were found.** Every reader below holds its own opinion about what a dash
means; the canon this cell built is only as good as the readers that consult
it, and these four do not.

1. **THE FIRST ONE THAT MATTERS — `analysis/structurer/tokens.py` inverts BOTH
   attested sign glyphs, generically, on a live path.** `money_value` (:139)
   tests `text.startswith("-")` for ASCII only, then ends
   `return -abs(value) if negative else abs(value)`. `parse_money` had already
   recovered the sign correctly; the `abs()` throws it away:

   ```
   token          money_value      parse_money
   -1,234.56        -1234.56          -1234.56    agree
   −1,234.56 (U+2212) +1234.56          -1234.56    INVERTED
   –1,234.56 (U+2013) +1234.56          -1234.56    INVERTED
   ```

   `MONEY_RE` (:65) admits ASCII and parentheses only, so the tokenizer path
   inverts identically. This is worse than a stale private class: it CALLS the
   shared grammar and then discards its answer, so fixing the canon cannot
   reach it. And it is not one issuer's layout — the structurer is the
   generic unclaimed-layout reader, so this is the sign rule for every
   document no registration claims. Blast radius TODAY is small (the
   structurer is opt-in off, and the one archive document in reach already
   fails), which is exactly why it should be fixed before the path is turned
   on rather than after. Not taken here: `analysis/structurer/` is not this
   cell's file, and the fix wants a differential against the shared grammar,
   which is a reader-by-reader job.
2. **`analysis/structurer/summary.py:127` is a FOURTH date-range class** —
   `(?:-|–|—|to|through|thru|au|until)` in `_RANGE_RE`, an alternation mixing
   dashes with words. Carries U+2013 and U+2014 but not U+2212, so card 4's
   guard is silent on it by design. Not repointed: `PERIOD_DASH` is
   dash-only and this needs the word alternatives, so it is a genuine local
   superset rather than a copy — recorded for completeness of the ledger.
3. **`analysis/regions.py:40` re-implements half of `normalize_sign_glyphs`** —
   `value.strip().replace("–", "-")` handles U+2013 and misses U+2212, so a
   Regions cell set with a true minus sign loses its sign. Same ABSENCE shape
   as finding 1 and equally invisible to card 4's guard. Regions is
   offline-inexecutable per §WIRING, so this could not be measured end to end;
   recorded rather than touched.
4. **`ocr/column_grid.py:62`** admits U+2212 in its money-cell class and not
   U+2013 or the em dash — the opposite half-opinion, in the geometry layer,
   outside `analysis/` and so outside card 4's scan (whose boundary is the one
   every other guard in that file uses). Named for the geometry cell.
5. **`balance_by_date._PERIOD_RE` is a date range built out of the SIGN
   class** — `mm/dd/yyyy {MINUS_CLASS} mm/dd/yyyy`, at
   `analysis/balance_by_date.py:369`. Inert under this cell (`MINUS_CLASS` is
   byte-identical), and deliberately NOT repointed: `PERIOD_DASH` is one glyph
   WIDER, so moving it could claim documents the family does not claim today.
   Widening is a coverage change with its own sweep, not a canon change. The
   module's other three `MINUS_CLASS` uses are genuine sign reads (the printed
   `+`/`-` operator that opens a term line) and are correct as they stand.
   `tests/test_shared_parser_utils.py` states the exclusion explicitly so the
   repointing test is not read as a claim about the whole platform.

**And the two this branch owns:**

6. **MGD-C1 — the raising family quotes the token it refuses, and THIS BRANCH
   WIDENED IT.** `parse_decimal`, `parse_decimal_mixed_separator`,
   `parse_grouped_float`, `parse_trailing_minus_dropped` and
   `parse_french_amount` all `raise ValueError(value)` with the printed token
   as the message, and `webapp/worker.py` returns `str(exc)` as the job error
   — so statement content can cross the exception boundary. The law batch 4
   closed for `read_money` (§MG-C2 D1) is still open one layer down, in the
   same module.

   The priority is higher than "inherited", and the correction matters:
   card 1 did not merely leave this open, it ADDED a caller. Before this
   branch `parse_signed_decimal("—$500.00")` returned a number and reached no
   raise at all; now it raises `ValueError("— 500.00")`, carrying the
   document's own text to a user-visible job error. The em-dash path is
   unreachable on today's archive, so nothing leaks today — but this branch
   converted a dormant boundary defect into one with a live caller, and that
   is the argument for taking the card next rather than eventually. Not fixed
   here: it changes exception messages across a dozen parsers and wants its
   own sweep.
7. **MGD-C2 — the fintech row grammars absorb an unread sign glyph rather
   than refusing the row, and the arithmetic backstop has a hole at zero.**
   Measured in MGD6, in three shapes. `mercury._ROW_RE`'s `type` group and
   `wealthsimple._ROW_TAIL_RE`'s `description` group are lazy any-character
   groups, so a glyph the sign class does not admit is swallowed and a
   neighbouring money cell becomes the amount — welded (`—$10.00`) the BALANCE
   column is read as the amount, spaced (`— $10.00`) the amount cell is read
   unsigned. Both are a debit booked as a credit; both are caught by the
   balance walk.

   **At an amount of ZERO they are not caught.** `-0.00` and `+0.00` are the
   same number, so the walk still reaches the printed balance, the document
   VALIDATES, and the glyph the bank set as a sign is published as description
   text (`"Coop —"`). The financial figures are right and the record of what
   the bank printed is wrong. So the guarantee is "fails closed for non-zero
   amounts", never the unqualified version, and it rests on arithmetic rather
   than on grammar — a future row shape without a balance column would have
   neither. All three shapes are pinned. Zero attested inputs today, which is
   why a refusal rule was NOT added: an unattested refusal is the same
   over-reach as an unattested sign glyph.
8. **`ANALYSIS_STAGE_VERSION` needs NO bump for this cell.** Zero archive
   documents change output. Ocean's call at merge, as always, but nothing here
   forces it.

# §CURRENCY — the currency-evidence platform card (CURRENCY-1, batch 5)

Branch `wave5-currency`, base `b524f72` (registry 71, v12, OCR v3, suite 4,240).
Gustavo's standing invariant, verbatim: *"Currency should be derived from
document evidence when available and must not be silently asserted by a schema
default when the document proves otherwise. If RBC or any other pinned expected
result moves, use the formal truth-set ceremony before changing expectations."*

## CUR0. Summary

| Documents publishing a currency today | 2,524 claimed (CAD 388 / USD 2,136); 872 unclaimed publish nothing |
| Documents whose PRINTED evidence contradicts what we publish | **9**, in 2 registrations, and nowhere else on the platform |

| `analysis/schema.py` | untouched. A default is right where no evidence exists; the invariant governs documents that PROVE a currency |

Revised after Ocean's adversarial review (BLOCK, narrow — behaviour sound, six
findings in code-adjacent record plus one real contradiction). What the review

## CUR1. The census — who publishes currency today, and from what

Twenty-five explicit currency assignments exist across 19 modules; the other
~46 registrations publish the `analysis/schema.py` default `"USD"` implicitly.
Sorting them by *what the value is derived from* is the census the card needed,
and it has four classes, not two:

| Class | Registrations | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| **A. Read off the page** | `bmo` (`Currency: XXX`, CAD fallback), `cibc` (the ISO code on the closing-balance row) | Already correct. The pattern the rest should look like |
| **B. Constant, but gated by a REQUIRED detection marker that carries the currency** | `wealthsimple` (`_GRID_RE` matches only `AMOUNT (CAD) BALANCE (CAD)`), `releve_facturation` (`_PRODUCT_RE` requires `COMPTE COURANT CANADIEN`, and the parser returns `None` without it) | Correct *by construction* — a document in another currency is never claimed. Reads as a hardcode; is not one. Both now say so, and `wealthsimple` has a test that fails if detection is ever widened |
| **C. Constant, ungated, and the document names the currency anyway** | `desjardins` (`PCA USD DESJARDINS CORPORATE BUILD-UP ACCOUNT` is printed; `currency="USD"` was written) | The invariant's target even where the value happens to agree: a CAD issue of the same product would have been published as USD |
| **D. Constant or schema default, and the document names nothing** | `bmo_ca_business` (127 docs), `scotiabank` (79 of 81), `community_section` (61), `td_canada_french` (13), `rbc` English (151 of 169), and every US registration | The default STANDS, and the ambiguity is named (§CUR5). Nothing here is inferred from an address, a folder or a filename |

## CUR2. THE ORACLE BAR, and the traps that set it

The bar is Gustavo's: a currency code, a locale-bound product line, or an
explicit symbol convention the layout proves. No geography, no folder, no
filename. The archive supplies four concrete reasons the bar has to be
*anchored to layout furniture* rather than to a token scan — each of these is
a real document, and each is pinned by a negative test:

1. **`Af 'CURRENCY KLR Enterpriees, LL`** — the OCR of a deposit-slip image on
   the **pinned** `Misc/KLR.May 31,2026 (1).pdf`. A labelled-ISO reader with an
   open code set publishes `currency="KLR"` on a pinned document. Every reader
   here validates against a closed set.
2. **`e-Transfer received PHILIPPESEGUIN CADWKEFS`** — RBC prints `CAxxxxxx`
   e-Transfer references in its ledger. A bare `\bCAD\b` scan reads a
   customer's reference as the account's denomination.
3. **`Funds transfer credit TT KM CAPITAL C`** — a posting on the **pinned**
   `RBC/Chequing Statement-JAN+.pdf`. An unanchored search for the `U.S. Funds`
   words reads a transfer TYPE as a denomination, and moves a pinned document.
4. **`CAD DRAFT 11512638 3,009.95 JAN21`** — TD prints a draft's currency in
   its ledger on eight documents. The draft's denomination is not the
   account's; on a USD account the two disagree.

And the filename hazard, stated correctly (this paragraph asserted the opposite
in the first revision, and Ocean was right to reject it). **Measured: all
twelve currency-named RBC files agree with their page — the six named
`CAD Statement-1718 …` print `CAD CHEQUING ACCOUNT`, the six named
`USD Statement-1046 …` print `U.S. Funds`. No archive filename disagrees with
what its document prints.** The case for the boundary is therefore not that
today's names would mislead; it is that the agreement is luck. Filenames are
operator-supplied metadata (R-4b), F-PROVENANCE measured 7 of 10 sampled
parsers reading financial evidence out of them, and a rename must not be able
to move a published reading. Both new readers carry a filename-boundary test
exercised through `admissible_text` (§CUR7, D-4).

Two more that shaped scope rather than a regex:

5. **`inter-currency transfer / 0390352/CAD 1.378237`** — Desjardins prints an
   FX *rate* with its counter-currency. All 6 Desjardins documents print both
   `USD` and `CAD` for this reason; only the product line states the account.
6. **`Account Information Currency:  CAD`** — the Scotiabank label belongs to a
   `Deposit Interest` statement bundled into the same PDF as the
   `Business Account` the parser publishes. It is evidence about a *different
   account*, so it is not read: **scotiabank is deliberately left alone** and
   named in §CUR5.

## CUR3. What was implemented

### CUR3.1 `analysis/rbc.py` — English reader (`_printed_currency`)

Two independent sites, both layout furniture and **both positionally
anchored**: the `U.S. Funds` denomination line (anchored at both ends of its
line, optionally sharing the title line) and the product name **inside the
`RBBDA…` mailing header** (`CAD CHEQUING ACCOUNT`, `US BUSINESS ACCOUNT`).
Disagreement between the two returns `None`, and `None` leaves the schema
default standing.

**D-1, the mailing-header anchor.** The first revision searched the whole
document for the product spelling while its own comment claimed the mailing
header. That gap is reachable: this family prints **88 postings that name an
account** — `Online Transfer to Deposit Account-5887`,
`ACCOUNT TRANSFER 06032-1122647` — so a customer who names an account
`CAD Chequing` puts the product spelling in the LEDGER, and
`Online Transfer to CAD Chequing Account-1718` would have been read as the
statement's denomination. Measured before anchoring: **twelve product-spelling
hits in the family, twelve of them on the `RBBDA…` line and none outside it**,
and 157 of 169 documents carry that line — so the anchor closes the shape at
zero cost, and the published result is byte-identical (12 USD / 6 CAD / 151
None before and after). Pinned by
`test_cur_negative_a_posting_naming_an_account_cannot_counterfeit_the_product`.

**D-2, the spelling table is literal.** The first revision matched
`(CAD|US)\s+(CHEQUING|BUSINESS)\s+ACCOUNT` — a four-way cross product admitting
`CAD BUSINESS ACCOUNT` and `US CHEQUING ACCOUNT`, which no document prints and
nothing had measured. It is now a two-entry table of the attested spellings
(`CAD CHEQUING ACCOUNT` 6, `US BUSINESS ACCOUNT` 6), with the unattested pair
pinned as reading nothing.

- 6 documents move **USD -> CAD** (the product line proves CAD)
- 12 keep USD, now *derived* from the page rather than defaulted onto it
- **151 print nothing and keep the default USD**, unchanged and named
- the French reader is untouched; `CDN TIRE MC`, a merchant on the pinned
  French statement, reads as nothing

### CUR3.2 `analysis/td_can.py` — native reader (`_native_printed_currency`)

The `Account Type` column's product suffix, anchored on the word `ACCOUNT`
(`ACCOUNT - CAD` / `- USD`), matched whether the column wraps it onto its own
line or not. Two different suffixes on one document returns `None`.

- 3 documents move **CAD -> USD** (they print `ACCOUNT - USD` twice each)
- 70 keep CAD, now derived
- 1 prints `BUSINESS / INVESTOR / ACCOUNT` — a product with no denomination —
  and keeps the layout default CAD
- the non-native `parse_td_canada_statement` and `td_canada_french` are
  untouched: neither has an archive document that prints a currency

**D-5 — the contradiction this branch created, and the fix.** The same header
line also fed `account_name`, as the FIXED string
`"BUSINESS CHEQUING ACCOUNT - CAD"`, written whenever the header printed
`BUSINESS CHEQUING`. Reading the denomination off the page without reading the
name off the same line published `currency="USD"` beside a name asserting
`- CAD` on the three U.S.-dollar statements — one payload contradicting itself,
from one printed line, on a field (`account`) that IS an audited column. Both
now come from one call to `_native_printed_currency`, so they cannot disagree.

Ocean's prescription offered the full printed string
(`BUSINESS CHEQUING ACCOUNT - USD EVERY DAY B`); **that is corrected here with
measurement.** Appending the plan token would move the published name on all 73
documents that print `BUSINESS CHEQUING` — six of them pinned — on an audited
column, for no correctness gain. Only the suffix was ever wrong, so only the
suffix is read. Measured effect: 70 names byte-identical, **3 names corrected
CAD -> USD (the same three documents as the currency), 0 pinned.**

### CUR3.3 `analysis/desjardins.py` — `_printed_currency`

The ISO code in front of the product name, validated against a closed
`{CAD, USD}`. Zero movement — all 6 archive documents print `USD` — but the
value is now the document's rather than the reader's, and `PCA`, the
three-letter account-type mark printed immediately before the product name,
cannot be published as a currency.

### CUR3.4 `analysis/wealthsimple.py` — the gate made explicit

No behaviour change. `stmt.currency = "CAD"` is class B: `_GRID_RE` is a
REQUIRED detection marker and matches only `AMOUNT (CAD) BALANCE (CAD)`, so a
document reaching that line has printed CAD over both money columns. The
comment now says which marker discharges it, and
`test_a_non_cad_activity_grid_is_not_claimed` fails if detection is ever
widened without the constant becoming a read.

### CUR4.1 The ceremony enumeration — EMPTY, and why that is a measurement

**Zero of the 109 pinned documents move, on any of the four fields.** The
enumeration table below is empty because the population is empty, and the
population was measured three ways:

1. The 9 movers' content hashes are disjoint from the pinned 109 (the diff
   instrument checks membership per mover and reports 0).
2. All four pinned RBC statements were read end to end for any currency-ish
   token. They print `Funds transfer credit` postings and nothing else; the
   only currency word in the four is a transfer type. They are in the
   151-document no-evidence bucket, so the default stands and they do not move.
   **The `rbc` ceremony the batch-3 log anticipated is not triggered by an
   evidence-based reader** — it would only be triggered by inferring CAD from
   the institution, which the invariant forbids.
3. The six pinned `td_canada_native` documents all print `ACCOUNT - CAD` and
   already publish CAD; the pinned Desjardins document prints `USD` and already
   publishes USD; the pinned BMO document prints `Currency: CAD` and is already
   read.

### CUR4.2 Blast radius — the label, the UI, and no figure

**CORRECTED after review.** The first revision claimed "no production module
reads `Statement.currency`". That claim was **false, and false for a
methodological reason worth recording: the grep behind it was
`--include=*.py`.** The serving layer is JavaScript.

What is true:

* **No Python module reads it.** `analysis/metrics.py`, `analysis/reconcile.py`,
  `analysis/adb.py`, `analysis/serialization.py`, `analysis/revenue.py`,
  `analysis/count_semantics.py` and `analysis/bank_repairs.py` contain zero
  references (the one hit in `adb.py` is the word "currency" in a rounding
  docstring). No metric, no reconciliation verdict, no integrity flag and no
  balance depends on it — which the differential confirms independently
  (`outcome` movers: 0).
* **`webapp/static/app.js` reads it, and it formats every money string in the
  UI.** `statement.currency || "USD"` at the two context sites (the main
  transaction table and the statement modal), threaded into
  `renderTransactionRows` and into `formatMoney`, which calls
  `Intl.NumberFormat("en-US", {style: "currency", currency})`. Under `en-US`
  that renders CAD as `CA$1,234.56` rather than `$1,234.56`.
* **So the nine movers DO change what an analyst sees**: the six RBC and three
  TD statements now render their amounts as `CA$…`/`$…` according to what the
  document prints. That is the correct rendering and the point of the card —
  a Canadian-dollar statement was being displayed with a bare `$` — but it is a
  visible change, not an inert one, and it is stated here rather than left for
  someone to discover in the UI.
* `benchmark/compare.py` is the only other reader; on-demand, gitignored.

The corpus gate and all three audit CSVs still never pinned the field, so a
pinned currency mover — had there been one — would have been a
**gate-invisible** change that nonetheless altered the analyst's screen. That
is the same blindness class batch 3 found for review<->validated movement, and
it is the strongest argument in this card for the gate item in §CUR6.

**Audit CSVs:** `currency` is **not** an audited column in any of the three
(`docs/adb-audit-results.csv`, `docs/balance-metrics-audit-results.csv`,
`docs/new-statement-audit-results.csv` — checked by header). It is not in
`tests/data/parser_expectations.json` either, and `corpus_gate.py` does not
mention it. So even a pinned currency mover would not have been a CSV change;
it would have been a gate-invisible one, which is worth recording.

## CUR6. Cards for Ocean and Gustavo

1. **RBC's 151 (decision, not a defect).** RBC prints `U.S. Funds` on its
   U.S.-dollar statements and prints nothing on the others. Whether *absence*
   of that line may be read as CAD is an inference from a negative about a
   layout convention, and it is outside the bar as written — so it was not
   taken. If Gustavo rules that a layout whose only denomination marker is
   `U.S. Funds` proves CAD by its absence, 151 documents move USD -> CAD
   **including all four pinned RBC statements**, and that ruling DOES need the
   formal ceremony. Evidence for the ruling is in §CUR1.1 and §CUR5.
2. **`scotiabank` multi-statement PDFs.** The `Currency:` label is per-account
   and this layout bundles accounts. Reading it correctly needs the
   account-block boundary the parser does not model today. Carded, not taken.
3. **`desjardins.account_name`** is still the hardcoded string
   `"USD Desjardins Corporate Build-Up Account"` while the product line it
   copies is now read for the currency. Deriving the name from the same match
   is a one-line change with a pinned-field consequence (`account` is an
   audited column in `balance-metrics-audit-results.csv`), so it is carded
   rather than taken inside a currency card.
4. **`shopify_balance`** prints `(USD)` column headers on 3 of 16. Adding the
   read changes nothing today and would gate the constant the way
   `wealthsimple` is gated. Small, safe, out of this card's scope.
5. **Class B is worth naming as a platform pattern.** Two registrations already
   discharge the invariant through a REQUIRED detection marker rather than a
   read. That is *better* than a read — it fails closed at dispatch instead of
   publishing a fallback — and it is invisible unless the comment says so. Any
   future currency constant should either be read or be gated, and should say
   which.
6. **THE RESIDUAL THIS CARD KNOWINGLY LEAVES (D-3): an inadmissible but REAL
   ISO code.** Every reader here validates against a closed, attested set —
   `{CAD, USD}` for Desjardins, two literal product spellings for RBC, the two
   suffixes for TD. That is what stops `PCA` and the OCR garble `KLR` from
   being published. It also means a **genuine** code the archive has not shown
   us — a EUR issue of the Desjardins product, say — falls into the same
   "prints nothing" branch as `PCA` and publishes the USD default **beside a
   page that says EUR**. That is precisely the "asserted by a schema default
   when the document proves otherwise" shape the invariant forbids, and it is
   left standing deliberately rather than closed by widening to all of ISO
   4217 on zero evidence.

   **The rule for closing it, which must not be got wrong: a newly attested
   code extends the closed SET. It never softens the fallback.** Publishing an
   unvalidated captured token is the `KLR` defect; publishing the default over
   a stated code is this one. The only safe third option, if this ever appears
   in a real document, is to refuse the currency field outright (leave it
   unset) rather than to guess — which needs a schema decision, so it is
   Gustavo's, not this card's. Recorded in the `_ADMISSIBLE_CURRENCIES`
   comment in `analysis/desjardins.py` so the next reader of that code finds
   it.

7. **The 13 archive documents with no OCR artifact** are outside every count in
   this card. They are the run of record's 13 deferred; they publish nothing,
   so they cannot carry a currency either way.

Method notes, for reproduction. Family populations come from LIVE detection
replay, never from a `rows.csv` `parser_id` column (the cache-hit hole, W3
#COUNTSP3). Document text comes from the OCR artifact store by DIRECT file path
(`webapp_data/artifacts/ocr/**/*.json`, keyed on `input_sha256`); the
`webapp_data` sqlite index was never opened. The archive and both caches were
read-only throughout, and no vendor call was made — **$0**. Of the 3,409
distinct archive shas, 3,396 have an OCR artifact with pages; the other 13 are
the run of record's deferred and are outside every count here.

**Artifact preference, and the ±1 it can cost.** The store holds up to three
OCR settings keys per document. This survey prefers the live key
(`1E6B5BE5…`, `force_ocr=False, allow_local_ocr=True, allow_visual_ocr=False`)
and falls back to an older one only where the live artifact is absent or has no
pages. Exercised: **3,351 of 3,396 documents were read at the live key, 45 from
a fallback** — including **4 of the 169 RBC documents and 1 of the 74 TD
native**. A fallback artifact is text a previous OCR version produced, so for
those documents this survey's census is a reading of slightly different bytes
than a cold production run would see, and any single one of them could land on
the other side of a count. Every number in this card is therefore exact for the
bytes measured and ±1-per-fallback against a fully cold rerun; the nine movers
themselves are not affected — all nine were read at the live key, and all nine
are confirmed independently by the differential AND by the per-family reader
confirmation.

## RS1. Card 1 — the seam

### RS1.1 What was actually there

Batch 4 wired `parse_native_woodforest` into all six copies by hand and pinned
them with an AST drift guard. Measured on the base tree, the six copies were
not merely equivalent — they were one computation written six times:

```
ocr/pipeline.py                 _native_statement  ['pdf_bytes', 'source_file']
adb_debug.py                    _native_statement  ['pdf_bytes', 'source_file']
adb_forensic_audit.py           native_statement   ['pdf_bytes', 'source_file']
balance_forensic_audit.py       native_document    ['pdf_bytes', 'source_file']
build_corpus_cache.py           native_document    ['pdf_bytes', 'source_file']
deterministic_coverage_audit.py native_statement   ['pdf_bytes', 'source_file']

distinct base ladder bodies (docstrings stripped): 1 over 6 modules
```

That measurement is load-bearing twice over. It says the batch-4 guard was
green for the right reason, and it says a byte-identity sweep through ONE of
the six entry points covers all six: they call the same seven module-level
functions from `ocr.native_text`, in the same order, with the same keyword.

### RS1.2 What it is now

`ocr/native_text.py::native_statement` holds the ordered ladder — the natural
home, because every copy already imported its rungs from there. The six
consumers **bind** it:

```python
from .native_text import native_statement as _native_statement      # ocr/pipeline.py
from ocr.native_text import native_statement as _native_statement   # adb_debug.py
from ocr.native_text import native_statement                        # adb_forensic_audit.py
from ocr.native_text import native_statement as native_document     # balance_forensic_audit.py
from ocr.native_text import native_statement as native_document     # build_corpus_cache.py
from ocr.native_text import native_statement                        # deterministic_coverage_audit.py
```

Binding rather than a delegating wrapper, deliberately. A wrapper is a body,
and a body can drift — someone adds a rung to one wrapper and the AST guard is
back. There is now no body to drift, and the six call sites keep the names they
already used, so nothing below the import changed: `parse_statement` still
calls `_native_statement`, `tests/test_pipeline.py` and five other test modules
still monkeypatch `ocr.pipeline._native_statement`, and
`tests/test_corpus_gate.py` still monkeypatches
`adb_forensic_audit.native_statement` / `balance_forensic_audit.native_document`.

### RS1.3 The drift guard, retired into a single-source assertion

`tests/test_native_rung_parity.py` no longer compares six extracted call lists.
It asserts the thing the comparison was approximating:

1. **identity** — every consumer's ladder name *is*
   `ocr.native_text.native_statement`, checked at runtime on the imported
   modules, not by AST similarity;
2. **the completeness scan, rekeyed** — no module outside `ocr/native_text.py`
   calls a rung at all, so a seventh copy cannot appear. The old scan keyed on
   the literal text `or parse_native_pdf_text(`, which a delegating consumer no
   longer contains; the new one keys on the rung names the ladder itself calls,
   read out of `native_statement`'s AST, so a new rung is covered automatically
   and `analysis/`'s unrelated `_parse_native_summary` family is not swept up;
3. **the other half of the GEOM-1 drift** — every `parse_native_*` the module
   defines is wired into the ladder (7 of 7), no rung is called twice, and the
   generic rung is still last. Batch 4's failure was a rung in one copy and not
   the others; with one copy that is impossible, and the remaining failure mode
   is a rung added to the module and never put in the ladder at all, which
   looks like working code and reads nothing.

## RS3. Card 2 — the crash class, and GEOM-1's attribution corrected

### RS3.1 The card's premise is measurably incomplete

The card says: *"`fitz.open` guarded; the `get_text('blocks')` loop is not.
Guard the loop."* Measured per rung on all four documents, at base:

```
navy_federal     -> RAISES FzErrorFormat: code=7: cycle in resources
td_canada        -> RAISES FzErrorFormat
wells_fargo      -> RAISES RuntimeError
woodforest       -> RAISES FzErrorFormat
desjardins       -> RAISES FzErrorFormat
first_citizens   -> RAISES FzErrorFormat
pdf_text         -> RAISES FzErrorFormat
```

**Every rung raises, and `_native_pages` is not the first one to.**
`parse_native_navy_federal` is rung 1 and extracts the whole document's text
itself, before `_native_pages` is ever called, so guarding only the
`get_text("blocks")` loop would have left the escape exactly where it was.
GEOM-1's attribution is not wrong, it is scoped to its own sweep harness, which
called `_native_pages` directly; through the ladder the exception comes out of
rung 1.

### RS3.2 The class cannot be caught by exception class

Same page, same defect, different extraction mode:

```
p1 get_text('text')   -> RuntimeError:   code=7: cycle in resources
p1 get_text('blocks') -> FzErrorFormat:  code=7: cycle in resources
p1 get_text('words')  -> FzErrorFormat:  code=7: cycle in resources
p1 get_text('dict')   -> RuntimeError:   code=7: cycle in resources
```

`FzErrorFormat` is also not reachable as an attribute of `fitz` or `pymupdf` in
this build (PyMuPDF 1.27.2.3), so it cannot be named in an `except` clause at
all. A guard written against the class named in the card would have missed the
two `text` call sites and been unwritable besides.

### RS3.3 The guard

One helper, `_page_text(page, *args, **kwargs)`, wraps every `page.get_text`
call in the module and converts whatever MuPDF raised into
`_UnreadableTextLayer`. Each rung catches that one class and returns None. Two
properties, both deliberate:

* **narrow.** A rung refuses only because the document's text layer is
  unreadable. A defect in a rung's own row logic still escapes, loudly — a bare
  `except Exception` around each rung would have turned a broken row reader
  into a silent fall-through to the generic rung, which is a bank-specific
  extractor quietly switching itself off, and is exactly the failure a coverage
  wave cannot see. `test_a_rung_defect_is_not_swallowed` pins it.
* **whole-document.** One unreadable page refuses the document. A partial read
  would hand a parser a statement with pages silently missing, and
  `parse_native_pdf_text`'s quorum gate (half the pages carry text) would
  accept it. `test_one_unreadable_page_refuses_the_whole_document` pins it.

Seven call sites routed: `_native_pages_cached` (`blocks`),
`_navy_transaction_rows` and `parse_native_navy_federal` (`text`+sort),
`parse_native_desjardins` (`text`+sort), `parse_native_wells_fargo`
(`text`, `blocks`), `_wells_rows` (`words`), `_fc_bands` (`dict`). The eighth
path, `parse_native_woodforest`, reaches MuPDF through
`ocr/column_grid.py::page_words`, which already swallows the failure — see
RS6.3.

All four are the same account, `Unidentified/c3f27791_3 BUSINESS CHECKING
X3774-*.PDF`. `fitz.open` succeeds and reports the page count; every page then
raises in every mode.

| content_sha256 | statement | pages | pages raising |
|---|---|---|---|
| `6f57be0899494df11bafb67741430a5a3537c623421d2a746232ea02b93af7bc` | 2026-01-31 | 4 | 4 |
| `64a4958471c2e1625b1918eadb97c4b491520bef5a560ab5e8ba94835a3c7645` | 2026-02-28 | 4 | 4 |
| `53906d0efdb5a5362d29af88a5d773882cbf19b40f7832ec43a6a2a9d3304035` | 2026-03-31 | 2 | 2 |
| `cdb8a6cc9f8efb5fac151979bfa9141697595f9b46a88a623a2db1d380df8629` | 2026-04-30 | 2 | 2 |

Outcomes, measured on both trees, identical for all four:

| Reader | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `parse_statement` (production, offline — what discovery calls) | `None` | `None` — **UNCHANGED** |
| `inspect_pdf` profile | `valid_pdf=True`, `classification=scanned`, `native_text_total_chars=0`, `malformed_pages=[all]` | identical |
| `deterministic_coverage_audit.audit_file` | `native_status=error`, `deterministic_status=error`, `error=FzErrorFormat: code=7: cycle in resources`, no quality/integrity fields | `native_status=no_native_text`, `deterministic_status=not_attempted`, `quality=needs_review`, `integrity_risk=review`, `integrity_flags=text_unavailable` |
| `build_corpus_cache.native_document` | raises — **aborts the whole cache build** | `None`, falls to local OCR |
| the native ladder itself | `FzErrorFormat` escapes | `None` |

**Production is unchanged, and not by luck.** `parse_statement`'s profile-driven
skip fires first: `native_text_total_chars == 0` on a valid PDF means no native
extractor can match, so the ladder is never called. `ocr/inspect.py::_page_texts`
has had the per-page guard all along, which is why the preflight can measure
zero characters on a document the ladder cannot survive. The crash class
therefore only ever bit the offline oracles, which call the ladder with no
profile gate — see RS6.2.

**Nothing became readable.** Every page raises in every mode, so the generic
rung cannot read what the crash previously killed; there is no coverage
movement to claim and none is claimed. The honest improvement is the oracle
rows above: an unhandled crash class became the module's own structured
`text_unavailable` refusal, and a cache build that aborted now completes.

  Unidentified/c3f27791_3 BUSINESS CHECKING X3774-2026-03-31.PDF   2/2 pages
  Unidentified/c3f27791_3 BUSINESS CHECKING X3774-2026-04-30.PDF   2/2 pages
exception classes observed             {FzErrorFormat, RuntimeError}
```

`text`+sort and `dict` were not probed archive-wide and the omission is
deliberate: every mode runs the same MuPDF structured-text extraction and
differs only in serialisation, they were confirmed to raise on all four known
documents, and they cost 10-16x the other three (measured on 250 documents:
`text`+sort 141.6 s and `dict` 201.6 s against `text` 11.8 s, `blocks` 12.5 s,
`words` 16.2 s). The 555-document ladder sweep in RS2 exercises `text`+sort and
`dict` for real on the families that use them and found no other mover.

Since the guard fires only where MuPDF raises, and MuPDF raises on exactly four
documents, the behaviour change is confined to those four by construction as
well as by measurement.

## RS6. Findings for Ocean

1. **The card's attribution needed correcting with measurement** (RS3.1).
   Guarding only `_native_pages`, as written, would have shipped a card that
   changed nothing: rung 1 raises first. Named here because the next reader of
   GEOM-1's note will otherwise inherit the same scoping.

2. **The oracles have no preflight and production does.** `parse_statement`
   routes on a `DocumentProfile`; `deterministic_coverage_audit`,
   `build_corpus_cache`, `adb_forensic_audit` and `balance_forensic_audit` call
   the ladder on raw bytes with no profile gate at all. That asymmetry is why a
   crash class could sit in the intake path for a whole wave while production
   never saw it — and it is a second-order oracle-fidelity gap of the same
   family as the one this card closed: the oracles do not run the routing
   production runs, only the rung production runs. Not fixed here (outside the
   named populations, and giving the oracles a profile skip would change what
   they measure). Worth a card.

3. **`ocr/column_grid.py::page_words` swallows the same failure into `[]`.** Its
   docstring says "Never raises", and an unreadable page therefore reads as a
   page with no words rather than as a refusal. It is unreachable for this class
   today (`parse_native_woodforest` gates on `_native_pages`, which now refuses
   first) and the module is not mine, so it is recorded rather than changed. It
   is the same hole one layer down.

4. **The finding was in the code before it was in a card.**
   `ocr/inspect.py::_page_texts` carries the comment "*duplicated by reference —
   that helper has no per-page error isolation*", naming `_native_pages` as the
   unguarded twin. The guard existed on one side of a deliberately duplicated
   pair for a full wave.

5. **No `OCR_STAGE_VERSION` bump is owed.** The rule in
   `webapp/artifact_cache.py` is "bump when the OCR ladder's output changes for
   unchanged settings". The ladder's output is byte-identical on 551 of 555
   sampled documents, and on the other four it produced nothing before (the
   call raised, so nothing was ever cached) and produces nothing now. No cached
   artifact can be stale. Stated explicitly because a v3 → v4 bump costs the
   whole archive a re-read.

6. **Possible merge point.** PREPARED-HANDOFF owns "the pipeline resolve-seam
   hunk"; if that is `ocr/pipeline.py` rather than `analysis/pipeline.py` it
   meets this branch's import-block rewrite at the top of the file. No other
   batch-5 handoff names any file this cell owns.

## RS9. Adversarial-review closures (Ocean, SHIP with four documentation-strength items)

All four are addressed in code rather than prose where code was possible; two
of them turned out to be real defects rather than wording, and one of the new
tests found a third. Byte-identity re-proven after the closures: the same 555
documents swept again, **0 records differ from the reviewed branch**, 0 escaped
exceptions, and the only difference from base is still the same 4 crash
documents.

### RS9.1 Clause 2 was overclaiming, and the binding list was unpinned

"A seventh copy cannot appear without failing here" was false. The scan matched
`ast.Name` calls only — the same blind spot as the batch-4 guard it replaced —
so an ALIASED import (`from ocr.native_text import parse_native_pdf_text as
generic`) or an ATTRIBUTE call (`native_text.parse_native_pdf_text(...)`) would
have walked straight past it.

Both holes are now closed rather than merely disclosed: the scan flags any
module outside the ladder home that *imports* a rung under any alias, and any
call by plain name **or** attribute. What remains open is dynamic access
(`getattr`, `importlib`), which no AST scan can see, and the module docstring
now says exactly that instead of claiming completeness. Clause 1 (object
identity) is named as the one that holds regardless, because it checks objects
rather than text.

`LADDER_BINDINGS` is no longer hand-maintained on trust. A new test derives the
consumer set FROM THE REPOSITORY — every module importing `native_statement`
from the ladder home, absolute or relative, plus the name each binds it under —
and asserts it equals the dict. A seventh consumer, or a renamed binding, now
fails there instead of silently sitting outside the identity check.

**A finding from writing the negative tests.** The three new scans are exercised
against synthetic sources that SHOULD trip them (plain call, aliased import,
attribute call) and sources that should not (`_parse_native_summary`, an
unrelated import). Doing that caught a bug in my own `_is_ladder_home`: a
relative `from .native_text import native_statement` in a module OUTSIDE the
`ocr` package was being credited to the ladder home, because the level check
fell through to the absolute-name branch. Fixed, and the case is pinned. A
guard whose failure path is never exercised is a guard nobody has tested.

### RS9.2 The diagnostic loss — restored, not carded

Correct and worth fixing: `_UnreadableTextLayer` carried MuPDF's message and
every rung dropped it, so the oracle traded `FzErrorFormat: cycle in resources`
for a generic `no_native_text` — archive-wide, a structurally corrupt PDF
became indistinguishable from an ordinary scan.

`_native_pages_cached` now returns `_PageRead(pages, refusal)` and the module
exposes `text_layer_refusal(pdf_bytes) -> str | None`. It is a reason channel,
not a second reader: the answer comes from the ladder's own memoised read, so a
caller that got `None` and wants to know why pays nothing and re-reads nothing.
Only the extraction sets a refusal — a PDF that fails to open, or a missing
PyMuPDF, answers `None` exactly as before.

Wired into the coverage oracle (in scope, and where the regression actually
showed). For the four documents:

```
error           native PDF text layer unreadable: page 1 FzErrorFormat: code=7: cycle in resources
integrity_notes native text unavailable and local OCR did not produce usable
                statement text; text layer unreadable: page 1 FzErrorFormat: ...
```

`native_status`, `deterministic_status`, `quality`, `integrity_risk` and
`integrity_flags` are **unchanged** — the reason is added, no classification
moves — and a document with a readable-but-empty text layer keeps its previous
row verbatim, which is pinned by a test.

Note for the record: production never lost this diagnostic. `inspect_pdf`
already records `malformed_pages` for these documents (all pages, on all four),
and production routes on that profile rather than on the ladder. The loss was
confined to the oracle row, and so is the repair.

### RS9.3 `_page_text`'s catch — narrowed, because the docstring's promise is
the valuable half

The reviewer's `srot=` demo was right: `except Exception` meant a mistake in how
a rung CALLS `get_text` became a silent whole-document refusal, contradicting
the docstring two lines above it. Measured, rather than reasoned about:

```
corrupt page:  get_text("text")   -> builtins.RuntimeError
               get_text("dict")   -> builtins.RuntimeError
               get_text("blocks") -> pymupdf.mupdf.FzErrorFormat
               get_text("words")  -> pymupdf.mupdf.FzErrorFormat
   FzErrorFormat mro: FzErrorFormat -> FzErrorBase -> Exception
   i.e. the two families are SIBLINGS; catching RuntimeError does not catch
   FzErrorFormat, which is why both have to be named

our own mistakes: get_text("text", srot=True) -> TypeError
                  get_text("nonsense-mode")   -> AssertionError
```

So the catch is now `(RuntimeError, FzErrorBase)`, resolved lazily via
`_mupdf_text_errors()` because this module imports PyMuPDF inside functions.
`TypeError`, `AssertionError` and anything else propagate — pinned by test.

The resolver has a failure mode of its own: if `FzErrorBase` ever moves it
would fall back to `RuntimeError` alone and the guard would silently re-open
for `blocks`/`words`. A test asserts the family IS resolved here rather than
letting that pass, and the test's own `FzErrorFormat` stand-in is derived from
the REAL `FzErrorBase` so it exercises that half of the tuple for real instead
of being caught as a RuntimeError subclass by accident.

Narrowing moves nothing: the archive census found no third exception class on
3,615 documents, and the 555-document sweep re-run after the change escapes
nothing and differs from the reviewed branch in 0 records.

### RS9.4 Prose

`ocr/pipeline.py` now reads "It is bound here under `_native_statement` — the
name `parse_statement` has always called and the suite monkeypatches —". The
`_UnreadableTextLayer` docstring's "every text extraction in this module" is
qualified to "every `page.get_text` call IN THIS MODULE", with
`ocr/column_grid.py::page_words` named inline as the path outside the guard
that answers `[]` rather than refusing, cross-referenced to RS6.3, and with the
note that it is unreachable for this class only because woodforest gates on
`_native_pages` first.

# §LCPERIOD — the recall card that turned out to be a third core processor

## L0. Summary

The card (W3 §SCANB S9.9) named 22 documents that print the second core
processor's period vocabulary in sentence case with long-form dates, and asked
for the period grammar to be widened so `core_processor_sectioned` could reach
them. **The characterization says they are not that template.** Twenty of the
22 are one platform whose only resemblance to the sectioned template is the
period SENTENCE; the other two are a third platform that merely prints the
same six words. So this cell registers the platform rather than widening a
grammar, and the issuer-specific reader that came first (`b1`) supersedes it —
§JHA-CELL's pattern, a third template over.

**20 documents print the template; 13 move `failed` to `validated`; nothing
moves down.**

| | before (base `b524f72`) | after |
|---|---|---|
| validated | 3 | **16** |
| failed | 17 | **4** |
| withheld | 0 | 0 |
| review | 0 | 0 |

All 13 are instrumented per document: both printed totals equal the published
totals, the summary's own identity closes, the printed day count equals the
span of the two printed dates, and the printed `DAILY BALANCES` grid agrees
with the walked ledger on every day in both directions — including its
pre-period cell, which is the platform's own second printing of the opening
balance. **822 transactions** published across the 13.

The 3 documents `b1` already reads are **3/3 byte-identical**, and so are all
39 documents of the §SCANB sectioned family: **0 of 42 rows differ** in the
full published payload.

## L1. The instrument

Every figure below comes from replaying the archive markdown through the real
pipeline (`analyze_markdown(parse_mode="deterministic")` +
`telemetry.record.classify_outcome`, the discovery runner's own call), with
the documents resolved from the D-3 OCR artifact store **by direct file path**
— the sqlite index was never opened, and the archive and the caches were never
written to.

Population re-derived from the artifact STORE, never from `rows.csv`: all
10,246 OCR artifacts were read, each payload envelope's own `input_sha256`
taken as the document identity, and the longest OFFLINE text kept (224
artifacts hold `document: null` — negative-cache entries — and are skipped).
**3,396 distinct documents have offline text**, which reproduces §SCANB S1's
figure exactly. Model census of the artifacts kept: `native-pdf-text` 8,769,
`native-pdf-text+wells` 672, `local-tesseract-ocr` 358, and four
layout-specialised native rungs; no hosted model, $0.

Base `b524f72` (v12, OCR v3, registry 71, suite 4,240). Branch base commit
`e935f98`, which differs from `b524f72` only in `docs/agent-handoffs/`.

## L2. The cohort, characterized before any code was written

### L2.1 The census reproduces, and then splits

the dated `mm/dd/yy THROUGH mm/dd/yy` form `core_processor_sectioned` requires
(the §SCANB cohort, reproduced exactly) and **22 without**. That is the card's
population, and it is not homogeneous:

| | documents |
|---|---|
| `Last statement: <Month D, YYYY>` + `This statement:` + `Total days in statement period: N` | **20** |
| `Total Days in Statement Period 31`, title case, no colon | 2 |

The 2 are `8ABEE7F32EC60078` and `F8E3E2E9F78F76E8`. They print

(31) $80,351.88`) — a different platform that shares six words and no
grammar. They are **out of this cell's population**, named here and carded at

### L2.2 The 20 share the period sentence and nothing else

Measured against the sectioned template, printing by printing:

| printing | `core_processor_sectioned` | this template |

| period | `TOTAL DAYS IN STATEMENT PERIOD 03/31/26 THROUGH 04/30/26: 30` | `Last statement: March 31, 2026` / `This statement: April 30, 2026` / `Total days in statement period: 30` |
| counts | `16 CREDITS <total>`, `M DEBITS <total>` | **none printed at all** |
| totals | inside the count rows | `Total additions` / `Total subtractions` |
| opening/closing | `LAST STATEMENT mm/dd/yy <fig>` / `THIS STATEMENT mm/dd/yy <fig>` | `Beginning balance $<fig>` / `Ending balance $<fig>` |
| statistics | `MINIMUM BALANCE`, `AVG AVAILABLE BALANCE`, `AVERAGE BALANCE` | `Low balance`, `Average balance`, `Avg collected balance`, `Interest paid year to date` |
| account | `<PRODUCT> ACCOUNT <number>` | `Account number <number> [Enclosures N]` |
| sections | `DEPOSITS` `OTHER CREDITS` `OTHER DEBITS` `CHECKS` | `DEBITS` `CREDITS` `CHECKS` |
| grid | `DAILY BALANCE`, in-period days only | `DAILY BALANCES`, opening on the day BEFORE the period |

Not one grammar is shared. Structural probes over the 20 confirm it as a

### L2.3 What widening the period grammar would have done

`core_processor_sectioned`'s two required markers are its period line and the
substring pair `LAST STATEMENT` / `THIS STATEMENT`, tested against
upper-cased text. **`Last statement:` upper-cases to a string containing
`LAST STATEMENT`**, so the second marker already fires on all 20. Widening the
first would have made that module claim all 20 and then decline all 20 at
`parse` — its summary strip, its account heading and its section names are all
absent — which is a detector that lies, and 20 documents added to the
`attempted` population of a reader that cannot read them.

And three of the 20 are `b1`'s, already `validated`. A second claim on them
resolves `ambiguous`, which routes them to review: **the recall card would
have regressed three documents.** That is the measurement that decided the
shape of this cell.

## L3. What a document has to prove

This platform prints **no transaction count**, so §SCANB's first gate does not
exist here. What it prints instead is a grid that OPENS on the opening
balance, and that is the stronger evidence: a dropped row moves its direction's
total AND every grid day after it, where a count check sees only the count.

Five printings, all of them, exactly:

1. the row total in each direction equals the printed total;
2. `beginning + additions - subtractions == ending`, the summary's own
   identity, checked against the printed closing balance;
3. the grid's PRE-PERIOD cell equals the printed beginning balance;
4. every in-period day of the grid equals the walked end-of-day balance, **and**
   every day the ledger posts on appears in the grid;
5. the printed day count equals the span the two printed statement dates
   describe — the period opens the day AFTER the last statement closed, which
   the grid's first cell independently confirms on every document.

Of the five, (1), (3), (4) and (5) are independent printings; (2) is a
function of figures (1) already checked. The grid is **REQUIRED**, unlike on
the sectioned template where it sits on top of two printed counts.

**Free evidence, deliberately not gated.** The bank prints `Average balance`
on 5 of the 13 publishers, and the platform's computed ADB agrees with it to
within a rounding convention every time:

```
computed ADB vs printed Average balance, the 5 that print one
  5DADFE8416F942AD     442.54  vs      442.86   (-0.32)
  7370DF5A42DF71E6  12,992.26  vs   12,992.17   (+0.09)
  79ACCAA2AD709795     491.82  vs      492.11   (-0.29)
  C505452E7046B8E0     539.58  vs      539.87   (-0.29)
  F5ED552BE8CF348F     997.44  vs      997.73   (-0.29)
```

**`Low balance` is NOT the grid's minimum, and is therefore not usable as a
sixth gate.** It agrees exactly on 3 of the 5 (`-387.40`, `19.53`,
`-1,096.74`) and disagrees on the other two — `79ACCAA2AD709795` prints
`-201.46` where the grid's lowest day is `-210.46`, and `7370DF5A42DF71E6`
prints `837.29` where the grid's lowest is `840.07`. It is an
available/collected-balance statistic, not a ledger one. Measured rather than
assumed, and left alone.

**The gate set's blind spot, named rather than left to be found.** Move value
between two rows that share a date AND a direction and all five printings
still hold. So does splitting one row into two on the same day and direction —
which a printed count WOULD catch, and this platform prints none. Both are
FORGERY signatures rather than OCR ones: a scan drops a row or mangles a
digit, which moves a total and every grid day after it, and does exactly that
on all four of the archive's refusing scans. Pinned as
`test_the_gates_are_blind_to_a_same_day_same_direction_redistribution`.

## L4. The issuer: this template does not print one

**`Statement.bank` is None on every document this reader publishes**, and that
is the SCAN-B hardening applied rather than a shortcut. The hardening is that
an issuer is published only from an arrangement in which the TEMPLATE bounds
the name on both sides, attested and fixtured. This template offers two
candidate fields and neither is one.

**The masthead line** prints the institution and then its address, with
nothing between them:

```
Direct inquiries to: 833-896-2850
Enterprise Bank & Trust PO Box 66940 St Louis MO 63166
```

Left edge only — §SCANB S3's refused arrangement exactly. A digit rule ends
`El Dorado Savings Bank 4040 El Dorado Road` in the right place and
`Enterprise Bank & Trust PO Box 66940` in the wrong one, and which it is
depends on which word of the address happens to carry the first digit. Worse
here than there: Lake City Bank prints the HOLDER's address block between the
contact field and its own, so the line is not even positionally stable.

**The closing courtesy sentence** is genuinely bounded on both sides — by the
template's own phrase on the left and the end of the line on the right — and
on the 17 sectioned documents it yields a clean name every time (Enterprise
Bank & Trust 8, Lake City Bank 5, El Dorado Savings Bank 4; the 3 B1Bank
documents yield the four-fold repeat the text layer prints). It was still
rejected, because a bound is not a role. Measured over the store, the same
full-line sentence yields:

```
   31  'us.'
    8  'Orange CO Airport Office'   <- a BRANCH, on this platform's own sibling arrangement
    4  'Simmons Bank. Thank you for banking with Simmons Bank. ...'
    2  'Wells Fargo.'
    2  'Farmers & Merchants Bank.'
    1  'United!'
```

A slot that names a branch office on a sibling layout is prose the issuer
chose, not a field the template reserves. Reading it would publish a wrong
name for a real bank, and a wrong name is worse than no name.

So `bank=None`, under the honest-unknown-issuer ruling of 2026-08-14. It costs
17 documents a label and no document its figures. Pinned as
`test_the_issuer_is_never_published_even_when_the_document_names_one`, and by
a mutant that reads the courtesy line and is killed.

**`account_name` is published only where the printing is unambiguous.** The
product name sits on its own line above the account field. On some documents
this text layer emits that line FOUR times over — fill, stroke and two shadows
of one printed string, which is also why the holder block above it reads
`RABBIT TWISTER HOLDINGS, LLC` four times. Publishing `Checking For Small
Business Checking For Small Business Checking For Small Business Checking For
Small Business` publishes a name no statement carries; collapsing it is a
REPAIR. So a line that is one token sequence repeated is declined and a line
printed once is published as printed: 8 of the 13 publishers name their
product (`Optima Business`, `Bb Enhanced Checking`), 5 publish None. A
whole-line rule, not a repeated-word one — `Business Business Checking` would
publish.

## L5. Four findings before merge, and what was done about each

### L5.1 The calendar-literal guard reads docstrings

`test_no_literal_calendar_fields_in_patterns` scans every string literal
containing an escaped `d` or `s`, and the module docstring quoted the escape
sequence while ALSO quoting real printed rows (`04-02`, `04-01-26`) as
evidence. The docstring now names the class in prose instead. The examples
stay: they are the evidence for the boundary rule, and the guard's own
docstring says it finds pinned calendar fields inside PATTERNS.

### L5.2 The clone guard was right, and the fix is a shared helper

`test_no_two_functions_in_analysis_share_a_body` found two functions
byte-identical between this module and `core_processor_sectioned`: `_once`
(read a summary row exactly once, decline a contradicted one) and `_sections`
(split a document into the runs of its own headings). Both are text-shape
utilities with the patterns supplied by the caller, so they were lifted to
`analysis/tables.py` as `unique_match` and `section_runs`, beside
`unique_line` (the same discipline over LINES) and `section_between`.

**Proven pure**, in its own commit `31cfda3` before the registration landed:
the 42-document family that reads through them — the 39 sectioned-template
documents plus `b1`'s 3 — is byte-identical in its full published payload,
**0 of 42 rows differing**, and the store-wide dispatch sweep is unchanged.
Six new unit tests, and two mutants aimed at the lifted bodies, both killed.

### L5.3 Two latent defects in the cheque-serial read

**The first, found by reviewing my own code.** The serial is read from the
text before the row, and that text started at the previous row's DATE, so it
still held the previous row's amount. A cheque the bank printed no serial for
would have published `Check 00` — a number the statement does not carry,
invented out of another row's money. The gap now starts at the previous row's
AMOUNT.

**The second, found by Ocean's review, and the same class one level up.** That
fix left the read END-ANCHORED over the whole gap, so ANY trailing digits
still fabricate a serial. Three constructions, all now fixtured:

| the gap carries | the old read publishes |
|---|---|
| `Continued on page 27` | `Check 27` |
| masked account furniture `XXXXXXXXXXXX0000` | `Check 0000` |
| furniture longer than the 200-char description truncation, ending `7654321` | `Check 765432` — a WRONG serial, not a missing one |

The third is the worst of the three and the one an end-anchored read makes
inevitable: truncation splits a token and the remainder is still digits.

The fix is structural rather than another anchor. The cheque section prints a
three-column grid — `Number Date Amount` — so the serial is the row's LEADING
CELL, read as the WHOLE of what the bank printed to the left of the date **on
that row's own line** (`_row_lead` + `fullmatch`). Furniture printed above the
row is a different line and cannot reach it however it ends; furniture a
flattened layer put ON the row's line is not a bare digit run and fails the
fullmatch. The gap's start stays load-bearing even so, because this platform
prints two rows on one line — pinned by
`test_two_cheque_rows_on_one_line_each_keep_their_own_serial`, which the
old date-anchored gap fails.

Neither defect is reachable on today's archive — the family prints ONE cheque
row and it is serialled — and all 13 published payloads are byte-identical
across both fixes. Four mutants, four killed.

### L5.4 The surviving mutants, measured rather than accepted

The review named three mutants its harness could not kill. Re-measured on this
tree, one of them IS killed and two survive, and reporting the count I was
given rather than the count I measured would have been the same substitution
this cell already had to correct once:

* **the ASCII right boundary — KILLED.** `_FIGURE_END` narrowed to `[0-9.,]`
  fails `test_an_amount_run_onto_a_word_is_refused`, which is one of this
  round's additions. The review saw it survive because it ran before that pin
  existed. Recorded as closed, not as inert.
* **the equivalent-mutant sign — survives, and cannot not.** Admitting a sign
  into `_FIGURE_TOKEN` changes nothing while `_magnitude` is `STRICT_UNSIGNED`;
  widening `_magnitude` to a signed format changes nothing while the regex
  stays unsigned. The two guards are redundant BY DESIGN, so no single-point
  mutant can be killed and a test that killed one would be pinning the other.
  A signed section figure refuses under every combination tried.
* **the unbounded summary strip — survives, and is belt rather than braces
  here.** Letting `_summary_region` run to the end of the document changes no
  outcome on any document measured, because this template does not reprint its
  summary labels in its disclosures the way the second core processor's does —
  which is exactly why §SCANB needs that boundary and this module's is
  precautionary. Kept, because the next issuer to print a disclosure block is
  not obliged to be as tidy, and named so nobody mistakes it for a proven
  guard.

## L6. Two corrections to §SCANB's glyph rationale

### L6.1 The ASCII digit class is a conservatism, not the guard S5 credits

§SCANB S5 says a Unicode-aware digit class "publishes a figure the bank never
printed" because it admits digits from other scripts. Measured: it does admit
them, and Python's `int()` and `float()` then map every one of them to its own
numeric value — `float` of the Arabic-Indic spelling of `250.00` is `250.0`,
`int` of the Arabic-Indic `24` is `24`. So a Unicode-class grammar reads the
look-alike as the figure the bank printed and publishes exactly what the ASCII
grammar publishes. **No outcome test can separate the two classes**, and the
mutation harness confirms it: swapping `[0-9]` for the Unicode class in this
module's row date is the one mutant the cell's tests could not kill by
outcome.

The class is kept — refusing an unexpected glyph is the right default for a
reader whose job is to publish only what it can read — and it is now described
accurately rather than credited with work it does not do. What the archive's
scans really substitute is LETTERS (`o` for a leading zero, a Cyrillic `Е`
inside `DATE`), and both classes refuse those.

### L6.2 The figure the bank never printed comes from the BOUNDARY

Chasing L6.1 found the real hole. With §SCANB's boundary class
`(?<![0-9A-Za-z.,/])`, an amount whose integer part a scan rendered in another
script matches the BARE sub-dollar alternative `.00`, because the character
before the dot is not in the class. The reader publishes **0.00 where the bank
printed 250.00**: precisely the failure the digit class is supposed to
prevent, arriving through the boundary instead.

This module's boundary classes are word-character classes for that reason.
Over the store both forms publish the identical 13 documents, so the stronger
one costs nothing. Pinned as
`test_an_amount_whose_integer_part_is_not_ascii_is_invisible_not_zero`, which
asserts the ASCII form's hole directly so the test cannot rot into a
tautology, and by two mutants that narrow the boundaries back to ASCII.

**`core_processor_sectioned` carries the same exposure.** It is gated rather
than open — such a figure breaks a printed total and the document refuses —
and it belongs to a shipped module this cell has no mandate to re-prove, so it
is carded at L7 rather than changed here.

alone and then declined all three at parse.

**L7.4 — the grid is required, and that is a deliberate strictness.** Three of
the four refusing scans print `DALY BALANCES` where the template prints
`DAILY BALANCES`. With the grid optional they would still refuse — their
ledgers are corrupted too — so the requirement costs nothing measurable today.
It is named because on a platform with no printed count, two gates is not
enough to publish on.

**L7.5 — a negative sub-dollar balance is unreadable.** `_balance` pads the
leading decimal before the sign is read, so a printed `$-.55` pads to nothing
and is refused. No document in the store prints one (measured), and the
refusal is fail-closed. The clean fix is a `LEADING_MINUS` variant that pads
AFTER the sign, which belongs to `analysis/money.py` and therefore to MG-D's
cell.

**L7.6 — a trailing-minus section figure would be read as a positive
magnitude.** The figure boundary excludes what may CONTINUE a number, not a
trailing sign, so `250.00-` in the CREDITS column is captured as `250.00` and
published as a credit. This template prints no trailing minus and no archive
document carries one; if one appeared the totals gate would catch it, because
a sign-flipped row misses its direction's total by twice its value. §SCANB
carries the identical exposure. Named rather than closed, because closing it
means diverging from the established form of the rule on a printing nobody has
made.

**L7.7 — `count_semantics` is deliberately not extended.** This registration
publishes no `stated_credit_count` or `stated_debit_count` at all — the
platform prints none — so the stated-count check has nothing to compare and
the table's UNSURVEYED default is silent, which is correct. Recorded so the
absence is a decision, as §SCANB S9.4 did for a different reason.

**L7.8 — `stated_daily_balances` excludes the grid's pre-period cell.** It is
a real printing and it IS used as a gate, but the field's contract is
in-period snapshots and `analysis/adb.py` treats an out-of-period one as a
defect of the statement (`bank_daily_balance_dates_valid`). Publishing it
would have withheld all 13. Named because it is a silent-looking choice with a
loud consequence.

**L7.9 — for PIPELINE-5's composition.** The 13 documents this cell publishes
all carry `bank=None`, so they join PIPELINE-5's `model_used` population and
the composed train's mover count grows accordingly. Named here because the two
cells cannot see each other; the arithmetic is Ocean's to verify at merge.

**L7.10 — the detect budget.** This registration adds two cheap required
markers and one substring, with NO normalization (case is load-bearing), which
is the cheapest shape a registration can have. Registry 71 to 72; the
affordability test projects to `PLANNED_REGISTRATIONS=80` and is green on this
tree.

**The card:** apply the approved honest-unknown-issuer policy (`bank=None`;
never infer the issuer from a filename, folder, template or branding) to
`fiserv_premier`'s four issuer-less refusals, carded at roughly +4 by §U7.3,
with the standing instruction to characterize the refusals before assuming any
of them publishes.

## FI0. Summary — an honest +0, and two corrections to the record

**Nothing moves. Nothing should.** The four documents are refused for two real,
measured reasons, and the missing issuer is not one of them.

| | claimed | published | refused |
|---|---|---|---|
| `fiserv_premier`, whole archive | 14 | 10 | **4** |

1. **The honest-unknown-issuer policy is already live in this module and is
   already correct.** `545166b` (batch 3, §UNID-B RC-D1) replaced the issuer
   refusal with `bank=None` in the same commit that made `_issuer` require the
   document's own web address to spell the name.
   `parse_fiserv_premier_statement` has had no issuer refusal since. The card's
   premise — "claimed and then declined for want of a printed issuer" (§UB7,
   restated at §U7.3) — describes the module as it stood *before* that commit.
   **Zero lines of policy to apply; +0 on that axis, structurally.**
2. **The period line is not absent.** The handoff, and `545166b`'s own D3, both
   record the refusal as over-determined because there is "no period line on
   any of the 4". All four print their period, twice: `Statement of Account
   <Month DD, YYYY> thru <Month DD, YYYY>` in the masthead, and the length
   separately as `Activity Summary Days in the Statement Period:  N`. What is
   absent is the *wording* `_PERIOD_RE` reads (`Statement Dates 4/01/26 to
   4/30/26 (30 days)`). That is a gap in this module, not a silence in the
   document, and the distinction decides the card: "the bank did not print it"
   closes it, "we do not read what the bank printed" keeps it open at a known
   price.

The real blocker is larger than either: these four print a **third issue** of
the template, whose ledger vocabulary this module does not read at all.

## FI1. The instrument

Every figure below is a live replay. The four documents' markdown was resolved
from the D-3 OCR artifact store **by direct file path** — the `webapp_data`
sqlite index was never opened — by recomposing the run's own cache key
(`cache_key(STAGE_OCR, content_sha256, ocr_settings_key(...))`), reading
`artifacts/ocr/<2>/<key>.json`, and rebuilding
`StatementMarkdown.to_markdown()` from the stored pages. All four are
`native-pdf-text`, 8 pages, `truncated_page_count: 0`, and both caches MISS in
the run of record — so the artifact is the run's own text, generated cold at
OCR v3.

The family sweep replays `fiserv_premier.detect` and
`parse_fiserv_premier_statement` over every artifact of the run's 3,380
distinct shas (16 have no offline artifact on disk), never over `rows.csv`
`parser_id` (the cache-hit hole, §COUNTSP3).

**The four chain across periods**: each closing balance is the next document's

### FI2.1 Cause 1 — the period, printed in two places instead of one clause

The two read issues print `Statement Dates 4/01/26 to 4/30/26 (30 days)`: the
dates and the length in one clause, which is what `_PERIOD_RE` matches. The
third prints the dates in the masthead heading and the length in the activity
strip, in long-form month names:

```
Statement of Account April 01, 2026 thru April 30, 2026
...
Activity Summary Days in the Statement Period:  30
```

Both facts are on the page. Neither is read. A parser with no period basis
cannot publish `period_start` / `period_end`, and every dated row it would
publish is bounded by `iso_within_period` against exactly that basis — so this
alone refuses the document, correctly and fail-closed.

### FI2.2 Cause 2 — a third ledger issue, in another registration's vocabulary

The module reads two ledger shapes: the `Transaction Activity` running grid and
the `Credit Transactions` / `Debit Transactions` split. These four print
neither. They print:

```
Deposits Date Description Amount
Other Credits Date Description Amount $
Debits Date Description Amount $
Checks Cleared            -> Date Check No Amount $
Daily Balance Information
Overdraft and Returned Item Fees
```

`_sections` matches none of those heads, all three buckets come back empty, and
the parser refuses at the final `else`. That is the correct outcome: an unread
ledger must never be published behind a summary that happens to close.

**That vocabulary is not new to the platform — it is `community_section`'s.**
Census over the run's artifacts, of documents printing `Deposits Date
Description Amount`:

```
documents printing the head                                          62
  claimed by community_section  (26 validated, 4 withheld, 2 review)  32
  claimed by mission_valley     (19 validated)                        19
  unclaimed / failed (Rogue Credit Union and siblings)                 7
  claimed by fiserv_premier and refused   -> THESE FOUR                4
```

The four are the only ones of the 62 that also print `Previous Balance`, the
parenthesised counts and `Statement of Account` — which is exactly the
conjunction `fiserv_premier` registers. It claims them at 0.5 and then declines,
and no other registration is offered them. `community_section`'s platform
registration legitimately does not claim them: it requires its own `Account
Summary Date Description Amount` grid and an `N Credit(s) This Period` row, and
these print the parenthesised strip instead.

So the fourth population is a genuine **hybrid**: one registration's summary
furniture over another registration's ledger furniture. It is not a defect in
either detector, and it is not fixable by widening one of them without
measurement.

### FI2.3 Is the ledger reachable? Yes, and the residual is one grammar rule

Measured, segmenting on the issue's own heads and carrying the section identity
across page breaks — the continuation header prints `Date Description Amount $`
with no section name, so a reader that resets at `--- Page` cannot tell a credit
continuation from a debit one. That carry is load-bearing, not cosmetic: mis-
carrying it files a credit as a debit.

```
             printed credits          read           printed debits           read
April        36 / 278,658.85    36 / 278,658.85     131 / 285,723.80    97 / 284,669.80
May          18 / 296,791.12    18 / 296,791.12     107 / 276,559.94    97 / 276,249.94
Jun 30       40 / 219,048.53    40 / 219,048.53     157 / 230,817.90   120 / 229,670.90
Jul 31       36 / 243,368.25    36 / 243,368.25     174 / 234,885.81   146 / 234,017.81
```

**Credits reconcile exactly — count and total — on all four.** The debit
residual is one row shape, and it is fully explained:

```
05/01 CHK# 00 AMT $579.45, NSF PAID ITEM FEE $31.00
```

The row's own amount is the LAST figure; the first is a REFERENCE to the item
that caused the fee. `_PLAIN_ROW_RE`'s description class is `[^$]`, so it cannot
span the reference, and its `(?=\s|$)` lookahead rejects `$579.45` because a
comma follows — so the row matches nothing and is dropped whole. Count of that
row per document: **34 / 10 / 37 / 28**, every one of them `$31.00`, and
34×31 = 1,054.00, 10×31 = 310.00, 37×31 = 1,147.00, 28×31 = 868.00 — exactly the
four residuals above, to the cent. The comma is doing accidental good work: it
makes the row fail rather than publish `$579.45` as a fee.

That is the whole of what stands between these four and a published ledger — a
rule for "the row's amount is its last money token, and an embedded `AMT $x,` is
a reference". It is a real money-grammar decision with a real hazard (a greedy
last-token rule tried here merged rows at section ends and lost 1–3 per
document), and it belongs to a scoped cell, not to this one.

## FI5. Carried findings for Ocean

1. **The card should be re-priced, not closed.** It is still worth +4, but it is
   a LEDGER card, not an issuer card: a third printed issue (§FI2.2) plus a
   second period wording (§FI2.1) plus one money-grammar rule for the embedded
   `AMT $x,` reference (§FI2.3). The issuer half is already shipped and is not
   what refuses anything. Suggested name: FISERV-ISSUE3.
2. **The right home for it is a question, not a given.** The ledger vocabulary
   belongs to `community_section` / `mission_valley`, which read it for 51
   documents today. A third `_sections` shape inside `fiserv_premier` duplicates
   a grammar that already exists twice over; lifting the section reader to a
   shared helper is the §SCANB/§JHA-CELL pattern and is the cheaper end state,
   but it touches two registrations and is therefore a ruling.
3. **The record carried two stale facts into this batch** (§FI0.1, §FI0.2), and
   both came from a differential written before a fix landed in the same wave.
   The generalisable lesson: a refusal cause recorded from `dispatch_outcome`
   is only true at the commit that produced it, and §UB7's `parser_declined`
   line survived four commits past the change that made it false.
4. **`_PLAIN_ROW_RE`'s `(?=\s|$)` lookahead is a guard nothing would notice
   being deleted — until now.** It is what makes a comma-terminated amount fail
   rather than publish. Measured over the ledger sections of all 10 published
   documents (62,431 characters of section text): **0 comma-terminated money
   tokens**. So on today's published population the lookahead is inert, and
   §FI2.3's 109 dropped fee rows across the four refused documents are the first
   measured evidence of what it buys. If FISERV-ISSUE3 is taken up, that
   lookahead is the thing its money-grammar rule must not simply relax.

# §MONEYPRIV — the raising family stops quoting the document

Batch 6, card 1. Base main `eef77c6` (branch point `8570bce`, the batch-6
handoffs), branch `wave6-moneypriv`, worktree `.claude/worktrees/mt6-moneypriv`.
Run of record `2026-08-16T000943.012887-0000-2e3ea385`. Owned files:
`analysis/money.py`, `tests/test_money_refusals_are_private.py`, this log.

**The card (W3 §MGD10 finding 6, MGD-C1):** the money-grammar raising family
carries the printed token in `ValueError(value)`, and `webapp/worker.py`
publishes `str(exc)` as the job error, so statement content can cross into the
durable store. Batch 4 closed this law for `read_money` (§MG-C2 D1: a refusal
never quotes the cell); the same module still quoted it one layer down, and
§MGD *widened* the exposure — before `wave5-mgd`,
`parse_signed_decimal("—$500.00")` returned a number; after it, that call
raises, so a dormant boundary defect acquired a live caller.

## MP0. Summary

**Eleven raise sites in one module, all of which put the printed cell in the
message; all eleven now name a reason instead. Zero archive movement, by
construction and by measurement.**

The card named five functions and five `raise ValueError(value)` statements.
The module actually held **eleven** leaking sites, because a refusal in this
family has two shapes and only one of them is written as a `raise`:

| shape | sites | what the user would have seen |
|---|---|---|
| explicit `raise ValueError(value)` | 7 | the cell, alone, as the whole message |
| the conversion's own error, escaping as the documented refusal | 4 | `could not convert string to float: '<the cell>'` |

The four inherited ones are the more dangerous half and the harder half to
see: `parse_grouped_float`, `parse_trailing_minus_dropped` and
`parse_french_amount` document "raises ValueError when the token is not a
number" and then let `float`'s own ValueError be that raise, so the leak is in
the standard library rather than in this file. `Decimal` is the quiet
counterpart — `InvalidOperation` says only `ConversionSyntax` — which is
exactly why `parse_decimal` and `parse_decimal_mixed_separator` had to write
their leak out by hand and the float three did not. The fourth is
`parse_digit_scrubbed`, which is not a member of the raising family at all
(§MP3).
